**San Diego City and County Continuum of Care (CA-601, Regional Task Force on Homelessness) and HHAP, County of San Diego share**
- Agency: Regional Task Force on Homelessness (RTFH, CoC lead and HMIS lead); County of San Diego HHSA, HCDS Office of Homeless Solutions (County HHAP administrative entity); City of San Diego (large city allocation)
- Type: grant
- Typical award: HHAP Round 6 (FY 2026-27 through 2028-29): County $12.1 million (accepted December 9, 2025), RTFH CoC $12.9 million, City of San Diego $25.8 million, from a joint regional application filed August 29, 2025. County HHAP rounds 1 to 6 total about $64 million ($9.99M, $4.57M, $12.79M, $10.5M, $14.1M, $12.1M); the region received $220.6 million in rounds 1 to 5 plus $46.2 million of Encampment Resolution Funds. County HHAP pays for Housing Our Youth, the Local Rental Subsidy Program ($6.6 million in Round 5), shallow rent subsidies, housing stability case management and harm reduction contracts, not capital. 2025 point-in-time count: 9,905 people, 5,714 unsheltered.
- AMI requirement: People experiencing or at risk of homelessness; HHAP-6 requires a regionally coordinated action plan, 10% youth set-aside, and allows Category 1 permanent housing uses including housing development and capital funding, rental assistance and operating support.
- Cycle: annual NOFA (next: RTFH's 2026 HHAP application period is open (see rtfhsd.org Grants and Contracts) alongside the FY 2026 HUD CoC NOFO; the County's HHAP-6 is already programmed to existing contracts. HHAP Round 7 depends on the state budget.)
- Layering notes: County HHAP is operating money, not a capital source, and the County's BHSA plan says it will spend all of it on existing youth, regional housing assistance and local rental subsidy programs as ARPA expires. A PSH developer should look to RTFH for CoC PSH or Rapid Rehousing operating funds and to the City of San Diego's much larger HHAP allocation for capital or operating subsidies inside the city (Pass 3). Coordinated Entry through RTFH is the referral source required by HCDS for homeless units in County-funded projects, and RTFH's CES is the official front door for BHSA housing interventions tied to homelessness.
- Source: https://sdcounty.legistar.com/LegislationDetail.aspx?ID=8186&GUID=BA2487AB-80B3-4A8B-88EB-EF4A4D6D05FC&Options=&Search=&FullText=1
- Confidence: verified (researched 2026-11-06)

**Tax-exempt multifamily bonds: County TEFRA approvals for CMFA, CSCDA and other JPA issuances (County not an issuer)**
- Agency: County of San Diego Board of Supervisors (TEFRA host approval through the Finance and General Government Group, Debt Advisory Committee concurrence); issuers California Municipal Finance Authority, California Statewide Communities Development Authority, California Public Finance Authority, California Enterprise Development Authority
- Type: bond
- Typical award: Project-sized conduit issuances approved as consent items roughly monthly. 2026 approvals include CMFA bonds for 2581 Commercial Street Apartments (70 units, up to $13 million, March 24 and August 18, 2026), four CMFA issuances on March 24, 2026 (up to $20M, $13M, $40M and $72M), Island Family Housing (CSCDA, August 18, 2026), Fallbrook Trails, Promenade and Seaward Affordable Apartments (CMFA, September 2026), Vista Lane Family Apartments reissuance (165 units, up to $55 million, December 9, 2025) and Fallbrook Senior Apartments (up to $26 million, November 4, 2025). The County collects about $991 per approval to recover staff costs and takes on no debt.
- AMI requirement: Federal bond and 4% LIHTC rules: at least 20% of units at 50% AMI or 40% at 60% AMI (or income averaging), 55-year CDLAC regulatory agreement.
- Cycle: rolling (next: Request the County TEFRA approval through the issuer (CMFA or CSCDA handle the notice and hearing); allow six to eight weeks before the CDLAC application deadline. Approvals appear on regular Board agendas; the Board also reapproves when terms change (reissuance on conversion to permanent, address corrections).)
- Layering notes: Neither the County nor the Housing Authority of the County of San Diego issues multifamily bonds; CMFA is the usual issuer, with County Board approval for projects in the unincorporated area and, in practice, for several City of San Diego addresses as well. Inside the City of San Diego the Housing Authority of the City of San Diego (through SDHC) is an active issuer and will be covered in Pass 3. Bonds alone do not trigger state prevailing wage, but County IHTF, HOME or PLHA in the same deal does. Pair the TEFRA timeline with the HCDS NOFA award (March 2027) and the 2027 second CDLAC/TCAC round that the NOFA rewards.
- Source: https://sdcounty.legistar.com/LegislationDetail.aspx?ID=8683&GUID=197FFBBE-5A88-4EB6-A06C-A6255DD07117&Options=&Search=&FullText=1

**Welfare Exemption (property tax), San Diego County Assessor**
- Agency: San Diego County Assessor/Recorder/County Clerk, Jordan Z. Marks; Institutional Exemptions unit, 1600 Pacific Highway, Suite 103, San Diego, CA 92101; (619) 531-5772; with the State Board of Equalization (Organizational Clearance Certificate)
- Type: tax abatement
- Typical award: Exemption of property taxes on units restricted to lower income households under Revenue and Taxation Code 214(g): full exemption for qualifying units in LIHTC or publicly financed projects and partial exemption for the qualifying share in mixed projects. In San Diego County the 1% base rate plus voter-approved debt applies to the exempt value, typically worth 1.1% to 1.25% of assessed value a year.
- AMI requirement: Nonprofit owner or limited partnership with a nonprofit managing general partner holding a BOE Organizational Clearance Certificate; recorded regulatory agreement (tax credits, bonds, HOME, PLHA, IHTF or County regulatory agreement) restricting rents to lower income households; BOE-267-L2 tenant data for projects without government financing or tax credits.
- Cycle: annual NOFA (next: Annual filing due February 15 each year (the Assessor's current instruction sheet, revised December 2025, states February 15, 2026); first-year claims on BOE-267 with BOE-267-L, L1, L2 and L-A supplements as applicable; late filings through December 31 receive a partial exemption.)
- Layering notes: Standard underwriting item for every LIHTC or County-financed deal in the region. The County's 55-year regulatory agreement and the inclusionary affordable housing agreements qualify as recorded restrictions. File the Organizational Clearance Certificate copy with the first claim and use the San Diego forms posted at sdarcc.gov. Mixed-income inclusionary projects owned by for-profits do not qualify and should instead seek a restricted assessed value under Revenue and Taxation Code 402.1.
- Source: https://www.sdarcc.gov/content/dam/arcc/assessor/forms/property-tax-exemption-and-exclusion-forms/267WELFIRST.pdf
- Confidence: verified (researched 2026-11-06)


### San Joaquin County

**Affordable Housing Density Bonus, Development Title Chapter 9-401 (unincorporated county)**
- Agency: San Joaquin County Community Development Department
- Type: density bonus
- Typical award: State-law density bonus codified in Chapter 9-401 (2026-10 code edition): 20% base bonus for 10% low-income, 5% very low-income or senior projects; 5% for 10% moderate-income for-sale units; 20% for 10% very low-income units for veterans, transition-age youth or homeless households; 35% for qualifying student housing; sliding scale up to 50% (2.5% per 1% very low-income above 5%, 1.5% per 1% low-income above 10%); land donation bonus 15% to 35%; floor area ratio bonus in the R-H zone for infill near transit with 20% of units at or below 50% AMI; 100% lower-income projects per Government Code 65915. One to four incentives or concessions by affordability tier plus parking reductions; the County may exceed these amounts (9-401.060).
- AMI requirement: 55-year rental affordability (longer if required by financing); for-sale units sold to qualifying buyers with equity sharing; affordable units integrated with and indistinguishable from market-rate units; replacement of existing affordable units required.
- Cycle: rolling (next: By application; pre-application response within 90 days; streamlined ministerial approval under 9-401.120 for eligible infill projects with at least 10% of units at or below 80% AMI (60 or 90 day review, deemed approved if missed).)
- Layering notes: San Joaquin County has no county housing trust fund, no county housing bond and no inclusionary ordinance; the County's own capital for multifamily is limited to HUD pass-through funds administered by the Human Services Agency Neighborhood Preservation Division (sjchsa.org), while the regional gap lender is the SJCOG-sponsored San Joaquin Regional Housing Fund and the main voucher and development partner is the Housing Authority of the County of San Joaquin (HACSJ). The unincorporated county has no inclusionary ordinance and no in-lieu fee, so the density bonus and concessions are the only land-use subsidy; the 2023-2031 Housing Element (HCD submittal revised January 2025, adopted and revised June 30, 2026 to transfer RHNA to the new City of Mountain House, 8,808 to 5,113 units) sets a quantified objective of 100 lower-income units through the bonus and commits to fee deferrals for affordable subdivisions. The ministerial pathway in 9-401.120 carries state prevailing wage and skilled workforce requirements for larger projects under Government Code 65913.4, so model labor costs before electing it. Most multifamily sites in the unincorporated county (French Camp, Garden Acres, Lodi and Stockton fringe) are constrained by water and sewer service, which the Housing Element names as the largest constraint. Source is the published Development Title chapter on gocodebook.com (County code host); confirm current text with Community Development at (209) 468-3144.
- Source: https://gocodebook.com/library/us/ca/san-joaquin-county/development-title/series-400-additional-use-and-development-regulations/chapter-9-401-affordable-housing-density-bonus
- Confidence: verified (researched 2026-11-07)

**Behavioral Health Services Act (BHSA) Integrated Plan FY 2026-29, housing interventions**
- Agency: San Joaquin County Behavioral Health Services (Health Care Services Agency)
- Type: other
- Typical award: Three-year plan totaling $295,750,706 approved June 2, 2026 (5-0). The County requested a transfer of 7% from the housing component to Behavioral Health Services and Supports, leaving housing interventions at 23% of BHSA funds. Estimated housing intervention expenditures: $18,790,266 in year one and $42,013,536 in year two; the continuum table shows housing services of $37.0 million, $41.6 million and $37.8 million across the three years. Planned uses: project-based rental subsidies for about 150 people a year (64 permanent, 86 interim; 350 units), operating subsidies for about 116 people (228 units, property management staffing for SRO and transitional-to-permanent apartments), landlord outreach and mitigation for about 100, and two capital projects (a 50-unit tiny home project and the 33-unit Edison House, both braided with other funds, unit availability June 30, 2027, BHSA share capped at $450,000 per unit).
- AMI requirement: Individuals with serious behavioral health conditions who are homeless or at risk; at least 50% of housing intervention funds for chronically homeless households; PSH setting types and Housing First.
- Cycle: rolling (next: Plan effective July 1, 2026 through June 30, 2029 with annual updates each June. Behavioral Health Services completed a request for qualifications for housing developers in 2025-26 (RFQ 25107) and will work with the pre-qualified pool: Central Valley Low Income Housing Corporation, Delta Community Developers Corporation, Domus Development LLC, Mahogany and Oak Real Estate, Mutual Housing California, RHCB Development LP, Self-Help Enterprises and Visionary Home Builders of California.)
- Layering notes: San Joaquin County has no county housing trust fund, no county housing bond and no inclusionary ordinance; the County's own capital for multifamily is limited to HUD pass-through funds administered by the Human Services Agency Neighborhood Preservation Division (sjchsa.org), while the regional gap lender is the SJCOG-sponsored San Joaquin Regional Housing Fund and the main voucher and development partner is the Housing Authority of the County of San Joaquin (HACSJ). BHSA is the County's largest discretionary housing stream and the realistic source of project-based operating subsidy for PSH units in the unincorporated county and Stockton; capital is limited to the two named projects, so new deals should pitch rental or operating subsidies for behavioral health set-aside units rather than construction money. Behavioral Health Services also carries Homekey+ (Bridge to Home, $15,900,896 agreement with CVLIHC approved January 13, 2026) and Behavioral Health Bridge Housing Round 3 contracts, and is building the SJ BeWell campus with a $38.2 million BHCIP Round 2 award (March 2026). Pre-qualification through the BHS RFQ is the entry point for developers. The Board file (source) links the board order, the 490-page DHCS Integrated Plan submission (FileOpen.aspx?Type=4&ID=45761) and the June 2, 2026 presentation.

- Agency: San Joaquin County Human Services Agency, Neighborhood Preservation Division
- Type: grant

Davis-Bacon applies to HOME-assisted projects of 12 or more units and to CDBG-assisted projects of 8 or more units; state prevailing wage applies to public subsidy. The Neighborhood Preservation pages moved from sjgov.org to sjchsa.org in 2026; the 2025-2029 Consolidated Plan and 2026-2027 Annual Action Plan are posted there.

It is grant money and does not by itself trigger prevailing wage, but it is always paired with public funds that do. Recorded at county level because the plans are county Medi-Cal plans and the money flows through countywide vehicles; figures are from the SJCOG March 11, 2026 announcement (source), the June 18, 2026 fund packet and the Lodi Commons FONSI.
- Source: https://sjcog.org/CivicAlerts.asp?AID=688
- Confidence: verified (researched 2026-11-07)

**Homekey+ and Behavioral Health Bridge Housing, County-sponsored projects**
- Agency: San Joaquin County Behavioral Health Services (Homekey+, BHBH) and Veterans Services Office
- Type: grant
- Typical award: Bridge to Home (Central Valley Low Income Housing Corporation): Homekey+ agreement for $15,900,896, January 13, 2026 through March 31, 2027, with a $12,785,399 appropriation in the FY 2025-26 Behavioral Health budget. Behavioral Health Bridge Housing Round 3: fourth amendment with CVLIHC (August 1, 2024 to June 30, 2027), $281,000 to the City of Manteca (March 1, 2026 to June 30, 2036) and $1,500,000 to Mahogany and Oak Consultancy (June 2, 2026 to June 30, 2027). HHAP-5 $1,000,000 for the SJ BeWell Tiny Home Village. HACSJ's Edison House (33 PSH units, 14 for veterans) is a state Homekey+ awardee. News reports describe a February 2026 Board consent action authorizing Veterans Services to apply for up to $38,500,000 of Homekey+ for a campus-style veterans housing village in French Camp near San Joaquin General Hospital; that item was not located in the Board files opened this pass.
- AMI requirement: Homekey+ and BHBH serve people experiencing homelessness with behavioral health conditions and veterans; PSH with 55-year restrictions for Homekey+ capital.
- Cycle: rolling (next: State Homekey+ applications are by state NOFA; the County sponsors applications case by case with Behavioral Health Services or Veterans Services as co-applicant. No County solicitation is open.)
- Layering notes: San Joaquin County has no county housing trust fund, no county housing bond and no inclusionary ordinance; the County's own capital for multifamily is limited to HUD pass-through funds administered by the Human Services Agency Neighborhood Preservation Division (sjchsa.org), while the regional gap lender is the SJCOG-sponsored San Joaquin Regional Housing Fund and the main voucher and development partner is the Housing Authority of the County of San Joaquin (HACSJ). The County's role is co-applicant and contract manager rather than lender; developers bring the site and the County brings match, operating funds (BHSA, BHBH, HHAP) and services. CVLIHC is the County's primary operator and Mahogany and Oak and HACSJ are the other repeat partners. Confirm the French Camp veterans village application status with the Veterans Services Office; the figure comes from a news summary of the February 2026 agenda rather than an opened Board file.

**Permanent Local Housing Allocation (PLHA), County formula allocation**
- Agency: San Joaquin County Human Services Agency, Neighborhood Preservation Division
- Type: grant
- Typical award: HCD formula allocation to the County: $919,667 (2024 allocation year), $985,099 (2025), estimated $5,747,919 for the 2024-2028 five-year plan; for 2019-2023 the County was eligible for an estimated $7,571,813 and had received $5,587,686 by early 2026. The County directs its PLHA to Activity 6 (emergency shelter and navigation center operations). 2026 NOFA: $1,884,922 from the 2022 and 2023 allocations; seven grant agreements approved June 30, 2026 (City of Manteca $206,324, City of Tracy $206,324, Gospel Center Rescue Mission $206,324, St. Mary's Community Services $206,324, Haven of Peace $400,000, HOPE Ministries $280,000, McHenry House of Tracy $379,626) running through June 30, 2030.

- Layering notes: San Joaquin County has no county housing trust fund, no county housing bond and no inclusionary ordinance; the County's own capital for multifamily is limited to HUD pass-through funds administered by the Human Services Agency Neighborhood Preservation Division (sjchsa.org), while the regional gap lender is the SJCOG-sponsored San Joaquin Regional Housing Fund and the main voucher and development partner is the Housing Authority of the County of San Joaquin (HACSJ). The County's PLHA five-year plan does not fund multifamily capital, so PLHA is not a County gap source for tax credit deals here; it sustains shelter operations that otherwise compete with HHAP. Stockton, Lodi, Tracy and Manteca receive their own PLHA formula allocations and may use them differently (Pass 3). County allocation figures are from the HCD 2024-2028 PLHA NOFA allocation tables; the 2019-2023 figures and the Activity 6 plan are from the County PLHA public notice (source).

**Project-Based Vouchers, Housing Authority of the County of San Joaquin (HACSJ)**
- Agency: Housing Authority of the County of San Joaquin (PHA code CA024), 2575 Grand Canal Boulevard, Suite 100, Stockton
- Type: other
- Typical award: HACSJ administers 5,380 Housing Choice Vouchers and 910 public housing units (FY 2026-27 Annual Plan). PBVs are awarded through Requests for Proposals for existing, new construction or substantially rehabilitated housing serving persons with disabilities, veterans and families; a past RFP offered up to 130 PBVs for existing units. FY 2026-27 project-basing: Tracy Apartments Phase I 32 PBVs plus 22 RAD and tenant protection vouchers (54 units), Lodi Commons 32 PBVs plus 22 ACC units (estimated PBV subsidy $152,172 a year), Edison House 19 PBVs plus 14 HUD-VASH (33 units), Grant Street Apartments 24 PBVs.
- AMI requirement: HUD PBV rules: households at or below 50% AMI at admission with 75% at or below 30% AMI; 15 to 20 year HAP contracts; HACSJ is not a Moving to Work agency so the 20% program cap and PBV competitive selection rules apply (exception for projects selected through a prior competitive public process).
- Cycle: rolling (next: No open PBV RFP found on hacsj.org procurement as of November 7, 2026; HACSJ reports it cannot apply for additional vouchers because of funding shortfalls, so new PBVs come from existing voucher authority. Monitor hacsj.org/resources/procurement and Public Purchase.)
- Layering notes: San Joaquin County has no county housing trust fund, no county housing bond and no inclusionary ordinance; the County's own capital for multifamily is limited to HUD pass-through funds administered by the Human Services Agency Neighborhood Preservation Division (sjchsa.org), while the regional gap lender is the SJCOG-sponsored San Joaquin Regional Housing Fund and the main voucher and development partner is the Housing Authority of the County of San Joaquin (HACSJ). PBVs are the main operating subsidy for PSH and senior deals in the county and underwrite debt on Measure-K and Regional Housing Fund projects; HACSJ attaches PBVs to its own Delta Community Developers Corp. projects and to partner projects. Davis-Bacon applies to PBV new construction and rehabilitation of nine or more units. HACSJ also runs HUD-VASH, Family Unification and Emergency Housing Vouchers (EHV sunset noted in 2026) and launched CASH SJC in August 2026, a $4.75 million CDSS-funded direct cash program for about 250 seniors on its waitlists. The 2026-27 Annual Plan (effective October 1, 2026) is the source; PBV program description is on hacsj.org/portfolio-item/project-based-voucher.

- Confidence: verified (researched 2026-11-07)

**San Joaquin Regional Housing Fund (SJRHF) gap loans, SJCOG**
- Agency: San Joaquin Regional Housing Fund Inc. (501(c)(3) subsidiary of the San Joaquin Council of Governments), fund manager Harris and Associates
- Type: loan
- Typical award: Round 1 (June 2026) committed $11,850,000 in gap loans to four projects: Airport Way Apartments, Manteca (TPC Housing) $2,850,000; The Junction, Tracy (CRP Affordable Housing and Community Development) $3,000,000; Lodi Commons at Salas Park, Lodi (San Joaquin Housing Authority) $3,000,000; The Don Shalvey Apartments, Stockton (Visionary Home Builders) $3,000,000. Alternates: Countrywood Cottages, Escalon; Casa De Mariposa and The View at Channel, Stockton. $750,000 held in reserve. Capitalization net of administration: $4,750,000 HCD Local Housing Trust Fund grant, $5,000,000 SJCOG Measure K smart growth local match, $2,850,000 Health Net grant ($12.6 million total; $13 million plus gross including $75,000 from the San Joaquin Community Foundation). Enterprise reports the round supports 421 affordable homes.
- AMI requirement: 55-year regulatory agreement minimum; LHTF dollars prioritize extremely low and very low income units in new construction and permanent rental housing; Measure K match requires infill and smart growth locations; Health Net dollars are flexible but prioritize low-income units. Preference for sites near transit and services.
- Cycle: annual NOFA (next: Round 1 closed; funding commitment letters carry a one-year term with a one-year extension option tied to tax credit outcomes. No Round 2 date is set; SJCOG is seeking new capital and the Advisory Committee meets quarterly (March 4, June 3, September 2 and December 2, 2027). An ADU pilot of about $300,000 in REAP 2.0 funds is in design. Contact Joann Martinez, SJCOG, (209) 235-0582.)
- Layering notes: San Joaquin County has no county housing trust fund, no county housing bond and no inclusionary ordinance; the County's own capital for multifamily is limited to HUD pass-through funds administered by the Human Services Agency Neighborhood Preservation Division (sjchsa.org), while the regional gap lender is the SJCOG-sponsored San Joaquin Regional Housing Fund and the main voucher and development partner is the Housing Authority of the County of San Joaquin (HACSJ). This is the only countywide gap lender and the first new local soft money in the county in years; awards of $2.85 million to $3 million were sized to close 4% bond and LIHTC deals already in the pipeline, and funds disburse only after all other financing is secured. Loan terms: 3% simple interest or the Freddie Mac 30-year rate, 55-year term extendable 25 years, annual payments from 50% of residual receipts shared pro rata with other public lenders, 1% origination fee, debt service coverage of 1.15 or better in year one (TCAC minimum operating expenses per Title 4 Section 10327 unless justified). Public money from the fund is treated as a public subsidy for prevailing wage. The SJRHF board is the SJCOG board (Escalon, Lathrop, Lodi, Manteca, Mountain House, Ripon, San Joaquin County, Stockton, Tracy). Source is the June 18, 2026 Advisory Committee agenda packet with the award table and underwriting summaries; guidelines are in the April 13, 2026 packet (sjcog.org/AgendaCenter/ViewFile/Agenda/_04132026-1710).
- Source: https://www.sjcog.org/AgendaCenter/ViewFile/Agenda/_06182026-1726
- Confidence: verified (researched 2026-11-07)

**Welfare Exemption (property tax), San Joaquin County Assessor**
- Agency: San Joaquin County Assessor-Recorder-County Clerk, Office of the Assessor, 44 North San Joaquin Street, Second Floor Suite 230, Stockton, (209) 468-2630
- Type: tax abatement
- Typical award: Full exemption of the ad valorem property tax on qualifying low-income rental housing (about 1% of assessed value plus voter-approved debt each year), applied by unit share for LIHTC and other restricted projects under Revenue and Taxation Code 214(g).
- AMI requirement: Property owned and operated by a qualifying nonprofit or a limited partnership with a nonprofit managing general partner holding a BOE Organizational Clearance Certificate; units restricted to lower-income households by regulatory agreement or tax credits; BOE-267 series claim forms filed with the Assessor.
- Cycle: annual NOFA (next: February 15, 2027 for the 2027-28 roll; claims filed February 16 through December 31 receive a partial exemption; late deadlines roll to the next business day.)
- Layering notes: San Joaquin County has no county housing trust fund, no county housing bond and no inclusionary ordinance; the County's own capital for multifamily is limited to HUD pass-through funds administered by the Human Services Agency Neighborhood Preservation Division (sjchsa.org), while the regional gap lender is the SJCOG-sponsored San Joaquin Regional Housing Fund and the main voucher and development partner is the Housing Authority of the County of San Joaquin (HACSJ). Standard California process: the Assessor page lists rental housing for lower-income households and HUD-financed elderly or disabled housing among eligible uses and requires a new claim every year. Budget the first-year supplemental and the partial-exemption rule when closing late in the year. Assessor name is on the office leadership page, not the exemption page.
- Source: https://www.sjgov.org/department/assessor/tax-savings-exemptions/welfare-exemption
- Confidence: verified (researched 2026-11-07)


### San Luis Obispo County

**Behavioral Health Services Act (BHSA) Housing Interventions and capital development RFP, 2026-2029 Integrated Plan**
- Agency: San Luis Obispo County Behavioral Health Department
- Type: grant
- Typical award: Housing Interventions budget $6,930,885 (FY 2026/27), $6,792,267 (FY 2027/28), $6,656,422 (FY 2028/29), 30% of BHSA. Funds about 107 PSH beds, 86 assisted living and board and care beds, 10 time-limited beds, FSP housing, landlord mitigation and participant assistance. Capital development: yes, one project in Year 1 via an RFP for a minimum of two units at up to $450,000 of BHSA per unit, braided with other funds, available by June 30, 2027, with by-right provisions required. Behavioral Health Bridge Housing beds start Year 2.
- AMI requirement: BHSA-eligible adults with serious mental illness or substance use disorder experiencing or at risk of homelessness; half of housing funds for chronic homelessness.
- Cycle: rolling (next: Capital development RFP expected in FY 2026/27 (units by June 30, 2027). Plan submitted to DHCS March 2026, final June 30, 2026; annual updates follow.)
- Layering notes: San Luis Obispo County's Department of Social Services Homeless Services Division (HSD, Devin Drake, Director; George Solis, Principal Administrative Manager; HSDgrants@co.slo.ca.us) runs one combined annual Action Plan NOFA each fall for CDBG, HOME, ESG, HHAP, PLHA, Title 29 and County General Fund Support on the Neighborly portal, and is the Continuum of Care collaborative applicant and administrative entity (CA-614). The Department of Planning and Building runs Title 22 land use incentives and assesses the new Title 31 in-lieu fee; the Behavioral Health Department holds BHSA; the Housing Authority of San Luis Obispo (HASLO) and its San Luis Obispo Nonprofit Housing Corporation, Paso Robles Housing Authority and Peoples' Self-Help Housing are the main developers; and the private nonprofit San Luis Obispo County Housing Trust Fund is the local CDFI gap lender. The Urban County covers the unincorporated area plus Arroyo Grande, Atascadero, Morro Bay, Paso Robles, Pismo Beach and San Luis Obispo (Grover Beach is outside). The County repealed its inclusionary ordinance on June 7, 2022 and replaced it in October 2025 with a voluntary Regional Housing Incentive Program and Regional Housing Fund. slocounty.ca.gov opens directly but rate-limits bursts (HTTP 429); Legistar web API is not enabled for the County. The capital set-aside is tiny (two units), so BHSA matters mainly as an operating and rental subsidy source for PSH units in a larger project. Transitions-Mental Health Association is the County's main housing partner. Contact Behavioral Health about committing operating subsidies to units in a Homekey+ or LIHTC project.

- Agency: San Luis Obispo County Department of Planning and Building

- Typical award: HCD awarded the County a Prohousing Designation in October 2025 for lowering permit barriers for affordable housing, incentivizing density through land use changes (Action 1 multifamily update) and creating the Regional Housing Fund. Designation gives projects in the unincorporated county priority or bonus points in state programs including the Prohousing Incentive Program, AHSC, Caltrans planning grants and others.
- AMI requirement: Not applicable to the designation.
- Cycle: rolling (next: Designation is active; the County may apply for Prohousing Incentive Program funds in HCD's next round.)
- Layering notes: San Luis Obispo County's Department of Social Services Homeless Services Division (HSD, Devin Drake, Director; George Solis, Principal Administrative Manager; HSDgrants@co.slo.ca.us) runs one combined annual Action Plan NOFA each fall for CDBG, HOME, ESG, HHAP, PLHA, Title 29 and County General Fund Support on the Neighborly portal, and is the Continuum of Care collaborative applicant and administrative entity (CA-614). The Department of Planning and Building runs Title 22 land use incentives and assesses the new Title 31 in-lieu fee; the Behavioral Health Department holds BHSA; the Housing Authority of San Luis Obispo (HASLO) and its San Luis Obispo Nonprofit Housing Corporation, Paso Robles Housing Authority and Peoples' Self-Help Housing are the main developers; and the private nonprofit San Luis Obispo County Housing Trust Fund is the local CDFI gap lender. The Urban County covers the unincorporated area plus Arroyo Grande, Atascadero, Morro Bay, Paso Robles, Pismo Beach and San Luis Obispo (Grover Beach is outside). The County repealed its inclusionary ordinance on June 7, 2022 and replaced it in October 2025 with a voluntary Regional Housing Incentive Program and Regional Housing Fund. slocounty.ca.gov opens directly but rate-limits bursts (HTTP 429); Legistar web API is not enabled for the County. Cite the designation in AHSC, Multifamily Housing Program and Infill Infrastructure Grant applications for unincorporated sites. Pair with Regional Housing Incentive density and the Housing Trust Fund.

**Regional Housing Fund and Regional Housing Grant (County Code Title 31, adopted October 21, 2025)**
- Agency: San Luis Obispo County Department of Social Services (grant) with Department of Planning and Building (fee collection)
- Type: grant
- Typical award: New fund capitalized by Regional Housing Incentive in-lieu fees ($30,000 per Incentive Point initially, range $30,000 to $50,000, ENR-indexed from July 1, 2026 and adjusted 5% up or down from July 1, 2029 based on program use), plus any General Fund, grants or private contributions. 75% goes to the Guaranteed Affordable Housing Account for the Regional Housing Grant and 25% to a Public Transportation Support Account. The County said the program is meant to fill the funding gap for roughly 280 already-approved affordable units. No awards yet and no balance published.

- Cycle: annual NOFA (next: Annual awards recommended by Social Services to the Board; the first Regional Housing Grant round depends on fee receipts and had not been announced as of November 8, 2026. Watch the Action Plan NOFA each September.)

**Regional Housing Incentive Program (Title 22 Chapter 22.12.010, adopted October 21, 2025)**
- Agency: San Luis Obispo County Department of Planning and Building
- Type: density bonus
- Typical award: Voluntary program for multifamily projects wholly inside an Urban Reserve Line. Projects accrue Incentive Points (two per on-site very low income unit, or by paying the Title 31 in-lieu fee of $30,000 per point through June 30, 2026, indexed to ENR construction costs after) and spend them on standards relief and density increases that count as base density before the state density bonus. Very low income units funded with government grants or tax credits do not earn points unless the project is 100% affordable (very low, low and moderate). Phase 2 (Actions 7 and 8, introduced November 4, 2025, scoped April 21, 2026) would add ministerial permitting for participating projects.
- AMI requirement: On-site units restricted to very low income under Section 22.12.030 Housing Affordability Standards (long-term covenants); in-lieu option carries no on-site units.
- Cycle: rolling (next: Not applicable; requested with the land use permit. Inland ordinance effective 30 days after October 21, 2025 adoption; Coastal Zone version pending Coastal Commission certification.)

**Urban County Action Plan NOFA: HOME and CDBG affordable housing development loans**
- Agency: San Luis Obispo County Department of Social Services, Homeless Services Division
- Type: loan
- Typical award: 2027 Action Plan NOFA (issued September 28, 2026, applications due October 30, 2026): HOME estimated $690,900 available for projects (allocation $767,667), CDBG $1,418,895 across the Urban County (County share $368,732 for projects; cities $30,236 to $371,200 each). 2026 Action Plan (approved April 7, 2026) put $499,969 of HOME into one affordable rental project and CDBG into rehab, shelters and a recuperative care facility. Recent HOME and Title 29 layered projects: Rolling Hills III (Templeton, 28 units, Peoples' Self-Help Housing), Cambria Pines (33 units, $373,418 HOME/PLHA/Title 29 in 2025), Monterey Family Apartments (50 units), Balay Ko on Monterey (56 senior units) and Arroyo Terrace (63 units), the last three by HASLO's nonprofit.
- AMI requirement: HOME: 90% of households at or below 60% AMI, 20% of units at 50% AMI in projects of five or more HOME units; affordability 20 years for new construction (longer under County agreements); 25% HOME match and 15% CHDO set-aside. CDBG: 51% low and moderate income.
- Cycle: annual NOFA (next: 2027 Action Plan applications closed October 30, 2026; draft housing recommendations hearing February 2027; Board of Supervisors approval April 2027; FY 2027/28 awards begin July 1, 2027. The 2028 Action Plan NOFA is expected in September 2027.)

The County repealed its inclusionary ordinance on June 7, 2022 and replaced it in October 2025 with a voluntary Regional Housing Incentive Program and Regional Housing Fund. slocounty.ca.gov opens directly but rate-limits bursts (HTTP 429); Legistar web API is not enabled for the County. Scoring (100 points) weights scope and expertise (40), funding readiness (15), cost effectiveness and unit count (20), entitlement readiness (10), site standards, vulnerable population targeting and alignment with the Countywide Plan to Address Homelessness (15). ### San Mateo County

**Behavioral Health Services Act (BHSA) housing interventions and MHSA/BHSA capital through the Affordable Housing Fund**
- Agency: San Mateo County Health, Behavioral Health and Recovery Services (BHRS), with the Department of Housing administering capital awards
- Type: loan
- Typical award: Three-Year Integrated Plan FY 2026-27 to FY 2028-29 approved by the Board June 9, 2026 (Behavioral Health Commission hearing closed March 5, 2026). Housing Interventions expenditures $24,427,542 (FY 2026-27), $24,374,720 (FY 2027-28), $24,374,720 (FY 2028-29); capital development $6,152,822 then $6,100,000 a year (24% of the component, near the 25% cap) delivered through the DOH Affordable Housing Fund NOFAs, where the AHF 14 round carried $5,000,000 of MHSA/BHSA capital at up to $200,000 per restricted unit; the plan lists nine capital projects and a 65-unit PSH pipeline at up to $450,000 per unit. Operating subsidies $3,540,627 plus $2,182,327, bundled rental and operating subsidies about $1,160,000 to $1,460,000, rental subsidies $1,000,000; $12,900,025 a year (51%) dedicated to chronically homeless people; 64 people a year in operating-subsidized units. San Mateo joined the state Flex Pool Technical Assistance Academy.
- AMI requirement: MHSA/BHSA units for BHRS-referred adults with serious mental illness or substance use disorder who are homeless or at risk: 30% AMI with PBVs or 20% AMI without, Housing First, on-site supportive services; 55-year County regulatory agreement through the AHF loan.
- Cycle: annual NOFA (next: Apply through the AHF NOFA (next round expected fall 2027) and meet with BHRS before applying; the plan runs July 1, 2026 to June 30, 2029 with annual updates. Ask BHRS about operating subsidies and transitional rent for MHSA/BHSA units, which the AHF NOFA counts toward its homelessness preference requirement.)
- Layering notes: San Mateo keeps BHSA capital at the statutory maximum and routes it through the same AHF loan documents as Measure K, so a PSH sponsor can get Measure K plus about $200,000 per BHSA unit in one award with BHRS operating subsidy behind it. State funds trigger prevailing wage. Plan read from the Board attachment on Legistar (final plan PDF, opened); the smchealth.org copies returned 404.
- Source: https://sanmateocounty.legistar.com/LegislationDetail.aspx?ID=94826&GUID=9A552B75-9564-4B1D-A51C-4144E6EBF1C3&Options=&Search=&FullText=1
- Confidence: verified (researched 2026-11-06)

**Daly City/San Mateo County Continuum of Care (CA-512) and HHAP**
- Agency: San Mateo County Human Services Agency, Center on Homelessness (CoC lead agency and HHAP administrative entity for the County and CoC)
- Type: grant
- Typical award: HHAP joint County and CoC allocations: Round 1 $3,431,246 (Feb 2020), Round 2 $1,597,106, Round 3 $4,375,129, Round 4 $4,658,201, Round 5 $5,237,946 (County $2,564,722, CoC $2,673,224), Round 6 $5,026,361 (County $2,430,522, CoC $2,595,839; accepted June 10, 2025, awarded March 2, 2026, usable through June 30, 2029), about $24,300,000 in all. State accountability site: $19,300,000 HHAP rounds 1 to 5 to the County ($13,800,000 obligated, $11,800,000 spent by mid-2025); Encampment Resolution Funding $16,000,000 in the area, $14,100,000 to the County. HHAP-6 supports operations of the 240-unit Navigation Center in Redwood City. HUD CoC program FY 2024 awards to CA-512: $817,332 (Shelter Plus Care sponsor-based $368,857, Vendome $303,133, Redwood Family House $145,342). State ESG CoC share $188,054 (2024). 2024 PIT: 2,130 people, 1,145 unsheltered, 3,454 year-round beds. Homekey: Casa Esperanza, Redwood City (former Comfort Inn, 51 PSH units, $15,978,232 Homekey plus up to $7,697,170 ARPA match, operated by Episcopal Community Services since 2025 under a 55-year ground lease with County Housing Voucher Program operating subsidies) and a Ramada conversion in South San Francisco with ECS; Homekey+ co-applicant RFP (Jan 15 to Feb 5, 2025) to pair developer teams and sites with County match for 2025 applications.
- AMI requirement: People experiencing or at risk of homelessness per HUD and state definitions; CoC permanent housing through Coordinated Entry; HHAP-6 must obligate 75% and spend 50% by June 30, 2027.
- Cycle: annual NOFA (next: HHAP-7 is available to HHAP-6 grantees; the CoC runs the HUD NOFO each summer. For capital, the County route is the Homekey+ co-applicant process through the Department of Housing and the AHF NOFA's homelessness preference units; HHAP itself funds shelter and services.)
- Layering notes: A small CoC (about $800,000 a year in HUD renewals) and modest HHAP, so homeless capital comes from Measure K and Homekey rather than CoC money; the County uses its own Housing Voucher Program and HACSM PBVs for operating subsidy at Homekey sites. HHAP figures from the County HSA HHAP page and Board item 25-554 (opened), HCD allocation lists and accountability.ca.gov; Homekey details from Board item 25-249 and the Homekey+ RFP page.

**HACSM Moving to Work funds for affordable housing development (through the Affordable Housing Fund)**
- Agency: Housing Authority of the County of San Mateo (MTW Activity 2011-16 and development activity) with the Department of Housing
- Type: loan
- Typical award: HUD has approved HACSM's use of unspent HAP reserves (MTW funds) for affordable housing development in steps: $4,000,000 originally, $8,000,000 (FY 2013), $10,000,000 (FY 2016), $25,000,000 (FY 2020), $35,000,000 (FY 2024) and $65,000,000 (FY 2025). The FY 2027 MTW Plan reports $65,000,000 of MTW funds approved for the Affordable Housing Fund, including $7,900,000 for Ridge at Ralston in Belmont and $8,600,000 for 493 Eastmoor in Daly City.

- Cycle: annual NOFA (next: Allocated through the AHF NOFA when HACSM has reserves to contribute; next AHF round expected fall 2027. Ask DOH whether HACSM funds are in the pool before applying.)
- Layering notes: Unusual source: HUD lets this MTW agency lend its unspent voucher money as capital, and the County has pushed the ceiling to $65,000,000. It arrives inside an AHF award as a zero-interest residual receipts loan, which helps cash flow versus the County's 3% Measure K loan. Federal HAP money carries Davis-Bacon and Section 3; state prevailing wage applies through the County loan. Read from the FY 2027 MTW Annual Plan PDF (opened).

**Housing Endowment and Regional Trust of San Mateo County (HEART) developer loans**
- Agency: HEART of San Mateo County, joint powers authority of the County and 20 cities and towns; 2905 S. El Camino Real, San Mateo; Armando Sanchez 650-204-5640
- Type: loan
- Typical award: HEART reports $57,000,000 invested in affordable housing development. Two products: QuickStart (up to five years, predevelopment, acquisition, construction or rehab, principal deferred to maturity) and SemiPerm (five to 15 years including extensions, interest-only or amortized on a 30-year schedule with balloon, for acquisition, predevelopment, refinancing and rehab). Rates are described as favorable and competitive and quoted on request; origination fee 2% of loans up to $2,000,000 and 1.5% above, $3,000 application fee, borrower pays lender legal and third-party costs; loan size depends on project financials and repayment source. Recent County relationships: a $2,400,000 agreement (June 16, 2026) for HEART to run the County's mobile home replacement loan program, and a $450,000 HEART loan in HEART-SV's plan to take over Visitacion Gardens in Brisbane (May 2026). Funded projects include Montara at Bay Meadows, Ocean View, Peninsula Station, Trestle Glen, Hillcrest Senior, Serenity Senior, Fair Oaks Commons, The Village at the Crossing and 2000 South Delaware.
- AMI requirement: Up to 120% AMI (workforce) with a 55-year affordability covenant on a number of units commensurate with HEART's share, deferring to other funders' covenants when sufficient; projects must be in a member jurisdiction (the County and 20 cities and towns: Atherton, Belmont, Brisbane, Burlingame, Colma, Daly City, East Palo Alto, Foster City, Half Moon Bay, Hillsborough, Menlo Park, Millbrae, Pacifica, Portola Valley, Redwood City, San Bruno, San Carlos, San Mateo, South San Francisco, Woodside and the County) with an adopted or under-review housing element.
- Cycle: rolling (next: Rolling; contact HEART for current rates and available funds. The 2026 Board report notes HEART is restructuring programs (first-time homebuyer loans ended Jan 28, 2026). HEART also runs an ADU design center and received state LHTF matching grants in past rounds.)
- Layering notes: HEART is bridge and acquisition money, not permanent gap financing: use QuickStart to tie up a site or carry predevelopment until an AHF award and tax credits close, then take out the loan. Member dues are population based and the County administers HEART, so it reads as a county-level source even though cities co-own it. Public agency funds, so assume state prevailing wage applies to construction financed with HEART loans. Term sheets (May 24, 2023) and member list opened on heartofsmc.org.
- Source: https://www.heartofsmc.org/programs/for-developers/
- Confidence: verified (researched 2026-11-06)

**Inclusionary Affordable Housing Ordinance (2004) with 2026 rezoning amendments, County affordable housing impact fees, and state density bonus**
- Agency: San Mateo County Planning and Building Department, 455 County Center, Redwood City; impact fees deposited to the Department of Housing's Housing Trust Fund
- Type: density bonus
- Typical award: Multifamily projects of five or more units in the unincorporated area must make 20% of units affordable, typically to lower income households (a rental project of five to nine units may provide its one required unit at moderate income; ownership projects may provide half at moderate income), with in-lieu fees, off-site units, land dedication or rehabilitation of existing affordable units allowed at the County's sole discretion. Ordinance 4927 (adopted Oct 6, 2026) removes those alternatives and the moderate-income option in the new R3-MD, PC-HD and TS-MU districts rezoned April 21, 2026 in Colma, Broadmoor and the Harbor Industrial area: 20% on site at low, very low or extremely low income. Affordable housing impact fees on residential and non-residential development were adopted in 2016 from a multi-jurisdictional nexus study and fund the AHF ($100,000 offered in each of AHF 13 and 14 for unincorporated projects); a new Multi-Jurisdictional Inclusionary Housing and Non-Residential Linkage Fee Study (Strategic Economics, $619,135, Dec 2025 to June 2027, County share $51,681) will reset fee levels for the County and ten cities. Density bonus follows Government Code 65915; the County enforces state law and has no local bonus beyond it.
- AMI requirement: Inclusionary units at lower income rents or prices for the ordinance term (long-term covenants recorded at entitlement); state density bonus units 55 years for rental.
- Cycle: rolling (next: Not applicable; applies at entitlement. Expect revised impact fee levels after the nexus study concludes in mid-2027. Unincorporated areas include North Fair Oaks, Colma, Broadmoor, Harbor Industrial, the Midcoast and Emerald Hills.)
- Layering notes: North Fair Oaks and the Colma and Broadmoor rezoning areas are where County inclusionary rules bite; 100% affordable projects satisfy them automatically and take the state density bonus. In-lieu fees and impact fees are small (about $100,000 a year reaches the AHF) because unincorporated development volume is low. Density bonus alone does not trigger prevailing wage. Sources: County inclusionary ordinance page (the ordinance PDF is image-only), Board items 26-817 and 25-1053 and the Oct 6, 2026 Board presentation and Ordinance 4927 (opened).
- Source: https://smcgov.org/planning/inclusionary-affordable-housing-ordinance
- Confidence: verified (researched 2026-11-06)

**Permanent Local Housing Allocation (PLHA), San Mateo County entitlement**
- Agency: San Mateo County Department of Housing (HCD entitlement grantee)
- Type: grant
- Typical award: 2019-2023 five-year formula estimate $7,257,300 (CY 2021 funds $2,068,889). Calendar year 2022 and 2023 funds of $1,831,715 ($1,036,938 plus $794,777) were authorized Dec 2, 2025 and awarded by HCD in July 2026 after the County's housing element came into compliance; $824,272 is committed through AHF 13 (moved from Laurel Landing to Rotary Gardens on Aug 25, 2026) and the balance is being allocated over the counter. HCD 2024-2028 Formula Allocation NOFA estimates: CY 2024 $849,022, CY 2025 $909,428, five-year $5,306,388.
- AMI requirement: County PLHA plan funds Activity 1 (rental development for extremely low to moderate income households with 55-year covenants through the AHF process) and Activity 6 (homeless services, shelter and navigation center operations and case management); 2024 HCD rule requires 40% of new funds for affordable owner-occupied workforce housing unless amended.
- Cycle: annual NOFA (next: PLHA is offered through the AHF NOFA, the Winter NOFA and over-the-counter processes as HCD releases each year's funds; CY 2022 and 2023 money must be spent on HCD's deadlines, which drove the Aug 2026 reallocation. Ask DOH whether CY 2024 and 2025 funds will appear in the fall 2027 AHF round.)
- Layering notes: Small and lumpy because HCD withheld San Mateo's PLHA for several years over housing element compliance; the County treats it as a swap source inside AHF awards (PLHA to the project closing soonest, Measure K to the slower one). State funds trigger prevailing wage. Figures from Board items 25-1006 and 26-706 read through the Legistar API and the HCD 2024-2028 PLHA NOFA.
- Source: https://sanmateocounty.legistar.com/LegislationDetail.aspx?ID=95103&GUID=5E955EF2-AB26-4DAB-8CC5-3ABE4B451365&Options=&Search=&FullText=1
- Confidence: verified (researched 2026-11-06)

**Project-Based Vouchers, Housing Authority of the County of San Mateo (HACSM, Moving to Work agency)**
- Agency: Housing Authority of the County of San Mateo, a division of the Department of Housing, 264 Harbor Blvd, Belmont, 650-802-3300; housing@smchousing.org
- Type: other
- Typical award: HACSM assists about 4,600 households and project-bases 1,930 vouchers (FY 2027 MTW Plan), with 36 new PBVs planned for 493 Eastmoor Avenue in Daly City (72 units). As an MTW agency since 1998 HACSM may project-base up to 40% of budget authority (raised from 35% in FY 2021) and awards PBVs through periodic RFPs: the last offered 200 Section 8 PBVs and 35 HUD-VASH PBVs for new construction (released Dec 2022, due Dec 30, 2022, awards Jan 2023), with at least 25% of PBVs as supportive housing units, 50% on two- and three-bedroom units, and a per-project cap of about 50% of units (waivable for supportive housing). In Jan 2025 DOH told Homekey+ applicants no PBVs were available. HACSM also provides HAP contracts up to 20 years and the County Housing Voucher Program (local funds) for Homekey sites such as Casa Esperanza.
- AMI requirement: Households at or below 50% AMI at admission with ELI targeting; supportive housing units for homeless and special needs households referred through Coordinated Entry; new construction only in the last RFP; 20-year HAP contracts with extensions.
- Cycle: rolling (next: No PBV RFP open as of Nov 2026 and none since Dec 2022; the AHF NOFA states applications may not assume PBVs without an existing HACSM award letter. Watch the DOH NOFAs, Bids and Proposals page and the annual MTW Plan (FY 2027 plan posted 2026) for the next solicitation. HACSM covers the entire county; no city in San Mateo County runs its own housing authority.)
- Layering notes: HACSM is the operating subsidy partner for every County-funded PSH deal and uses MTW flexibility to award PBVs in bulk (1,930 outstanding), but supply is tight and awards come through RFPs rather than the AHF NOFA. A HAP contract is not a prevailing wage trigger; Davis-Bacon applies to PBV new construction or rehab of nine or more contract units. HACSM also recycles MTW HAP reserves into the Affordable Housing Fund (separate record). Sources opened: 2022 RFP page and PDF, FY 2027 MTW Annual Plan, Homekey+ RFP Q&A.

**San Mateo County Affordable Housing Fund (AHF) annual NOFA (Measure K, County impact fees, MHSA/BHSA, PLHA, HOME)**
- Agency: San Mateo County Department of Housing (DOH), Housing and Community Development division, 264 Harbor Blvd, Building A, Belmont; Raymond Hodges, Director; applications through OpenGov (procurement.opengov.com/portal/smcgov)
- Type: loan
- Typical award: AHF 14.0 (released April 20, 2026, pre-application meeting by April 30, applications due May 20, 2026): $29,347,311 offered, made up of $24,247,311 Measure K ($19,000,000 new FY 2026-27 plus $5,247,311 recaptured), $100,000 County impact fees (unincorporated projects only) and $5,000,000 MHSA/BHSA. Ten applications sought more than $70,000,000 for 810 units. Board awards Aug 25, 2026: $24,347,311 to six projects totaling 459 units: Sand Hill Rise City, Redwood City $9,389,000 (94 units); Mercy Housing 555 Kelly, Half Moon Bay $6,575,000 (40); Related 1051 Mission, South San Francisco $3,545,414 (158, plus $9,495,420 from AHF 11); MidPen 626 Walnut, San Carlos $3,000,000 (95, County-owned site); Novin 3051 Edison, North Fair Oaks $1,537,897 Measure K and impact fees (70); Habitat Ladera, Portola Valley $300,000 (2 ownership units). AHF 13.0 (NOFA June 2, 2025, due July 3, 2025): $41,146,470 to nine projects on Oct 7, 2025 from $19,000,000 new Measure K, $18,022,198 recaptured Measure K, $824,272 PLHA, $100,000 impact fees, MHSA and HHAP. Since 2013 the AHF has awarded more than $400,000,000 to 63 projects and 4,522 units (2,339 occupied, 588 under construction, 1,595 in predevelopment).
- AMI requirement: Units typically 30% to 60% AMI with a 55-year County regulatory agreement from completion (57 years from recording of the deed of trust); at least 5% of low-income units (or two units) reserved with a preference for people experiencing homelessness at 30% AMI with tenant-based subsidies and referrals held open 60 days; MHSA/BHSA units for behavioral health referrals at 30% AMI with PBVs or 20% AMI without; studio and one-bedroom rents assumed at no more than 50% AMI and larger units at 60% AMI.
- Cycle: annual NOFA (next: The DOH funding page lists the next Affordable Housing Development NOFA for fall 2027; AHF 14 closed in May 2026 and its awards were approved Aug 25, 2026. Recaptured funds are offered between rounds through an over-the-counter process (NOFA Appendix C). Pre-application meetings are mandatory and applications require third-party commitments of at least the lesser of $1,000,000 or $20,000 per unit.)
- Layering notes: The Peninsula's main gap source: about $19,000,000 of new Measure K sales tax a year plus recaptured funds, MHSA/BHSA capital, HACSM Moving to Work money and whatever HOME and PLHA the County holds, all run through one annual NOFA. Terms (Appendix D): 3% simple interest from certificate of occupancy, 55-year term, annual payments of at least 50% of residual receipts to the County (two-thirds pooled pro rata when other public soft lenders share), deferred developer fee paid only from the borrower share, DOH will not cut its rate unless the host city and state lenders do the same. Measure K and impact fees do not trigger Davis-Bacon, but the application requires a state prevailing wage determination and all projects must comply with the County Living Wage Ordinance, so budget prevailing wage. Awards are explicitly sized to make 4% and 9% tax credit, AHSC and Homekey+ applications competitive and ranked on readiness. The NOFA does not award PBVs; HACSM must issue its own commitment letter. Documents opened: AHF 14 NOFA PDF and Appendix D underwriting guidelines, the July 29, 2026 HCDC hearing deck, and Board items 25-838 and 26-679 via the Legistar API.
- Source: https://www.smcgov.org/housing/ahf14-nofa
- Confidence: verified (researched 2026-11-06)

**Tax-exempt multifamily bonds: County TEFRA approvals for CMFA, CSCDA and CEDA issuances (County not an active issuer)**
- Agency: San Mateo County Board of Supervisors with the County Attorney (TEFRA hearings); bonds issued by the California Municipal Finance Authority, California Statewide Communities Development Authority or California Enterprise Development Authority
- Type: bond
- Typical award: The County is a member of CMFA, CSCDA and CEDA and holds the required TEFRA hearings for projects in the unincorporated area or where it is the member jurisdiction: CMFA bonds up to $11,000,000 for Mercy Housing's 42-unit 903 Oceana Boulevard rehabilitation in Pacifica (April 7, 2026), plus CMFA (May 6, 2025), CEDA and CSCDA (June 10, 2025) hearings. CMFA shares part of its issuance fee with the County. No County-issued multifamily housing revenue bonds were found in 2025 or 2026 Board records.
- AMI requirement: CDLAC and Section 142(d) minimums (20% at 50% AMI or 40% at 60% AMI) under the JPA issuer's regulatory agreement; County loans in the same project add 55-year County restrictions.
- Cycle: rolling (next: Schedule the TEFRA hearing with the County Attorney's office at least seven days after newspaper notice and before the CDLAC application; the Board hears these on consent. For projects inside cities, the city holds the hearing.)
- Layering notes: Expect to use CMFA or CSCDA as issuer in San Mateo County; the County's role is the TEFRA approval and a small fee share, with no County credit or staff involvement. Bonds alone do not trigger state prevailing wage; AHF, HOME or HACSM money in the deal does. Board item 26-255 read through the Legistar API.

**Welfare Exemption (property tax), San Mateo County Assessor-County Clerk-Recorder**
- Agency: San Mateo County Assessor-County Clerk-Recorder and Elections (ACRE), Mark Church, Assessor; 555 County Center, Redwood City; 650-363-4500; institutional exemptions unit via smcacre.gov contact page
- Type: tax abatement
- Typical award: Full or partial exemption of property tax on units occupied by households at or below 80% AMI under Revenue and Taxation Code 214(g); worth roughly 1.1% or more of assessed value a year depending on the tax rate area. ACRE posts the full BOE-267 series (267, 267-L, L1, L2, L3, L4, H, O, R and income worksheets) and notes the annual BOE-267-A is issued by the office rather than downloaded.
- AMI requirement: Nonprofit or LP with eligible nonprofit managing general partner holding a BOE Organizational Clearance Certificate (plus a Supplemental Clearance Certificate for LP low-income housing); units restricted by recorded regulatory agreement or occupied by households at or below 80% AMI; BOE-267 first filing and annual supplemental affidavits by Feb 15 (late claims receive a reduced exemption under Rev. and Tax. Code 270).
- Cycle: rolling (next: 2027-02-15 (annual claim deadline for the 2027-28 roll). File the first claim on acquisition so the construction period is covered.)
- Layering notes: Standard in every tax credit operating budget; San Mateo's high assessed values make this the largest operating subsidy most projects receive. ACRE's institutional exemptions and forms pages (opened) list forms and the OCC and SCC requirements but no local deadline text or direct phone; the BOE county contacts page gives the main number.
- Source: https://smcacre.gov/assessor/institutional-exemptions-forms

**Winter NOFA: HOME Consortium, Urban County CDBG, ESG and PLHA (annual federal and state funds round)**
- Agency: San Mateo County Department of Housing, Housing and Community Development division, as HOME Consortium lead and Urban County CDBG grantee
- Type: loan
- Typical award: FY 2026-27 Winter NOFA (issued Dec 2, 2025, applications due Jan 15, 2026, HCDC hearing March 12, Board April 21, 2026) sources: CDBG $2,315,528 plus $347,644 program income and returned funds; HOME $1,485,482 plus $1,428,857 program income and returned funds; federal ESG $208,430; state ESG $165,356; PLHA $0 (held pending housing element compliance); City of East Palo Alto minor home repair $125,000; total $6,076,297. Uses: $2,000,000 HOME for new affordable housing and preservation, $717,035 HOME CHDO set-aside left unallocated for an over-the-counter award, $620,815 CDBG rehab and public facilities, $493,716 Section 108 loan repayment (Trestle Glen). The December 2025 notice estimated about $5,000,000 in total CDBG, HOME and related funds; a separate capital projects guideline listed about $3,317,010 CDBG for capital and $1,738,713 for community development based on FY 2025-26 levels.
- AMI requirement: HOME: households at or below 80% AMI at HOME rents, 55-year County regulatory agreement (HOME units become AHF-restricted units for the balance of the 55 years when the HOME period is shorter); CDBG: low and moderate income benefit; County loan terms as in the AHF underwriting guidelines.
- Cycle: annual NOFA (next: FY 2027-28 Winter NOFA to be released Dec 1, 2026 after the HCDC needs hearing on Oct 22, 2026; applications are typically due mid-January with Board approval in April. Housing capital applicants should also watch the fall AHF round.)
- Layering notes: Urban County: unincorporated area plus Atherton, Belmont, Brisbane, Burlingame, Colma, East Palo Alto, Foster City, Half Moon Bay, Hillsborough, Menlo Park, Millbrae, Pacifica, Portola Valley, San Bruno, San Carlos and Woodside. HOME Consortium: the Urban County plus Redwood City, San Mateo and South San Francisco (Daly City is its own entitlement, Pass 3). Federal money is small next to Measure K, so HOME usually appears as a $1,000,000 to $2,000,000 piece inside an AHF-funded project. Davis-Bacon applies to HOME projects with 12 or more assisted units and CDBG projects with eight or more; County loans also carry state prevailing wage and the County Living Wage Ordinance. ### Santa Clara County

**2016 Measure A Affordable Housing Bond (Housing Bond)**
- Agency: County of Santa Clara Office of Supportive Housing (OSH), Housing and Community Development Division
- Type: loan
- Typical award: $950 million general obligation bond approved November 8, 2016. As of October 2026 the Board had committed $879.2 million; 65 multifamily rental developments in 12 cities received about $747 million ($714.3 million in Supportive Housing Development Program rounds 1 through 14 and off-cycle awards plus $11.9 million acquisition loans and $90.5 million County acquisitions). Individual commitments range from $1.0 million (The Veranda, Cupertino, 19 units) to $42.3 million (Mosaic Court, Milpitas, 134 units); Gateway Tower (220 units, San Jose) revised January 13, 2026 to $25,560,000, about $116,182 per unit.
- AMI requirement: Board goals by category: PSH for persons with disabling conditions, rapid rehousing units, ELI (30% AMI) and VLI (50% AMI) units, plus 300 mixed-income units and homeownership. 4,800 rental unit goal exceeded (5,255 goal units approved, 109%). Long-term County regulatory agreement recorded on each project.
- Cycle: closed/inactive (next: No new application round. As of October 2026 the remaining $67.8 million is reserved for three developments on County-owned land and one affordable homeownership development (Branham Station, VTA TOD). About $6.4 million of program-generated income is available to recommit to multifamily rental projects.)
- Layering notes: santaclaracounty.gov subdomains (osh, asr, bhsd, news, files) returned HTTP 403 to automated access on 2026-11-07; records were built from the Board of Supervisors IQM2 legislative files (sccgov.iqm2.com), the County Housing Element, Santa Clara County Housing Authority documents, HCD and BOE pages. The County's November 3, 2026 implementation report (first annual report, year 10 of a 10-year plan) states the bond is nearly fully deployed: 65 approved rental developments with 6,846 units (2,693 supportive), 38 in operation, 17 under construction, four fully financed and six in predevelopment; $30.5 million in program-generated income received, $23.5 million recommitted. Measure A averaged about $6 of outside funding per $1 of County bond money and has been the standard local soft source behind 4% and 9% tax credit deals in Santa Clara County; in 2025, 11 County-funded projects won tax credit awards. Awards are made through the over-the-counter Supportive Housing Development Fund NOFA (see separate record) and paired with SCCHA project-based vouchers (3,000 plus PBVs deployed). Do not confuse with the November 4, 2025 Measure A, a five-eighths cent County sales tax for safety-net services that is not a housing fund. The Board is studying a future housing fund (June 2, 2026 report) but no successor measure is on the November 2026 ballot; the statewide $10 billion housing bond (AB 736/SB 417) is the near-term pipeline source. County loans require state prevailing wage as public funds.

- Confidence: verified (researched 2026-11-07)

**Continuum of Care CA-500 (San Jose/Santa Clara City and County) and HHAP funding**
- Agency: County of Santa Clara Office of Supportive Housing (OSH) as CoC lead and collaborative applicant; City of San Jose and the CoC are co-applicants for HHAP
- Type: grant
- Typical award: HHAP Round 6 allocations (HCD, based on the 2024 PIT count): Santa Clara County $11,860,491.01; San Jose/Santa Clara City and County CoC $12,667,208.31; City of San Jose $25,329,964.46. The County's delegated HHAP-6 authority is $24,528,000 (County plus CoC shares); the state notified the region of its award March 17, 2026. The County is also administering about $10 million HHAP-2, $28 million HHAP-3, $25.8 million HHAP-4 and $27.9 million HHAP-5. HUD CoC program grants to the County total about $35.1 million for 23 renewals (2026-27) and the region receives roughly $48 million a year; the 2026 CoC competition application authority is up to $38.1 million for 24 grants.
- AMI requirement: Households experiencing homelessness referred through coordinated entry; Housing First required by the regional MOU; at least 10 percent of HHAP for youth.
- Cycle: annual NOFA (next: HHAP-6 obligation and expenditure deadlines run through June 30, 2030 under the amended agreement. HUD vacated its 2026 CoC NOFO after federal litigation; the County delegated authority to apply for up to 24 CoC grants when the competition reopens.)

HUD's proposed 30 percent cap on permanent housing in the 2026 CoC round puts about 1,600 PSH households at risk per OSH (October 2025 coverage). ### Santa Cruz County

**Affordable Housing Impact Fee (AHIF): exemption for deed-restricted affordable units and fee fund**
- Agency: Santa Cruz County Community Development and Infrastructure, Planning Division, Housing Section
- Type: fee waiver
- Typical award: Current rates (2026 Affordable Housing Guidelines, Chapter V): market-rate rental units $2 per habitable square foot (ADUs of 750 square feet or less exempt); ownership projects of fewer than seven units $2 to $15 per square foot scaled by unit size and project size (5 or more homes $15 per square foot at all sizes); non-residential $3 per net new square foot ($1 for agricultural barns). Deed-restricted affordable rental units, Measure J units and subsidized housing are exempt, and density bonus projects that include affordable rental units may qualify for a waiver of the fee on the market-rate units. Fees fund the AHIF account used in the County housing NOFA. The September 1, 2026 KMA nexus study supports maximum fees of $17.30 to $24.50 per square foot, far above current rates.
- AMI requirement: Exemption applies to units deed-restricted to lower income households; waiver on mixed-income projects negotiated with Housing staff in exchange for a set number of affordable rental units.
- Cycle: rolling (next: Fees are due at building permit (Planning Director may defer to occupancy for hardship). Watch for a Board fee update in 2027 following the 2026 nexus and feasibility studies.)
- Layering notes: Santa Cruz County housing programs sit in the Community Development and Infrastructure Department (CDI) Planning Division, Housing Section (HousingProgramsInfo@santacruzcountyCA.gov, (831) 454-2332), which runs the Measure J inclusionary program, the Affordable Housing Impact Fee, LMIHAF, PLHA and the County housing NOFA; the Human Services Department's Housing for Health Division (H4H, the CoC CA-508 lead) runs HHAP, Homekey and homeless programs; Behavioral Health holds BHSA; and the Housing Authority of the County of Santa Cruz (HACSC) supplies vouchers. The County is a non-entitlement jurisdiction for CDBG and HOME. County programs apply only to the unincorporated area (about half the population); Santa Cruz, Watsonville, Capitola and Scotts Valley run their own programs (Pass 3). cdi.santacruzcountyca.gov, santacruzcountyca.gov PDFs, santacruzhealth.org and housingforhealthpartnership.org open normally; the Board's IQM2 portal (santacruzcountyca.iqm2.com) renders by script and could not be listed, so Board items were taken from NOFA appendices and press coverage. The AHIF is both a cost the affordable developer avoids (exempt units) and the source of part of the County NOFA money; at $2 per square foot on rentals it raises little, which is why the NOFA is capped at $500,000 per award. Other County development fees (roadside, parks, drainage) are not waived for affordable projects in the guidelines. Source is the 2026 Affordable Housing Guidelines PDF (August 2026 revision).

**Density bonus, enhanced density bonus and priority processing (County Code Chapters 17.12 and 17.10.040)**
- Agency: Santa Cruz County Community Development and Infrastructure, Planning Division
- Type: density bonus
- Typical award: State density bonus law implemented in Chapter 17.12 (last amended Ordinance 5286, 2018) with a County enhanced density bonus (Section 17.12.065) above the regular 35% state bonus: projects providing at least 21% low income units earn 36.5% rising 1.5 points per percentage point to a 50% maximum bonus at 30% low income units. Priority processing under Section 17.10.040 for standard-density projects with 25% or more affordable units and for density bonus projects with 35% or more affordable units.
- AMI requirement: Government Code 65915 thresholds (5% very low, 10% low, senior, moderate for-sale) with 55-year recorded restrictions; enhanced bonus requires 21% or more low income units.
- Cycle: rolling (next: Requested with the development application; 2024 and 2025 state law changes (AB 2694, AB 1287) apply directly even where the 2018 chapter text lags.)
- Layering notes: Santa Cruz County housing programs sit in the Community Development and Infrastructure Department (CDI) Planning Division, Housing Section (HousingProgramsInfo@santacruzcountyCA.gov, (831) 454-2332), which runs the Measure J inclusionary program, the Affordable Housing Impact Fee, LMIHAF, PLHA and the County housing NOFA; the Human Services Department's Housing for Health Division (H4H, the CoC CA-508 lead) runs HHAP, Homekey and homeless programs; Behavioral Health holds BHSA; and the Housing Authority of the County of Santa Cruz (HACSC) supplies vouchers. The County is a non-entitlement jurisdiction for CDBG and HOME. County programs apply only to the unincorporated area (about half the population); Santa Cruz, Watsonville, Capitola and Scotts Valley run their own programs (Pass 3). cdi.santacruzcountyca.gov, santacruzcountyca.gov PDFs, santacruzhealth.org and housingforhealthpartnership.org open normally; the Board's IQM2 portal (santacruzcountyca.iqm2.com) renders by script and could not be listed, so Board items were taken from NOFA appendices and press coverage. The enhanced bonus to 50% is a real local incentive for mixed-income projects in the urban unincorporated area (Live Oak, Soquel, Aptos) where zoning density is low; 100% affordable projects rely on state law's unlimited bonus near transit. Source is Chapter 17.12 text on gocodebook.com.
- Source: https://gocodebook.com/library/us/ca/santa-cruz-county-planning/title-17/chapter-17.12-density-bonus

**Measure J inclusionary housing program (County Code Chapter 17.10)**
- Agency: Santa Cruz County Community Development and Infrastructure, Planning Division, Housing Section
- Type: other
- Typical award: Requirement dating from the 1978 Measure J initiative: ownership projects of seven or more units provide 15% of units as affordable for-sale homes (Section 17.10.030); alternatives are payment of the Affordable Housing Impact Fee at the unified fee schedule rate (17.10.034), the existing unit conversion program (17.10.037), a financial contribution to a nonprofit off-site project that yields more units than required (17.10.036), or 15% on-site rental units affordable to low income households for the life of the units (17.10.039). Rental projects pay the impact fee unless they provide the 15% rental units. Fees are deposited in the Measure J trust fund (17.10.087). The 2026 Affordable Housing Guidelines (August 2026) govern pricing, resale and eligibility.
- AMI requirement: For-sale units priced for moderate and lower income buyers under County guidelines with resale restrictions in perpetuity; rental alternative units at low income rents in perpetuity under a recorded rent regulatory agreement.
- Cycle: rolling (next: Applies with each entitlement. The County released a Keyser Marston residential nexus study on September 1, 2026 and an inclusionary feasibility study; the Housing Advisory Commission's 2026-27 work program includes recommendations on the Affordable Housing Impact Fee, so fee or percentage changes may come to the Board in 2027.)

**HOME and CDBG, Solano County (state non-entitlement status; 2024 CDBG planning grants)**
- Agency: California HCD state CDBG and HOME programs; Solano County Department of Resource Management as applicant
- Type: grant
- Typical award: No county HOME or CDBG entitlement. State CDBG 2024 awards to the County of Solano: $300,000 Affordable Housing Development Site Feasibility Study and $300,000 Pocket/Cottage Housing Feasibility Study (Resolution 2024-213 of Dec 10, 2024; award Sept 3, 2025; $559,909 contract with Lisa Wise Consulting approved May 5, 2026, through June 30, 2028). No County of Solano award appears in HCD's HOME 2022-2023 awardee list. Fairfield, Vacaville and Vallejo are HUD entitlements (Pass 3).

- Cycle: annual NOFA (next: Follow HCD state HOME and CDBG NOFAs. The County's feasibility studies run May 2026 to August 2027 (public workshop Aug 27, 2026, survey closed Sept 7, 2026) and will identify five potential housing areas in the unincorporated county; a developer solicitation could follow in 2027-2028.)
- Layering notes: Negative finding for capital: the County has no HOME or CDBG construction pipeline of its own. The CDBG-funded studies matter because they are the County's first step toward sponsoring affordable multifamily or cottage housing on unincorporated sites under the 2023-2031 Housing Element (adopted Feb 6, 2024). A developer wanting state HOME in Dixon, Rio Vista or the unincorporated area needs the County or city to apply as grantee. HOME and CDBG carry Davis-Bacon (CDBG 8+ units, HOME 12+ units) and state prevailing wage.

- Type: grant

Earlier: 2020 award $128,234; 2023 allocation $560,188 (Five-Year Plan amendment affirmed by the Board July 23, 2024). Cities of Fairfield ($390,910 in 2021), Vacaville and Vallejo ($505,369 in 2021) receive their own entitlement shares (Pass 3).
- AMI requirement: PLHA statute: rental assistance at or below 60% AMI unless the plan targets up to 120% AMI (150% in high-cost areas); 55-year covenant for rental development. County five-year plan governs uses.
- Cycle: annual NOFA (next: HCD releases formula allocations annually; the County files a plan amendment and resolution each round (last affirmed July 23, 2024). No County NOFA to developers found. The 2020 Housing Authority MTW plan proposed using about $25,000 a year of County PLHA for down payment assistance to FSS graduates.)
- Layering notes: About $570,000 to $600,000 a year, more than Napa or Sonoma's county share, but the County has not published how it programs the money. Ask the County Administrator's Office whether the 2024-2028 plan funds multifamily gap loans, ADUs or homeless services before counting it. State funds, so prevailing wage applies to construction.
- Source: https://www.hcd.ca.gov/sites/default/files/docs/grants-and-funding/plha/2024-2028-plha-formula-allocation-nofa.pdf
- Confidence: verified (researched 2026-11-06)

**Project-Based Vouchers, Solano County Housing Authority (Dixon, Rio Vista and unincorporated area)**
- Agency: Solano County Housing Authority (SCHA), administered under contract by the City of Vacaville Housing Authority, 40 Eldridge Ave Suite 2, Vacaville, 707-449-5675
- Type: other
- Typical award: HCV-only agency authorized for 290 vouchers in its 2020 Moving to Work plan (255 leased; 20 HUD-VASH, 13 Mainstream), listed at 372 vouchers by a 2024 directory. The 2020 MTW plan set aside up to 60 vouchers for project-basing. PBV waitlists opened for Silvey Villa senior units in Dixon (Aug 2024), new PBV lists on Jan 7, 2025, and eight units at Prospera at Homestead, Dixon (June 10, 2025).
- AMI requirement: Households at or below 50% AMI (75% of admissions at 30% AMI); PBV units limited to 25% of a building unless serving elderly, disabled or supportive services households.
- Cycle: rolling (next: No PBV RFP found. Owner proposals go to the Vacaville Housing Authority staff who run SCHA; the Vacaville Housing Authority's own Dec 2024 RFP awarded 85 PBVs to the Elan Apartments in Vacaville (city program, Pass 3).)
- Layering notes: SCHA covers only Dixon, Rio Vista and the unincorporated county; Fairfield, Vacaville, Vallejo, Suisun City and Benicia have their own housing authorities (Pass 3). Small voucher pool, so PBV awards run 8 to 20 units per project, typically on Dixon deals that also take County Housing Trust Fund money. SCHA is a Moving to Work agency (2020 plan), which allows local PBV flexibilities. PBVs alone do not trigger state prevailing wage; Davis-Bacon applies to PBV new construction or rehab of 9 or more contract units. Vacaville's housing pages (cityofvacaville.gov) returned 403 to automated access; the MTW plan on solano.legistar.com is the opened source.
- Source: https://solano.legistar.com/gateway.aspx?M=F&ID=68d29896-8ed9-449f-b711-96eb02a7dc29.pdf

**Public facilities fee waiver or deferral for affordable housing (none adopted, Solano County)**
- Agency: Solano County Department of Resource Management (County Code Chapter 11, Article X public facilities fees)
- Type: fee waiver
- Typical award: None. In Jan 2024 The Hampstead Companies asked the Board to waive $672,829 in public facilities fees for Prospera at Homestead, which would have cut the Housing Trust Fund loan to $2,500,000; the Board did not act and funded the full $3,200,000 loan instead.
- AMI requirement: Not applicable.
- Cycle: closed/inactive (next: No waiver or deferral program exists; requests are handled case by case through the Board.)
- Layering notes: Negative finding. Budget the County's public facilities fees in full for unincorporated and Dixon deals and ask for a Housing Trust Fund loan instead. If a waiver were granted it would count as public funds under Labor Code 1720(b)(4). City fee waivers and deferrals are Pass 3.
