- Typical award: Requirement, not a subsidy. Applies to subdivisions of five or more parcels or condominiums and rental projects of five or more units. Ownership projects of 5 to 19 units pay the in-lieu fee ($12,000 per unit per the Housing Element, set by resolution) for every unit. Ownership projects of 20 or more units and rental projects of five or more units provide either 20% of units affordable to moderate income households (120% AMI) or 10% affordable to low income households (80% AMI), restricted 55 years; projects with 10 or more inclusionary units must make 10% of them three bedroom. Alternatives with a Commission or Council infeasibility finding: in-lieu fee, land dedication, off site units, or equivalent methods; the Council may waive or reduce the obligation for economic hardship and may assist developers with subsidies or design flexibility (17.08.020(H)).
- AMI requirement: 20% moderate or 10% low income, 55-year recorded affordable housing agreement; ADUs do not count toward the requirement; off site units do not count toward a receiving site's density bonus.
- Cycle: rolling (next: Applies at the first approval through an affordable housing plan; agreement recorded with the final map or before building permit. Ordinance 780 (adopted December 9, 2025 as the Housing Element implementation package) amended 17.08.010 to add special needs groups and set a citywide minimum density of 50% of the maximum (17.03.110).)
- Layering notes: The 20% moderate option is the loosest inclusionary standard in the county and lets market rate rental projects avoid low income units entirely; a developer wanting state density bonus concessions must instead hit the 65915 thresholds, and inclusionary units count toward the bonus. 100% affordable projects satisfy the requirement and generate no fee. In-lieu revenue flows to the Affordable Housing Fund record above. Code text read on ecode360 (source_url); the December 9, 2025 second reading staff report and ordinance were opened on the City's CivicWeb host.
- Source: https://ecode360.com/47985322
- Confidence: verified (researched 2026-11-08)

**Calistoga Measure D 1% Transient Occupancy Tax for affordable and workforce housing (Resolution 2018-072, effective January 1, 2019)**
- Agency: City of Calistoga Administrative Services Department; City Council allocates
- Type: grant
- Typical award: Special tax of 1% on hotel stays (TOT 12% to 13%) held in a separate account and restricted to affordable and workforce housing programs and services, including land acquisition and donation, building acquisition, rehabilitation and demolition, housing construction, mobile home preservation, housing subsidies and preservation of expiring subsidies. Campaign estimate about $512,325 a year; an annual Government Code 50075.3 report is required. Uses: backfill of deferred fees for the Lincoln Avenue Apartments (78 units) and the proposed ADU Fee Assistance Program (annual transfer subject to appropriation). Council members questioned slow disbursement in 2024, so unspent balance is likely several million dollars; the balance was not found in a text document this pass.
- AMI requirement: Affordable and workforce housing; the City applies it to households up to 120% AMI for development and, for the ADU program, rentals at or below 160% AMI with a 10-year deed restriction.
- Cycle: rolling (next: No NOFA; allocated by City Council with the annual budget (FY 2026-27 budget adopted June 2026) and by resolution for specific projects. Confirm the fund balance with Administrative Services (707-942-2807).)
- Layering notes: Measure D is Calistoga's most flexible housing money (no nexus limits) and the natural source for moderate income units, fee backfill and land purchase (Council FY 2025-26 priorities include developing the City owned Earl and Eddy parcels). Combine with the Affordable Housing Fund for lower income units and the County fund. Parallel measures exist in Napa (F), St. Helena (E) and the County (I), each separate. Sources opened: October 6, 2026 ADU Fee Assistance staff report on CivicWeb (source_url, cites Resolution 2018-072 and the Measure D use restriction) and the Measure D City Attorney impartial analysis PDF (retrieved from calistogaca.gov via WebFetch because the site blocks scripts).
- Source: https://calistoga.civicweb.net/document/117944/
- Confidence: verified (researched 2026-11-08)

### City of Concord

**Concord Affordable Housing Fund and Concord Housing Fund (Housing Successor Low and Moderate Income Housing Asset Fund, SB 341 report FY 2024/25)**
- Agency: City of Concord Housing and Community Services Division (Housing Successor to the former Concord Redevelopment Agency)
- Type: loan
- Typical award: Housing Successor fund at June 30, 2025: available cash $3,063,558; FY 2024/25 deposits $1,020,949 (including a $615,049 Pavilion loan repayment and $222,705 in loan payoffs); FY 2024/25 expenditures $596,214 (mostly $334,957 in first-time homebuyer loans; no multifamily loan issued); housing loans receivable $33.9 million. The 2023 Housing Element reported a combined Housing Trust Fund balance of about $6.2 million including inclusionary in-lieu fees. - AMI requirement: Housing Successor funds must follow Health and Safety Code 34176.1: at least 30% to rental housing for households at or below 30% AMI, no more than 20% for 60% to 80% AMI, balance at or below 60% AMI; the City's five-year extremely-low-income test (July 2020 to June 2025) showed 0% spent on ELI rental housing, so the next multifamily award is likely to be steered to ELI units. City-funded projects carry long-term regulatory agreements (Rick Judd Commons is 55 years).

- Layering notes: Concord's own fund is modest (about $3 million liquid in the successor fund plus in-lieu balances) and is best used as the local match that unlocks County HOME, CDBG-Housing and Measure X awards (county records: Contra Costa County Affordable Housing Program, Measure X Housing Fund). Lakeside Recapitalization (RCD, Concord) received $2 million County HOME in May 2026 without City funds, showing County money can lead. The City's Resources for Housing Developers page points developers first to County Measure X and HCD. Gap order for a Concord deal: 4% credits and bonds, County HOME or Measure X, then a City successor-fund loan sized to the ELI set-aside, plus fee deferral under CDC 18.185.040(G). The OnBase agenda portal is JavaScript-only, so 2025 and 2026 council items could not be scanned for a NOFA; status taken from the Toolkit page (https://www.cityofconcord.org/1174/Affordable-Housing-Toolkit) and the SB 341 report (source_url).

**Concord Affordable Housing Incentive Program (CDC 18.185.060), Density Bonus Program (CDC 18.185.050) and Transit Station Overlay density increase**
- Agency: City of Concord Community Development Department, Planning Division (zoning@cityofconcord.org, 925-671-3152)
- Type: density bonus
- Typical award: Regulatory incentive, not a cash subsidy. Local alternative to state density bonus law for projects with at least 40% affordable units on parcels of 10,000 square feet or more in RM, RH, CO, NC, CMX, DMX and DP districts: RM density rises from 32 to about 45 units per acre (1 unit per 970 square feet, a 40% bonus), RH from 100 to about 145 units per acre (45% bonus), NC from 24 to about 33 units per acre plus FAR increases; reduced parking and other standard modifications; bonuses under 18.185.060 are not additive with 18.185.050. Separately, the Transit Station Overlay District grants a 25% density and floor area increase (Housing Element program to make it by right with objective standards). State-law density bonuses (Gov. Code 65915) are processed by the Community Development Department under 18.185.050; written findings are required to deny; an affordable housing agreement is recorded before building permit.
- AMI requirement: 18.185.060 rental eligibility: at least 20% of units at very low income plus another 20% at low or very low income (40% total); for-sale: 20% at low or very low plus 20% at up to 100% AMI. 18.185.050 follows state density bonus thresholds.
- Cycle: rolling (next: Applies at entitlement; no deadline. Concord completed its AFFH rezoning (at least 1,000 lower-income units of capacity in higher-resource areas) in March 2026 and allows multifamily by right in commercial and mixed-use districts when objective design standards are met.)
- Layering notes: The 40% affordability threshold for the local incentive program is high, so most mixed-income projects use state density bonus law instead; 100% affordable projects (which qualify for an 80% state bonus or unlimited density near transit) get the most value from the local program's FAR and parking relief in downtown districts. No City fee waiver program exists; fee deferral to first occupancy is available under 18.185.040(G) by affordable housing agreement. Pair with the County's conduit bond issuer and HACCC project-based vouchers (county records). codepublishing.com returned 403; chapter text read on the zoneomics mirror (source_url) and confirmed against the City's Affordable Housing Toolkit page.
- Source: https://www.zoneomics.com/code/concord-CA/chapter_4

**Concord Inclusionary Housing Ordinance (Concord Development Code Chapter 18.185.040, Ord. 24-1) and in-lieu fee (Fees and Charges Schedule, Res. 26-6042.1)**
- Agency: City of Concord Housing and Community Services Division (Sophia Huckabay, Housing Manager, 925-671-3387) with the Planning Division
- Type: other
- Typical award: Requirement, not a subsidy. Projects of 5 or more units: ownership projects 15% inclusionary (7.5% low, 7.5% moderate); rental projects 6% inclusionary (1% very low, 1% low, 4% moderate), with a fixed rotation order for each inclusionary unit. In-lieu fee effective July 1, 2026 (adjusted annually by a construction cost index): $20.13 per gross square foot of market-rate development for ownership projects and $15.10 per gross square foot for rental projects of 10 or more units; fractional-unit fee $256,497 x fractional unit (ownership) and $174,160 x fractional unit (rental). Rental projects may pay the fee for the whole obligation; ownership projects may pay only for fractional units or for 5 to 9 unit projects. In the five years before the 2023 Housing Element the City collected only about $170,000 in in-lieu fees.
- AMI requirement: Rental inclusionary units restricted 55 years and ownership units 45 years under a recorded Affordable Housing Agreement; density bonus units meeting the table income levels count toward the inclusionary requirement; projects of 1 to 4 units, replacement of units lost to natural disaster, and office-to-residential conversions of buildings commercial for at least 5 years are exempt.
- Cycle: rolling (next: Applies at entitlement; fee rate in effect at building permit. Fee schedule last adopted April 28, 2026 (Res. 26-6042.1) effective July 1, 2026; the schedule is readopted each spring. Housing Element Program 12.4 called for a fee update by July 2024, which produced the March 14, 2024 fee basis now indexed annually.)
- Layering notes: Low rental percentage (6%) and a relatively low rental in-lieu fee ($15.10 per square foot) mean most Concord apartment projects either build a handful of moderate-income units or pay the fee; this is why the City's inclusionary fund is small relative to Walnut Creek's. In-lieu revenue goes to a restricted fund alongside the Concord Housing Fund (see the Concord Affordable Housing Fund record). Chapter 18.185.040(G) also lets the City grant development incentives, including deferral of development fees until first occupancy (approved by the City Manager) and expedited processing, when an affordable housing agreement is signed. County Chapter 822-4 inclusionary ordinance does not apply inside Concord. codepublishing.com (the City's code host) returns 403 to automated access; chapter text was read on the zoneomics mirror (https://www.zoneomics.com/code/concord-CA/chapter_4) and the City's 2024 Inclusionary Housing Ordinance Summary Sheet (https://www.cityofconcord.org/DocumentCenter/View/13659). Fee amounts were read from the adopted July 1, 2026 fee schedule (source_url).
- Source: https://www.cityofconcord.org/DocumentCenter/View/15683/Fees-and-Charges-ScheduleJuly-1-2026Res-No-26-60421
- Confidence: verified (researched 2026-11-08)

- Agency: City of Concord Housing and Community Services Division and Planning Division (surplus land inventory, Housing Element sites program)
- Type: other

City-owned surplus sites declared May 24, 2022: Concord Town Center II, 1765 Galindo Street, 3.1 vacant acres zoned DMX, Housing Element site for 309 lower-income units and an MTC Priority Site; the City issued an RFP in January 2025 and as of November 2025 is negotiating with a selected developer for sale and entitlement. ### City of Davis

**Affordable Housing Ordinance (Davis Municipal Code Article 18.05, Ordinance 2646) and Rental Housing Inclusionary Guidelines (Resolution 25-002, in-lieu fee)**
- Agency: City of Davis Social Services and Housing Department, Affordable Housing Manager Iris Grace and Director Dana Bailey; Community Development Department for entitlements
- Type: density bonus
- Typical award: Requirement, not a subsidy. Rental projects of 20 or more units must provide 15% affordable units, half low income and half very low income (ordinance adopted July 2023). Resolution 25-002 (adopted January 7, 2025, 4 to 1) set the in-lieu fee for non-discretionary rental projects at $250,000 per required affordable unit and $125,000 for a fractional unit when the whole units are built on site. Staff had proposed $608,000 per unit (cost of the most recent all-affordable project) and the Council rejected $369,000. The fee is indexed annually by the construction cost index with a one-time payment or a multi-year option at a 10-year net present value. Ownership projects have separate land dedication and in-lieu options approved case by case.
- AMI requirement: 15% of rental units (7.5% low income at 80% AMI and 7.5% very low income at 50% AMI) with long-term covenants; alternatives (in-lieu fee, land dedication, Project Individualized Plan) must deliver equivalent affordability value and discretionary projects need Council approval of the alternative.
- Cycle: rolling (next: None (ordinance). Council on December 16, 2025 directed staff to amend the land dedication option as soon as possible; an amendment requiring land dedicators to also provide funding was introduced in March 2026 per local coverage. A broader revision of the ownership inclusionary rules is in progress. Verify current text with the Affordable Housing Manager, (530) 757-5602.)
- Layering notes: The ordinance is the engine behind Davis's two main local tools: in-lieu fees and negotiated contributions flow to the City Housing Trust Fund, and land dedication produces fully improved affordable sites (see the Housing Trust Fund and land dedication records). For a 100% affordable developer this means partnering with a market-rate applicant on a dedicated site, or seeking Housing Trust Fund gap money. Staff's October 21, 2025 informational report found production lagging RHNA and proposed a mandatory financial review when a developer claims infeasibility; Councilmembers asked staff to look at 10% extremely low income in place of part of the 15% requirement. Section 40.27.110 of the zoning code ties Article 18.05 to state density bonus law. Stack with county records: no Yolo County housing trust fund or county NOFA exists; Yolo County Housing project-based vouchers and the state CDBG and HOME competitions are the county-level layers. Access: cityofdavis.org (Akamai) returns 403 to scripts and to WebFetch; the Council minutes on documents.cityofdavis.org open and were used. The Resolution 25-002 text (showpublisheddocument/20364) and the October 21, 2025 staff report could not be opened.

**Affordable housing land dedication sites under Article 18.05 (Village Farms 16-acre dedication, Project Individualized Plan Exhibit E)**
- Agency: City of Davis Community Development Department and Social Services and Housing Department (Council subcommittee negotiates development agreements)
- Type: other
- Typical award: Land, not cash. Village Farms Davis (Development Agreement Exhibit E, approved December 16, 2025 and revised January 13, 2026) dedicates 16 acres to the City for 280 low and very low income units on fully improved sites (no more than 4 parcels, none under 2.5 acres), to be developed with a qualified affordable housing developer selected by the City, with the City to endeavor to add 80 moderate income units. Baseline features now require construction to commence on 100 affordable units before Phase 3 and no permits beyond the first 150 until that starts; the City holds an option after 150 units. Together with the $6 million Housing Trust Fund payment the package is valued by the applicant at over $6 million plus land.
- AMI requirement: 280 low and very low income units (plus up to 80 moderate) on dedicated land; affordability covenants set in the City's developer agreement.
- Cycle: rolling (next: City selection of the affordable developer for the Village Farms sites has not been scheduled; it depends on voter approval of the project (June 2026 Measure J/R/D vote) and on the first land dedication. Watch Council agendas and the Social Services Commission.)
- Layering notes: This is how 100% affordable developers get sites in Davis: the inclusionary ordinance's land dedication option plus Housing Trust Fund money, then compete for 9% credits, MHP, AHSC or HCD Super NOFA money. Vice Mayor Vaitla's December 2025 direction to amend the land dedication option (so dedicators also provide resources) led to a March 2026 ordinance introduction, so later projects should carry cash with the land. Earlier dedications (Cannery, Chiles Ranch, Bretton Woods) produced sites now built or in pipeline. Davis has no city-owned surplus land program beyond these dedications. Pair with Yolo County Housing PBVs and the CoC HHAP money for supportive units.

**CDBG and HOME entitlement allocations (2025-2029 Consolidated Plan, Resolution 25-061) and PLHA formula allocation**
- Agency: City of Davis Social Services and Housing Department, Housing and Grants Management (Director Dana Bailey)
- Type: grant
- Typical award: Davis is a CDBG entitlement city and a HOME participating jurisdiction. Council adopted the 2025-2029 Consolidated Plan and the Program Year One (2025) Annual Action Plan on April 15, 2025 (Resolution 25-061). Local coverage puts year one CDBG plus HOME at about $1.06 million; HOME has historically funded first-time homebuyer loans and rental project gap loans, CDBG funds public services, facilities and the Pathways to Employment and homelessness programs. HCD's 2024-2028 PLHA NOFA lists Davis at about $1.33 million over five years; staff told Council on February 18, 2025 that PLHA would be used for homeownership opportunities.
- AMI requirement: CDBG at or below 80% AMI; HOME at or below 80% AMI with at least 90% of rental assistance at 60% AMI and 20% of units at 50% AMI in projects with 5 or more HOME units.
- Cycle: annual NOFA (next: Program Year 2026-27 Action Plan process runs winter to spring 2027 (public hearing typically April). Confirm amounts and the HOME set-aside with the Grants Management office, (530) 757-5602.)
- Layering notes: Federal money is the only recurring Davis source for rental projects, but the annual HOME amount is small (hundreds of thousands) and competes with homebuyer uses; combine with Housing Trust Fund gap money and state credits. HOME triggers federal Davis-Bacon only at 12 or more HOME-assisted units; state prevailing wage applies when City funds are added. Davis also receives HHAP through the Davis, Woodland/Yolo County CoC (see county record) for supportive housing operations. Yolo County's own CDBG and HOME (state non-entitlement) cover only unincorporated areas, so there is no overlap. Blocked: the Grants Management page and the Consolidated Plan PDF on cityofdavis.org (403); the April 15, 2025 minutes on documents.cityofdavis.org were opened and record the adoption.

- Agency: City of Davis Social Services and Housing Department (Housing Trust Fund administered by the Affordable Housing Manager; Social Services Commission reviews affordable housing plans)
- Type: loan
- Typical award: Project-specific gap contributions sized by Council; no published NOFA or guidelines found. Revenue is in-lieu fees under Resolution 25-002 ($250,000 per unit) plus negotiated contributions from peripheral Measure J/R/D projects: Village Farms Exhibit E (approved December 16, 2025, revised January 13, 2026) commits $6,000,000 to the Housing Trust Fund ($2 million with dedication of the first land site, $1 million at the first building permit, $3 million before any Phase 3 building permit); Willowgrove's plan reportedly adds $1.8 million. Earlier years the fund was small (the 2023 single-family in-lieu fee was about $82,000 per unit) and the City has historically funded projects such as Paul's Place and Creekside from it. Current balance not published in any document opened this pass.
- AMI requirement: Low and very low income units with long-term covenants; Council direction prioritizes very low and extremely low income and deed-restricted ownership.
- Cycle: rolling (next: No NOFA. Contributions arrive with Village Farms and Willowgrove milestones only if voters approved the projects (Village Farms was placed on the June 2026 ballot and Willowgrove on the November 2026 ballot); verify election outcomes and timing with the Affordable Housing Manager, (530) 757-5602.)

Sized to projects on the dedicated land sites first (the Village Farms plan says the money should support affordable housing on the dedication sites but may be used elsewhere consistent with the plan). Layer as the last gap after 9% or 4% credits, HCD MHP or AHSC, Yolo County Housing project-based vouchers and the Davis CDBG and HOME allocations; City money is public funds and triggers prevailing wage. Councilmembers raised formalizing the fund into a structured trust (April 2026). Davis has no RDA successor housing fund. - Agency: City of Davis Community Development Department, Planning Division
- Type: density bonus
- Typical award: Regulatory. Section 40.27.110 (Ordinance 2322, 2008) allows deviations from zoning standards in accordance with the density bonuses and incentives provided for affordable housing by Article 18.05 and state density bonus law (Government Code 65915). Davis has no local enhancement beyond the state schedule; Article 18.05 alternatives (in-lieu fee, land dedication) are the local layer.

### City of East Palo Alto

**Affordable Housing Preservation Program (over-the-counter fund)**
- Agency: City of East Palo Alto Housing Division
- Type: loan
- Typical award: Council allocated just over $2 million to the program; applications accepted over the counter once the NOFA is released (anticipated March 2026 or later, launch planned for 2026). Draft guidelines (November 26, 2024) were developed with the County Equity Innovation Fund and HEART.
- AMI requirement: Conversion of market-rate housing to income-restricted housing or preservation and extension of existing restrictions; anti-displacement focus.
- Cycle: rolling (next: Over the counter after NOFA release; status of the 2026 release not confirmed. Contact housing@cityofepa.org, (650) 853-3189.)
- Layering notes: County layer: every San Mateo County city project competes for the County Affordable Housing Fund NOFA (AHF 14 closed July 15, 2026, next fall 2027), HEART bridge loans and HACSM project-based vouchers; city money is usually the first commitment that unlocks those. Small but flexible; pairs with the County's preservation financing and the Bay Area Preservation Pilot. The City's broader funding plan (Affordable Housing Strategy 2024-2028, adopted February 6, 2024) commits 50% of Measure HH office parcel tax revenue ($2.50 per square foot on office over 25,000 square feet, 2018) to creation and preservation of affordable housing, cites capacity to fund up to 122 units in 100% affordable developments, and adds Measure JJ gross receipts tax revenue (about $1.45 million to $1.7 million a year, approved November 2024); the City has not posted a new-construction NOFA, so developers should approach the Housing Division directly. Source is the preservation program page.
- Source: https://www.cityofepa.org/housing/page/affordable-housing-preservation
- Confidence: verified (researched 2026-11-07)

**Inclusionary Housing Ordinance (Chapter 18.37) with in-lieu fees and Affordable Housing Commercial Linkage Fee**
- Agency: City of East Palo Alto Housing Division, 1960 Tate Street
- Type: other
- Typical award: Requirement, not a subsidy. Projects of 5 or more units: rental 20% on-site (5% at 35% AMI, 10% at 50% AMI, 5% at 60% AMI) or, with Council approval, 25% off-site or an in-lieu fee of $299,200 per required unit (FY 2025-26); for-sale 20% on-site (10% median, 10% moderate) or 25% off-site or $268,800 per unit in lieu. Projects under 5 units pay a per-unit share ($59,840 to $239,360 rental). Commercial linkage fee (Resolution 118-2020, effective October 31, 2020, ENR-indexed each April 1) applies to office, R&D and medical office; retail, restaurant, service and hotel are charged $0; the City plans to update it in 2027 after the multi-city nexus study.
- AMI requirement: Ordinance 425 (November 19, 2019) and Guidelines (Resolution 142-2020); income limits follow HCD; SB 9 lot splits exempt (September 2025); in-lieu fees reset each July (FY 2025-26 adopted July 16, 2025).
- Cycle: rolling (next: Applies at entitlement; fee schedule updated each July (comprehensive fee schedule effective July 18, 2026). East Palo Alto is a 2026 multi-city nexus study participant.)
- Layering notes: County layer: every San Mateo County city project competes for the County Affordable Housing Fund NOFA (AHF 14 closed July 15, 2026, next fall 2027), HEART bridge loans and HACSM project-based vouchers; city money is usually the first commitment that unlocks those. East Palo Alto has the deepest rental targeting in the county (a 35% AMI tier) and uses the fees plus Measure HH and Measure JJ revenue to fund 100% affordable projects such as Colibri Commons and Light Tree; 148 inclusionary units were in the pipeline in 2024. Source is the City's inclusionary housing page; fee amounts from the in-lieu fee page and the linkage fee notice (updated October 16, 2026).

### City of Elk Grove

**City of Elk Grove Affordable Housing Fund and Affordable Housing Impact Fee (Municipal Code Chapters 16.88 and 16.89)**
- Agency: City of Elk Grove Housing and Public Services Division (fund and RFPs); Finance Department (fee collection)
- Type: loan
- Typical award: Fee-funded local gap loan fund. Current (2025) fees per the 2026 EPS nexus study: $6,396 per single or two-unit dwelling and $3,837 per multi-unit dwelling; nonresidential $1.05 commercial/retail, $3.11 hotel, $1.19 manufacturing, $1.28 warehouse and $0.00 office per square foot, indexed annually. Staff recommended (Sept 23, 2026 hearing) converting to per square foot: $3.59 single-unit, $3.29 owner-occupied multi-unit, $1.46 renter-occupied multi-unit, plus commercial $2.15 shopping center, $2.29 office, $0.39 industrial, $1,146.75 per hotel room and other categories (maximums supportable were $47.80, $43.80 and $19.50 per square foot). The City releases an RFP when the fund balance can support a project (generally about $5 million); the City reports $84 million lent to sixteen projects since inception (developer page, not opened this pass).
- AMI requirement: Fund restricted to housing for low and very low income households (HCD limits); 2026 update would also allow a local preference for City-based workers where fair housing law permits. Density bonus affordable units are exempt from the residential fee (Zoning Code 23.50.080).
- Cycle: rolling (next: No open RFP found as of 2026-11-08; watch elkgrove.gov/affordable-housing/developers and the City's purchasing RFP page. Outcome of the September 23, 2026 fee update hearing (ordinance amending 16.88 and 16.89 and a fee resolution) was not confirmed; contact Joshua Tovar, Management Analyst II, jtovar@elkgrove.gov, or the Housing and Public Services Division, (916) 683-7111.)
- Layering notes: Elk Grove is an impact-fee jurisdiction (like the City and County of Sacramento) with no inclusionary option, so market-rate rental projects pay the fee rather than build units; the 2026 renter-occupied rate was deliberately set low ($1.46 per square foot recommended) because the nexus study found multifamily infeasible at higher fees. Elk Grove is outside the SHRA lending area (SHRA finances in other cities only under cooperation agreements), so this fund, state sources and Elk Grove's own PLHA are the local layer. Past RFPs tied fund loans to City-owned sites (Sheldon Farms North and Old Town, 2023). elkgrove.gov and codepublishing.com return 403 to automated access; facts here come from the City's Sept 23, 2026 public hearing notice and the June 2026 EPS nexus study PDFs on elkgrove.gov.

**Fairfield affordable housing Fee Deferral Program (Municipal Code Chapter 5, Article I), Fee Credit Bank and Train Station Specific Plan fee reduction**
- Agency: City of Fairfield Community Development Department (Director approves deferrals and fee credits)
- Type: fee waiver
- Typical award: Deferral, not waiver: affordable projects defer certain building and development fees to certificate of occupancy or permanent financing. Fee Credit Bank: credits from demolished buildings (water and sewer connection fees, not school or Solano County public facilities fees) can be applied to affordable projects. Train Station Specific Plan area: 25% reduction in development fees for multifamily units above 24 units per acre. ADUs under 750 square feet exempt from park, Cordelia open space, sewer connection and County public facilities fees; all ADUs exempt from a long list of City fees. No published dollar value of deferrals.
- AMI requirement: Deferral: multifamily must be at least 50% moderate-income and 25% low-income units, 55-year rental covenant (45 years ownership). Fee credits: low- and moderate-income units with a covenant of up to 55 years.
- Cycle: rolling (next: Apply to the Community Development Department with the building permit; no cycle. The City was updating its AB 1600 traffic and Northeast (TSSP) fees in 2022-2023; confirm current fee schedule.)
- Layering notes: Deferral improves construction-period cash flow but fees are still paid, so budget them. Fee credits are a real reduction when a demolition site has banked credits; ask the Director for the current bank balance. Solano County public facilities fees cannot be deferred or credited by the City (County record: no County waiver program). A fee credit or reduction is public funds under Labor Code 1720(c) if above de minimis, hence unclear. Source is the HCD-posted October 2022 review draft of the 2023-2031 Housing Element (adopted February 7, 2023, certified April 10, 2023 per the City's housing element site, not opened); Chapter 5 of the Municipal Code itself is on a blocked code host.
- Source: https://www.hcd.ca.gov/housing-elements/docs/fairfield-6th-draft100622.pdf
- Confidence: verified (researched 2026-11-08)


### City of Folsom

**Density bonus and other developer incentives (Folsom Municipal Code Chapter 17.102)**
- Agency: City of Folsom Community Development Department, Planning Services
- Type: density bonus
- Typical award: State density bonus law implemented in Chapter 17.102 (Ord. 1145, 2011) for very low, low, moderate and senior households, with additional incentives or concessions per Government Code 65915(i), an added bonus for child care facilities, and resale and occupancy restrictions on moderate income units. Multifamily objective design standards were adopted in late 2025 to enable ministerial review.
- AMI requirement: Per state law (affordable rent defined as 30% of 50% or 80% AMI).
- Cycle: rolling (next: Rolling at entitlement.)
- Layering notes: No local enhancement beyond state minimums identified; the chapter predates recent state amendments and defers to Government Code 65915 where they conflict. The 2024 General Plan and Folsom Plan Area amendments added capacity for about 6,046 units in targeted multifamily areas, which is where bonus requests will land. Inclusionary projects may also request fee waivers or deferrals under 17.104.070 and Chapter 16.60.
- Source: https://www.zoneomics.com/code/folsom-CA/chapter_53
- Confidence: verified (researched 2026-11-08)

**Folsom Affordable Housing Loan (AHL) Program (Folsom Housing Fund 238 and Housing Trust Fund 221)**
- Agency: City of Folsom Community Development Department, Housing Services (loan consultant TDA, Inc.)
- Type: loan
- Typical award: Gap loans from the City's inclusionary in-lieu fee fund and commercial housing trust fund. Unaudited cash available for projects at June 30, 2025: $23.9 million (Fund 238 $22.8M, Fund 221 $0.9M, legacy funds $0.2M). Track record: 11 loans since 2005 totaling over $36 million supporting 1,095 units (e.g., a $2.7M conditional loan for 52 units in 2020). Guidelines adopted by Resolution 11427 on August 26, 2025 standardize terms and allow the City to issue NOFAs.
- AMI requirement: Minimum 55-year income, rent and affordability restrictions recorded senior to foreclosable liens; serves extremely low, very low and low income households; priority to sites outside concentrations of existing regulated housing and to Housing Element goals (seniors, large families, special needs). Fund 238 must spend at least 50% on construction or major rehab of multifamily rentals affordable to low and very low income households (Sacramento Housing Alliance settlement).
- Cycle: rolling (next: No NOFA issued as of 2026-11-08; the 2025 guidelines contemplate strategic NOFAs when resources are available, and staff planned a Council policy discussion on priorities for the housing funds. Requests may still be submitted ahead of tax credit rounds; contact Housing Services via the Community Development Department (Pam Johns, Director), (916) 461-6000.)
- Layering notes: The largest city-controlled pool in Sacramento County outside the City of Sacramento (about $23M) with few competing applicants, because Folsom's rental projects are scarce and the Folsom Plan Area south of Highway 50 generates most in-lieu revenue. Loans are repaid from 50% of residual cash flow after allowed expenses; operating and replacement reserves required for the 55-year term; underwriting and compliance aligned to TCAC and LIHTC rules. Folsom is outside the SHRA lending area (cooperation agreement needed), so this fund plus state sources is the local layer; a Folsom Plan Area MOU committing to 890 deed-restricted affordable units (2024 General Plan amendments, not opened this pass) creates sites. Chapter 17.104.070 also allows fee waivers or deferrals and density bonuses for inclusionary units. folsom.ca.us returns 403 to automated access; the staff report and resolution were read from the City's public agenda host.
- Source: https://mccmeetingspublic.blob.core.usgovcloudapi.net/folsomca-meet-20667254009747e4aa5f68a4d63539d6/ITEM-Attachment-001-3c80e00338b5420aafa72ac45dae4a5d.pdf
- Confidence: verified (researched 2026-11-08)

**Folsom Housing Trust Fund commercial development fee (Municipal Code Chapter 3.90, Fund 221)**
- Agency: City of Folsom Community Development Department (fee) and Housing Services (fund)
- Type: loan
- Typical award: Commercial linkage fee of $2.08 per square foot on new commercial development (established 2002), deposited in the Housing Trust Fund (Fund 221) and used mainly to fill financing gaps in affordable rental projects through the AHL Program. Fund 221 balance was $918,311 at June 30, 2025.
- AMI requirement: Fund supports affordable housing development; AHL Program 55-year restrictions apply to loans.
- Cycle: rolling (next: Deployed through the AHL Program (no NOFA as of 2026-11-08). Fee paid at building permit.)
- Layering notes: Minor source compared with Fund 238; Folsom's rate ($2.08) is below the City of Sacramento ($2.68 commercial) and above the County ($2.17). Chapter 3.90 text itself was not opened (codepublishing.com and folsom.ca.us return 403); the rate and balance come from the August 26, 2025 staff report on the City's public agenda host.
- Source: https://mccmeetingspublic.blob.core.usgovcloudapi.net/folsomca-meet-20667254009747e4aa5f68a4d63539d6/ITEM-Attachment-001-54dff11a603148f68a0203d4b6b13245.pdf
- Confidence: verified (researched 2026-11-08)

**Folsom Inclusionary Housing Ordinance (Municipal Code Chapter 17.104) and in-lieu fee (Ordinance 1359, Resolution 11510)**
- Agency: City of Folsom Community Development Department, Housing Services
- Type: other
- Typical award: Requirement, not a subsidy. For-sale residential projects of 10 or more units (and rental projects of 10 or more units receiving City assistance) must make 10% of units affordable: 3% very low income and 7% low income; market-rate rental apartments are exempt. In-lieu fee effective February 12, 2026 (replacing 1% of the lowest sales price): $3.00 per square foot for single-family for-sale units and $2.50 per square foot for multifamily for-sale units of 1,500 square feet or less, paid at building permit into the Folsom Housing Fund (Fund 238); at least 50% of fee revenue must go to lower-income rental development. Prior-year collections exceeded $3.8M, mostly from the Folsom Plan Area. Alternatives: land dedication, off-site units, acquisition-rehab or conversion of market-rate units, inclusionary credits, combinations.
- AMI requirement: Rental inclusionary units restricted at least 30 years (or longer if state law requires); for-sale units resale-restricted; projects of nine or fewer market-rate units exempt.
- Cycle: rolling (next: Applies at entitlement; fee per unit in effect at permit issuance. Council adopted Ordinance 1359 on January 13, 2026 (first reading December 9, 2025) and set fees by Resolution 11510 the same night; next review expected with the Housing Element cycle. Developers paying fees only need a letter of intent, not a full inclusionary housing plan.)
- Layering notes: Nearly all Folsom Plan Area builders pay the fee, which is why Fund 238 holds about $22.8M and funds the AHL Program (record above). Rental multifamily was kept exempt in 2026 despite AB 1505 authority, so apartment developers owe no inclusionary units or fee. Developers who provide more than 10% can bank and sell inclusionary housing credits for five years (17.104.070). The ordinance text was read from the City Council's January 13, 2026 agenda packet on the City's public agenda host and the zoneomics code mirror.
- Source: https://mccmeetingspublic.blob.core.usgovcloudapi.net/folsomca-meet-e0a349248e64470eac3fc0fa94532290/ITEM-Attachment-001-881e809b1b1f4a71b18b405a5e2e979f.pdf
- Confidence: verified (researched 2026-11-08)

- Agency: City of Folsom Community Development Department, Housing Services
- Type: loan
- Typical award: Largely spent. Fund 274 held $25,672 at June 30, 2025 from a 2006 $3.1M inclusionary payment ($2.7M went to the Granite City Apartments site on Sibley Street). Fund 280 held $149,695 of pre-2011 redevelopment bond proceeds that SB 107 (2015) let the City use for housing; over $9.6 million was invested in multiple affordable projects after redevelopment dissolved in 2012.

- Type: grant
- Typical award: Hayward has received over $15,000,000 in HOME funds since 1991 as a Consortium member (annual formula share), used for Glenn Berry, Sara Conner Court, Huntwood Commons, Tennyson Gardens, Leidig Court, Cypress Glen, Weinreb Place, Alta Mira and Mission Paradise, plus Project Independence tenant-based rental assistance ($500,000 renewed July 2026). Hayward is also a CDBG entitlement city; CDBG has funded predevelopment and acquisition. The County proposes to centralize HOME administration, compliance and allocation during the FY 2027-2029 term, with Consortium members reviewing future allocations.
- AMI requirement: 100% of HOME funds to households at or below 80% AMI with HOME rent limits; federal affordability period plus City regulatory agreement.
- Cycle: annual NOFA (Consortium allocation each program year) (next: FY 2027 allocation set spring 2026; future allocations may be awarded through the County's HOME Consortium RFP (county record) under the centralized model. Verify with the Housing Division.)
- Layering notes: Small annual amounts (several hundred thousand dollars) but the only recurring development money Hayward controls. Pairs with the County HOME Consortium RFP, Measure A1 and HACA PBVs. Hayward's December 2024 analysis identified weak local match, GHG scoring and a thin rent differential as reasons three of five recent projects struggled to win state funds, and cited an expected Prohousing designation as a strength.
- Source: https://hayward.legistar1.com/hayward/attachments/a14a28e1-41e1-4606-a74e-1b25ec86e353.pdf
- Confidence: verified (researched 2026-11-08)

**Hayward Affordable Housing NOFA (local housing funds with Alameda County Measure A1 base allocation; last round 2018)**
- Agency: City of Hayward Development Services Department, Housing Division, 777 B Street, Hayward; housing@hayward-ca.gov, (510) 583-4454
- Type: loan
- Typical award: 2018 NOFA: about $7,000,000 in local housing funds plus recommendations for Hayward's Measure A1 base allocation ($18,200,000 available at the time) and local match to position projects for the A1 regional pool. Maximum City loan 10% of total residential development cost of the affordable units; HOME per-unit limits for HOME-assisted units ($144,050 studio to $285,149 four bedroom in 2018); 24-month commitment with one-year extension. CDBG available for predevelopment or acquisition by request. No NOFA has been issued since; the City reports only one City-supported project remaining in the pipeline and limited general fund for housing.
- AMI requirement: Rental and supportive housing for lower income households; Measure A1 policies require at least 20% of units at 20% AMI for A1-funded projects; scoring favors special needs, homeless, larger units and deeper targeting.
- Cycle: closed/inactive (next: No open NOFA as of 2026-11-08. The December 2024 Housing Policy and Resource Committee report floated an annual general fund allocation for a regular NOFA but no funding was identified. Watch the Doing Business with Hayward page and the Housing Division mailing list.)
- Layering notes: Hayward's role is mainly as pass-through for its Measure A1 base allocation (county record) and HOME Consortium share; local dollars are limited to the Affordable Housing Trust Fund balance and CDBG. Developers should expect to rely on Measure A1, Measure W, HACA project-based vouchers and state sources with the City providing land (surplus sites), entitlements under the Streamlined Affordable Housing Overlay, and its Prohousing designation points. NOFA page and 2018 program description were opened on hayward-ca.gov.
- Source: https://hayward-ca.gov/content/notice-funding-availability-new-construction-affordable-rental-housing
- Confidence: verified (researched 2026-11-08)

**Hayward Affordable Housing Ordinance (HMC Chapter 10, Article 17; Ordinance 17-20, amended April 11, 2023), in-lieu fees (Resolution 17-167 as amended 2023) and Affordable Housing Trust Fund**
- Agency: City of Hayward Development Services Department, Housing Division, 777 B Street, Hayward; housing@hayward-ca.gov, (510) 583-4454
- Type: other
- Typical award: Requirement, not a subsidy. Applies to all projects of two or more net new units: on-site units, in-lieu fee, off-site units or alternatives. In-lieu fees (10 or more units, per sq ft of habitable space, 2023 schedule): high-density condominiums 35 units per acre or more $19.35; lower-density ownership under 35 units per acre $26.00; all other dwelling types including rental $23.46; plus 10% if paid at occupancy; projects of 2 to 9 units pay 50% to 89% of the calculated fee. Fees fund the Affordable Housing Trust Fund, used solely to increase and preserve housing for extremely low to moderate income households (land acquisition and development subsidies). Collections 2020 to mid-2026 total $8,926,851: $3,599,171 (2020), $2,193,532 (2021), $2,013,770 (2022), $199,507 (2023), $489,948 (2024), $378,237 (2025), $52,687 (2026 YTD).
- AMI requirement: On-site compliance percentages set in 10-17.205 (historically 10% of units for ownership and rental); local tenant preference policy in 10-17.805; 55-year rental affordability.
- Cycle: rolling (next: Applies at entitlement; fee per the annual Master Fee Schedule (FY 2027 schedule adopted June 2026). Verify current indexed amounts with the Housing Division.)
- Layering notes: Hayward's trust fund is small and shrinking because most recent developments provided on-site units rather than paying fees (City's December 2024 competitiveness analysis), so the City lacks local match for state applications. The AHO text on municode is script-blocked; requirements were read from the City's affordable housing page, Resolution 17-167 and the 2023 in-lieu fee resolution on Hayward Legistar. Compare Fremont ($44 per sq ft for-sale) and Berkeley ($62.83).
- Source: https://hayward-ca.gov/your-government/programs/affordable-housing
- Confidence: verified (researched 2026-11-08)

**Streamlined Affordable Housing Overlay District, HMC Section 10-1.2650 (Ordinance 24-04, April 2, 2024)**
- Agency: City of Hayward Development Services Department, Planning Division
- Type: density bonus
- Typical award: Entitlement streamlining, not a subsidy. Ministerial site plan and tentative map approval for housing on sites carried over from prior housing element cycles and listed in the 6th Cycle Housing Element lower-income inventory, provided the project meets the Housing Element minimum density assumptions and at least 20% of units are deed restricted for extremely low, very low or low income households for 55 years (rental) or 45 years (ownership); site must not meet Gov Code 65913.4(a)(6) exclusion criteria; objective standards and standard conditions apply.
- AMI requirement: At least 20% of units at low income or below, 55-year rental or 45-year ownership restriction.
- Cycle: rolling (next: Ministerial application any time; approval lapses per 10-1.2690.)
- Layering notes: Hayward has no local density bonus chapter; state density bonus requests are processed with site plan review (recent approvals include townhome projects with 10% to 11% affordable units). The overlay lowers entitlement risk on the inventory sites and pairs with state SB 35/SB 423 streamlining. Fee relief for affordable projects is not offered by the City. Code read on the zoneomics mirror because municode is blocked.

### City of Huntington Beach

**Affordable Housing (Inclusionary Housing) Ordinance, Huntington Beach Zoning and Subdivision Ordinance Sec. 230.26, and in-lieu fee**
- Agency: City of Huntington Beach Community Development Department, Housing Division (Charles Kovac, Housing Manager, charles.kovac@surfcity-hb.org; Gregory Hoang, Senior Housing Analyst, 714-536-5473)
- Type: other
- Typical award: Requirement, not a subsidy. New residential projects of three or more units (including conversions) must restrict at least 10% of units: rental units at the lower income level (or very low or extremely low at the developer's choice), ownership units at moderate income, with fractional units rounded up or paid as fee. In-lieu fees may be paid by ownership projects of any size and rental projects of 100 units or fewer, per a fee schedule set by Council resolution and indexed annually to Orange County new home prices; fees are paid before building permit (pro rata for phased projects) and deposited in the Affordable Housing Trust Fund. Land dedication is allowed at Council discretion. Projects that exceed the requirement on-site are eligible for reduced City fees (the 2025 Annual Progress Report cites over $1,000,000 of development impact fee exemptions for a 78-unit project with 8 ELI, 32 VL and 37 low units). A 6-1 Council vote amended the ordinance and the fee formula to make payment more flexible (date not confirmed).
- AMI requirement: Affordability term at least 55 years for rental and 45 years for ownership; affordable rental units built by a separate affordable developer on a parcel within an ownership project may not request City financial assistance; at least 40% of such units must have two or more bedrooms; interior standards equal to LIHTC minimums.
- Cycle: rolling (next: Applies at entitlement; fee per the current Council resolution at building permit. Council must review the Trust Fund and fee within 180 days after each fiscal year end (by late December).)
- Layering notes: A low 3-unit threshold but a fee-out for all ownership and all rental projects up to 100 units, so in practice most Huntington Beach projects pay the fee; the Trust Fund (next record) is the resulting local source. The ordinance's fee-reduction incentive is the only affordable housing fee relief found among the five cities. Housing Element status matters here: HCD's March 6, 2026 letter found the 2021-2029 element cannot be certified until the Program 2A and 2B rezonings (Affordable Housing Overlay) are complete, and the state litigation over the element continues, which exposes projects to builder's remedy and limits state funding points. Code read on the zoneomics mirror; Legistar attachments (HCD letter, 2025 APR) opened via the Legistar web API.
- Source: https://www.zoneomics.com/code/huntington-beach-CA/chapter_4
- Confidence: verified (researched 2026-11-08)

**Affordable Housing Density Bonus (Zoning and Subdivision Ordinance Sec. 230.14) and Affordable Housing Overlay (Beach and Edinger Corridors Specific Plan)**
- Agency: City of Huntington Beach Community Development Department, Planning Division
- Type: density bonus
- Typical award: Requirement and entitlement, not a subsidy. Sec. 230.14 implements Government Code 65915: 20% base bonus for 10% lower income units rising 1.5% per additional 1% to 35%, 5% base bonus for 10% moderate income for-sale units rising 1% per 1% to 35%, one to three incentives or concessions by affordability tier, land donation option under 65915(h). The Beach and Edinger Corridors Specific Plan Affordable Housing Overlay provides non-discretionary review for qualifying affordable projects, and the HBHA Pathways RFQ sought 100% affordable supportive housing at 60% AMI or less with by-right processing for projects with at least 20% affordable units.
- AMI requirement: State thresholds; 55-year rental covenants; in-lieu fees under Sec. 230.26 are calculated on units before the density bonus.
- Cycle: rolling (next: Applies at project application. Housing Element Program 2B (expand the Affordable Housing Overlay) is the rezoning HCD requires before certification; Resolution 2026-25 to adopt the element was heard June 2 and June 8, 2026.)
- Layering notes: Huntington Beach's local code mirrors the pre-2020 state schedule (35% cap), but state law controls and allows larger bonuses; the practical constraint is political and legal (Measure U voter control, State v. City of Huntington Beach over the Housing Element). Until the element is certified, projects may use builder's remedy and the City cannot earn Prohousing points. No local fee waiver ordinance beyond the Sec. 230.26 fee-reduction incentive. Density bonus does not trigger prevailing wage. Code read on zoneomics; HCD March 6, 2026 letter and Legistar matter list opened.
- Source: https://www.zoneomics.com/code/huntington-beach-CA/chapter_4
- Confidence: verified (researched 2026-11-08)

**Affordable Housing Trust Fund (Sec. 230.26.E and F) and City inclusionary loans**
- Agency: City of Huntington Beach Community Development Department, Housing Division; Huntington Beach Housing Authority
- Type: loan
- Typical award: In-lieu fees collected under Sec. 230.26 are placed in the Affordable Housing Trust Fund and may be used for predevelopment, land or air rights acquisition, rehabilitation, land write-downs, administration, gap financing or interest rate buy-downs on construction or permanent loans. Current balance and annual receipts were not published in an opened document. Example of use: the City holds an Inclusionary Housing promissory note on Pelican Harbor Apartments that was amended (First Amendment to City Inclusionary Housing Promissory Note) with a HOME note amendment and CMFA bond TEFRA approval on October 21, 2025 (Resolution 2025-65) to allow the project's refinancing; Five Points Senior Villas covenants were extended by amendment in August 2025.
- AMI requirement: Fund projects must have at least 50% of units affordable to very low and low income households with at least 20% very low income, under a recorded affordable housing agreement with 55-year covenants; Council may add permitted uses by resolution with the annual fee schedule.
- Cycle: rolling (next: unknown, verify with agency; no NOFA. Council reviews the fund annually within 180 days of fiscal year end. Request the fund balance from the Housing Division.)
- Layering notes: Small and reactive: Huntington Beach uses the Trust Fund and HOME CHDO reserve for project-specific loans and covenant extensions rather than rounds. Combine with the City's CDBG and HOME, County 2026 Supportive Housing NOFA loans ($95,000 to $105,000 per unit inside Huntington Beach), OCHA PBVs (Oasis Huntington Beach took 62) and OCHFT. The Huntington Beach Housing Authority is also the housing successor; its LMIHAF balance was not opened this pass. Public funds trigger state prevailing wage. Code text on zoneomics; Legistar matter 25-856 attachments list opened (the inclusionary note PDF itself is an image scan with no text).

- Agency: City of Huntington Beach Community Development Department, Housing Division (Charles Kovac, Housing Manager; Gregory Hoang, Senior Housing Analyst, gregory.hoang@surfcity-hb.org, 714-536-5473)

### City of Irvine

**Affordable Housing Credits Program (Irvine Zoning Ordinance Sec. 2-3-6)**
- Agency: City of Irvine Community Development Department (credits database and three-party credits agreements)
- Type: other
- Typical award: Market mechanism, not a subsidy. Projects that build more affordable units than the 15% requirement earn transferable credits in three income categories (extremely low or very low, low, moderate) that they may sell to market-rate projects or mixed projects with a shortfall; credits become available after building permits are issued for the excess units and a completion bond or certificate of occupancy is in place. A three-party credits agreement (buyer, seller, City) must be executed before the buyer's building permits; sale prices are not disclosed to the City.
- AMI requirement: Credits track the income level of the excess units; the receiving project satisfies its required affordable component at that level.
- Cycle: rolling (next: Agreement before building permit; City maintains the credits database on request.)
- Layering notes: For a 100% affordable developer this is a revenue source unique among the five Orange County priority cities: excess units can be monetized to market-rate builders in the same or other planning areas, effectively a private in-lieu payment. Confirm with the City how many credits are outstanding and the recent trading range. Read on the zoneomics mirror because cityofirvine.gov returned 403.
- Source: https://www.zoneomics.com/code/irvine-CA/chapter_2
- Confidence: verified (researched 2026-11-08)

**Affordable Housing In-Lieu Fee Fund (Irvine Zoning Ordinance Sec. 2-3-5.B.3.c; fee set by City Council resolution)**
- Agency: City of Irvine Community Development Department
- Type: loan
- Typical award: In-lieu fees are deposited in the City's affordable housing fund and used for projects serving low, very low and extremely low income households and Housing Element needs; the fee is set by Council resolution and determined at building permit (a legacy $17,000 per unit rate applied only to Irvine Business Complex projects filed before 2007). An Affordable Housing Requirement and In-Lieu Fee Update draft study was posted August 3, 2023 (per the City page title captured in search results), but the adopted schedule and the current fund balance could not be read because cityofirvine.gov blocked access. The City's FY 2023-25 budget reported a four-acre land conveyance to the Irvine Community Land Trust as part of its 100% affordable housing support.
- AMI requirement: Fund uses limited to low, very low and extremely low income households and Housing Element implementation; recipients record 55-year covenants under Chapter 2-3.
- Cycle: rolling (next: unknown, verify with agency; no NOFA located. Ask Community Development for the current in-lieu fee resolution, fund balance and whether a developer round is planned.)
- Layering notes: Because most Irvine builders provide units on-site or through credits, the in-lieu fund is smaller than Santa Ana's; its visible use is land and loans to Irvine Community Land Trust projects (Salerno, Parc Derian, Doria, Alegre, Sage Park) which then take LIHTC, HOME, OCHFT and County MHSA money. Public funds trigger state prevailing wage. Code section read on zoneomics; City pages (node 81916 and affordable housing pages) returned 403.
- Source: https://www.zoneomics.com/code/irvine-CA/chapter_2
- Confidence: needs_confirmation (researched 2026-11-08)

**Inclusionary Housing Ordinance, Affordable Housing Implementation Procedure (Irvine Zoning Ordinance Chapter 2-3, Secs. 2-3-1 to 2-3-11; Ord. 04-15, 24-13, 25-16)**
- Agency: City of Irvine Community Development Department, Planning Services and Housing staff
- Type: other
- Typical award: Requirement, not a subsidy. Residential projects must provide 15% of units as affordable: 5% extremely low or very low income, 5% low income, 5% moderate income (ownership units for very low or low earn 2:1 credit; extremely low units 1.6:1; three- and four-bedroom units 1.4:1 and 1.6:1). Projects with at least 10% very low or extremely low units satisfy the combined 10% lower income requirement. Alternatives (menu option) are allowed only when on-site units are infeasible or in the City's interest: converting market units for 55 years, extending expiring covenants 55 years, in-lieu fees set by Council resolution, transferring units to a nonprofit, buying affordable housing credits (Sec. 2-3-6), alternative housing (SROs, special needs, shelters at 1:1), or dedicating land or resources of at least equal value. Projects up to 100% affordable may be approved in any planning area and can only be denied under Government Code 65589.5(d). Community preference policy in Sec. 2-3-11.
- AMI requirement: Covenants of at least 55 years at the income level provided; bedroom mix must match the market units and affordable units must be dispersed; affordable housing plans and annual compliance reports required; revocation of entitlements for noncompliance.
- Cycle: rolling (next: Applies at entitlement; in-lieu fee amount determined at building permit under the current Council resolution (fee study drafted August 3, 2023; current schedule not confirmed). Chapter last amended June 24, 2025 (Ord. 25-16).)
- Layering notes: Irvine's 15% requirement is the highest of the five Orange County priority cities and is the engine behind the Irvine Company planning area affordable sites that nonprofits (Jamboree, C&C, Related, ICLT) build with 4% and 9% credits; a nonprofit taking an inclusionary site typically gets the land at low cost plus City or Irvine Community Land Trust support, then layers County MHSA/BHSA, OCHFT and OCHA PBVs. Sec. 2-3-7 states the City has no obligation to provide financial incentives, so there is no guaranteed city subsidy. cityofirvine.gov returned 403 to all fetch methods this pass; the ordinance was read on the zoneomics mirror.
- Source: https://www.zoneomics.com/code/irvine-CA/chapter_2
- Confidence: verified (researched 2026-11-08)

**Irvine Community Land Trust (ICLT) land and development partnerships**
- Agency: Irvine Community Land Trust, 501(c)(3) created by the City of Irvine in 2006, 503 Nightmist, Irvine 92618; Board chaired by Ryan Aeh (2026)
- Type: other
- Typical award: ICLT acquires or receives land (including City conveyances such as the four-acre site reported in the City's FY 2023-25 budget) and ground leases it to development partners so that units stay affordable permanently. Portfolio: Alegre Apartments, Doria Apartments, Parc Derian Apartments, Salerno Apartments (501 Nightmist) and Sage Park (affordable ownership); it reports hundreds of affordable units in Irvine and, since its 2017 mission expansion, elsewhere in Orange County. ICLT finances projects with LIHTC, HOME, Orange County Housing Finance Trust loans, FHLB AHP and HUD programs; dollar values of land contributions are not published.
- AMI requirement: Permanent affordability through recorded ground lease covenants; rental projects have served extremely low to low income households and Sage Park serves moderate income buyers.
- Cycle: rolling (partnerships negotiated with ICLT) (next: No solicitation open; contact ICLT through its partnerships page. Note the September 2026 governance dispute: ICLT directors wrote to the City Council on September 23, 2026 defending Resolution 26-803 (consultant contract, 5 to 1 vote), which could affect City-ICLT land conveyances.)
- Layering notes: ICLT is how Irvine converts inclusionary land dedications and City-owned parcels into 100% affordable projects without a city loan program; a developer partnering with ICLT gets site control at nominal ground rent and then stacks 4% or 9% credits, County MHSA/BHSA capital, OCHFT (Cypress Village Irvine took $3,500,000 in the 2024 OCHFT round) and OCHA PBVs. ICLT is a nonprofit, not a public agency, so its land alone does not trigger prevailing wage, but City land conveyed through it may. ICLT home, about, history, process, partnerships and properties pages and the September 23, 2026 letter opened on irvineclt.org.
- Source: https://irvineclt.org/our-process/
- Confidence: verified (researched 2026-11-08)

**Residential Density Bonus Standards (Irvine Zoning Ordinance Sec. 2-3-10)**
- Agency: City of Irvine Community Development Department, Planning Services
- Type: density bonus
- Typical award: Requirement and entitlement, not a subsidy. Implements Government Code 65915 to 65918 by reference: density bonuses, incentives and concessions, waivers and parking ratios per state law, documented in a density bonus housing agreement recorded as a condition of the discretionary approval; development standards may be modified under Sec. 2-3-10.C for projects providing the Chapter 2-3 affordable units.
- AMI requirement: State thresholds (5% very low, 10% low, 10% moderate for-sale, 100% affordable); 55-year rental covenants.

Irvine receives its own CDBG, HOME, PLHA and HHAP allocations (HHAP Round 6 $5,947,855 per the County record) but those pages could not be opened this pass. Irvine is not a Prohousing designated city per the HCD list opened 2026-11-08.

### City of Lincoln

**Lincoln 2021-2029 Housing Element Actions 2.6 and 2.7: project-by-project incentives (deferred development fees, reduced parking, expedited review) for affordable housing in Villages 1, 5 and 7**
- Agency: City of Lincoln Community Development Department, Planning Division (916-434-3370; 600 6th Street)
- Type: fee waiver
- Typical award: Negotiated, not codified. The Housing Element (adopted January 2023 per the City's 2025 Annual Progress Report, 2021 to 2029 cycle, RHNA 5,120 units) commits the City to offer incentives on a project-by-project basis for lower-income housing in Village 1, Village 5 and Village 7, including deferred development fees, reduced parking requirements, expedited application review and technical assistance (Action 2.7), and to provide financial or in-kind assistance and incentives beyond the density bonus for extremely low income housing (Action 2.6). Action 2.9 commits only to explore a local inclusionary program; none has been adopted. No dollar amounts, fee schedules or fund are attached.

- Layering notes: Lincoln's village specific plans (Lincoln Crossing, Village 7 and others) carry no fixed inclusionary percentage, unlike Roseville's 10% goal, so affordability in Lincoln depends on developer-by-developer agreements plus County and state money. The Consolidated Plan notes two-story height limits and two spaces per unit parking standards as constraints the City may relax for affordable projects. The Housing Element PDF itself could not be located on the redesigned lincolnca.gov site (housing element and general plan URLs returned 404); the actions were read from the City's 2026-30 Consolidated Plan, hence needs_confirmation.

**Lincoln CDBG entitlement program (first-time entitlement, 2026-2030 Consolidated Plan and 2026 Annual Action Plan)**
- Agency: City of Lincoln City Manager's Office (Nita Wracker; publiccomments@lincolnca.gov, 916-434-2427; 600 Sixth Street)
- Type: grant
- Typical award: Lincoln became a HUD CDBG entitlement city in 2026 with a first-year allocation of $272,325. The 2026-30 Consolidated Plan (public hearing May 12, 2026, submitted to HUD June 3, 2026) prioritizes community services and administration; it states the City has not yet set standards for subrecipients and will look for opportunities to support affordable housing with entitlement funds but does not program CDBG for housing development in year one. Stakeholders asked for local gap financing, PBV support and tax credit competitiveness funds, which the City said it will continue to evaluate.
- AMI requirement: CDBG national objectives (low and moderate income benefit); no housing development set-aside adopted.

### City of Menlo Park

**Below Market Rate (BMR) Housing Fund NOFA 2026/27**
- Agency: City of Menlo Park Community Development Department, Housing Division
- Type: loan
- Typical award: Approximately $4 million available for the production and preservation of permanent affordable housing, awarded competitively by the City Council; PlanetBids listing cites award sizes of about $300,000 to $800,000. Additional consideration for extremely low income units, special populations and preservation or rehabilitation of multifamily housing. Emergency shelters and transitional housing are not eligible. The prior round (January 2023) offered $1.5 million to $2 million; the City also contributed $1 million to a teacher housing project in November 2024.
- AMI requirement: Permanent affordability consistent with the BMR Housing Program Guidelines (October 21, 2025) and the Housing Element; priority to extremely low income and special needs units.
- Cycle: annual NOFA (next: Applications due 5:00 pm Friday, November 20, 2026 on PlanetBids (invitation 2026-100926-101526; questions closed November 6, 2026); Housing Commission review winter 2027, Council award spring 2027. Housing Element Program H1.I requires a NOFA at least every two years.)
- Layering notes: County layer: every San Mateo County city project competes for the County Affordable Housing Fund NOFA (AHF 14 closed July 15, 2026, next fall 2027), HEART bridge loans and HACSM project-based vouchers; city money is usually the first commitment that unlocks those. The BMR fund is capitalized by commercial in-lieu fees (office and R&D $23.26 per square foot in FY 2026-27) and residential in-lieu payments, so its size tracks Meta and life science approvals; $4 million is enough for one gap loan or a preservation deal and is typically paired with County AHF and HACSM PBVs. Source is the City's 2026 NOFA page; contact Arianna Milton, ANMilton@menlopark.gov, (650) 330-6705.

**Below Market Rate (BMR) Housing Program: residential inclusionary and commercial in-lieu fees (MPMC 16.96)**
- Agency: City of Menlo Park Community Development Department, Housing Division
- Type: other
- Typical award: Requirement, not a subsidy. Residential: 10 to 19 units at least 10% BMR, 20 or more units at least 15% BMR (very low, low and moderate income); 5 to 9 units provide a unit if feasible or pay a graduated in-lieu fee of 1% to 3% of sales price; for-sale projects of 10 or more may pay 3% of the sales price per market-rate unit in lieu; rental in-lieu fee set by Council resolution based on the cost of a one-bedroom unit. Each on-site BMR unit earns one additional market-rate unit up to 15% above zoned density. Commercial: buildings of 10,000 square feet or more provide BMR units or pay in-lieu fees of $23.26 per square foot (office and R&D, Group A) or $12.62 (other commercial and industrial, Group B) for July 1, 2026 to June 30, 2027, adjusted each July 1 by a five-year CPI shelter average.
- AMI requirement: BMR rents at or below 30% of the income category limit and no more than 75% of market rents; income categories from 30% to 120% AMI; one-year live or work preference; BMR housing agreement recorded before permits.
- Cycle: rolling (next: Applies at application; Menlo Park leads the 2026 San Mateo County multi-city nexus study (Strategic Economics) that may raise inclusionary percentages and add a residential impact fee later in 2026 or 2027.)
- Layering notes: County layer: every San Mateo County city project competes for the County Affordable Housing Fund NOFA (AHF 14 closed July 15, 2026, next fall 2027), HEART bridge loans and HACSM project-based vouchers; city money is usually the first commitment that unlocks those. The commercial in-lieu fee is the engine of the BMR fund (see NOFA record); office projects in the Bayfront and downtown specific plan areas often negotiate on-site or off-site BMR units instead. Source is the City's residential BMR requirements page; commercial rates from the companion commercial page and the October 21, 2025 Guidelines (Resolution 7003).

**Mill Valley Affordable Housing Requirements: inclusionary units and affordable housing impact fee, MVMC Chapter 20.80 (Ordinance 1295 of 2017, inclusionary update adopted 2026 under Housing Element Programs 7 and 11)**
- Agency: City of Mill Valley Planning and Building Department
- Type: other
- Typical award: Requirement, not a subsidy. Impact fee: 1% of construction valuation on single-family and small multifamily residential work at or above the valuation threshold ($100,000 in 2018, $105,000 in 2020, $130,000 in 2023, $142,000 from May 1, 2024, indexed to the California Construction Cost Index), paid at building permit into the Affordable Housing Trust Fund; collection was extended five years by Council resolution on March 20, 2023. The 2026 update lowered the inclusionary requirement from 25% to 15%, exempted 2 to 6 unit projects from building affordable units and waived their impact fee when units stay under 850 square feet (one bedroom), 1,000 (two bedrooms) or 1,200 (three bedrooms), and eliminated micro-unit caps. Fractional units of 0.50 or more may be met by an in-lieu payment calculated by applying the fraction to the impact fee formula.
- AMI requirement: Projects of 7 to 9 units: 15% affordable with at least one unit for moderate income households. Projects of 10 or more units: 15% affordable, at least half of the affordable units for low income households and the rest moderate income. Rental affordable units restricted in perpetuity or the maximum term allowed by law (20.80.060). Exempt: ADUs, micro units, projects below the valuation threshold, projects vested before November 1, 2018. Off-site units, land dedication or acquisition-rehabilitation alternatives at the City's sole discretion; Chapter 20.80.080 allows reducing moderate income unit counts when units are instead restricted to very low or low income.
- Cycle: rolling (next: Threshold adjusts each calendar year. Housing Element Program 11 requires a further look at inclusionary ratios at the 2028 RHNA mid-point; Program 12 calls for considering a commercial linkage fee and single-family impact fee changes with other Marin jurisdictions.)
- Layering notes: The 2026 drop from 25% to 15% (half low, half moderate) brings Mill Valley below Novato (20%) and the County (20%) and closer to San Rafael's 5% to 10%; combined with the Housing Overlay Districts (17 to 40 units per acre) it is meant to make 7-plus unit infill feasible on commercial corridors. The impact fee is the engine of the Trust Fund record above; no commercial linkage fee exists yet. The 2026 ordinance PDF (Attachment 1, as adopted per the City zoning updates page), the Zoneomics mirror of Chapter 20.80, the 2024 APR and the Housing Element were opened; the City's eCode360 host was not needed.
- Source: https://www.cityofmillvalley.gov/DocumentCenter/View/12336
- Confidence: verified (researched 2026-11-08)

**Mill Valley Affordable Housing Trust Fund (MVMC 20.80.070, Ordinance 1295, Resolution 20-26 Administrative Guidelines, Resolution 24-60 Local Housing Trust Fund match)**
- Agency: City of Mill Valley Planning and Building Department (Danielle Staude, dstaude@cityofmillvalley.org), with Housing Advisory Committee priorities and City Council approval of every award
- Type: loan
- Typical award: Funded by the 1% affordable housing impact fee on residential permits at or above the construction valuation threshold ($142,000 since May 1, 2024) plus inclusionary in-lieu payments and donations; collections were $345,000 by Feb 2020, roughly $300,000 a year per the Housing Element and about $600,000 a year per the 2024 Annual Progress Report, with about $1,000,000 unencumbered in 2024. Resolution 24-60 (Sept 5, 2024) committed $1,000,000 of Trust Fund match for an HCD Local Housing Trust Fund application ($1,200,000 requested; HCD's Round 5 applicant list shows the City with a self-score of 60) so that $2,400,000 total would be available: $1,000,000 ($500,000 grant plus $500,000 match) for Bayfront Terrace at 1 Hamilton Drive and $1,400,000 for other projects to be solicited. Loans at simple interest of no more than 3% as construction or deferred-payment permanent financing; up to 5% administration. Ongoing uses: Marin Housing Authority BMR administration, Home Match contract (up to $30,000 a year), Bayfront Terrace predevelopment, and the Lease to Locals pilot ($3,500 to $14,000 per converted rental, running through 2027).
- AMI requirement: Low income households per Chapter 20.80 covenants; LHTF-matched awards target 60% AMI and below with a 30% extremely low income set-aside. Projects must be inside Mill Valley, scored on feasibility, funding needed, unit count and location outside the very high fire severity zone. Council approves each award at a public hearing. The City adopted HCD's Uniform Multifamily Regulations for underwriting.

The City said it would announce a solicitation in early 2025 contingent on the HCD LHTF award; no award or solicitation was found on the City site as of November 2026, and the 2028 Mitigation Fee Act five-year review and impact fee extension decision are the next fixed milestones.)
- Layering notes: Mill Valley's fund is unusually well capitalized for a 14,000-person city because the 1% fee hits every large remodel; it is the only Marin priority city with a committed state LHTF match strategy. Money has gone almost entirely to the City's own site (Bayfront Terrace, EAH Housing, 45 units) and to tenure programs, so a third-party developer should expect the $1,400,000 remainder and future fee receipts (about $600,000 a year) as the ceiling. Layer under the Marin County Affordable Housing Fund (the County awarded 1 Hamilton $500,000 in 2022 and $1,000,000 total by 2024 per County documents cited in search results, not opened), County HOME ($360,000 to the Eden Housing Mill Valley rental project in FY 2026-27, see County record) and PLHA; CDBG and HOME flow through the Marin Urban County. City loans are public funds for prevailing wage. - Agency: City of Mill Valley Planning and Building Department
- Type: density bonus
- Typical award: Requirement framework, not a cash subsidy. Chapter 20.81 applies Government Code 65915 by reference (bonus, incentives, waivers, parking ratios; senior projects get no concessions unless state law requires). The 2024 Housing Overlay Districts, applied on top of base zoning to Housing Element sites, allow 17 to 40 units per acre (20 to 40 in the Opportunity Site overlay), 40-foot height, one parking space for units of 1,000 square feet or less, waived lot merger fees, and let projects also use State Density Bonus to modify standards; projects reserving 20% of units for lower income households get streamlined review. **Mill Valley development fee waivers for affordable housing (MVMC 5.32 as amended October 3, 2022, Housing Element Programs 14 and 23) and lot merger fee waiver in the Opportunity Site Housing Overlay**
- Agency: City of Mill Valley Planning and Building Department; City Council resolution for waivers
- Type: fee waiver
- Typical award: 100% waiver of City application processing fees for projects managed and operated by affordable housing organizations when at least 10% of units serve very low income households (Housing Element Program 14 text) or extremely low income households (Program 23 and 2024 APR wording), adopted by ordinance and resolution in October 2022. Lot merger fees are waived for projects using the Opportunity Site Housing Overlay (Ordinance establishing the overlays, 2024). Affordable projects are also exempt from the Chapter 20.80 impact fee. Dollar value depends on the City fee schedule; a handout on incentives was a 2024 work plan item.

- Cycle: rolling (next: Request at application. Confirm the exact MVMC 5.32 threshold (very low versus extremely low) with Planning before underwriting; the two City documents read describe it differently.)
- Layering notes: A processing-fee waiver is worth tens of thousands of dollars on a Mill Valley project, not a gap closer, but it counts as public funds under Labor Code 1720(b)(4). Stack with the Trust Fund, the housing overlays and State Density Bonus. Mill Valley's title 5 code text was not opened (eCode360 not attempted); terms come from the certified 2023-2031 Housing Element Chapter 4 (opened), the 2024 Annual Progress Report (opened) and the overlay ordinance (opened). marincounty.gov remained Cloudflare-blocked this pass; County programs are referenced from the Marin County records in this database.
