### City of Napa

**Napa 1% Transient Occupancy Tax for Affordable and Workforce Housing Fund (Measure F, November 2018)**
- Agency: City of Napa Housing Division
- Type: loan
- Typical award: Special tax of 1% on hotel and short term rental stays (TOT raised from 12% to 13%), effective January 1, 2019, dedicated solely to affordable and workforce housing projects, programs and services in the City of Napa. FY 2024-25 revenue about $2.8 million; fund balance at June 30, 2025 about $10.2 million unaudited, of which $4 million was formally reserved for specific projects. Measure F campaign estimate was $2.1 million a year. Awards are low or no interest deferred loans under the same rolling NOFA as the impact fee fund.
- AMI requirement: Households at or below 120% AMI. Under the NOFA the TOT fund is targeted primarily to the missing middle (81% to 120% AMI, rents at 30% of 110% AMI) and applications serving that band receive automatic full leverage points. 55-year rental and 45-year ownership regulatory agreements.
- Cycle: rolling (next: Rolling through the Neighborly portal under the combined Affordable Housing and TOT NOFA; City commits to a NOFA at least every two years. No 2025 or 2026 NOFA document found online as of 2026-11-08; confirm availability with the Housing Division (707-257-9628).)
- Layering notes: The only sizable local source in Napa County for moderate income and workforce rental or ownership units, which state programs rarely fund. Pairs with the impact fee loan (80% AMI units) in a mixed income project: impact fee dollars on the low income units, TOT dollars on the 81% to 120% AMI units. The County (Measure I) and the other four cities adopted parallel 1% TOT measures in 2018; each is a separate fund with its own geography, so a Napa city project cannot draw on the County or St. Helena funds. Sources opened: FY 2024-25 CAPER (source_url, fund balance and revenue), 2023 NOFA, Measure F argument in favor, HCD Prohousing designation release (Napa designated 2024) and Prohousing matrix.
- Source: https://www.cityofnapa.org/DocumentCenter/View/14760/CAPER-FY2024-25
- Confidence: verified (researched 2026-11-08)

**Napa Affordable Housing Impact Fee (NMC Chapter 15.94, Ordinance O2018-011) and alternative equivalent proposals**
- Agency: City of Napa Community Development Department (Chief Building Official) and Housing Division
- Type: other
- Typical award: Requirement, not a subsidy. Fee per gross square foot set by implementing resolution; schedule effective January 1, 2017 (phased in from May 2016): multifamily $4.05, single family and condominium $4.75, office and retail $3.55, hotel $6.00, industrial $3.50 per square foot. Collections ran $0.4 million to $3.6 million a year in FY 2014-15 through FY 2018-19 and about $1.7 million in FY 2024-25. An impact fee nexus study was underway in 2023 (Housing Element Program H2-2.7, fee schedule update due by 2028), so expect a higher schedule.
- AMI requirement: Exemption requires rents at 30% of 60% AMI (low), 30% of 50% AMI (very low) or 30% of 30% AMI (extremely low) with a 55-year rental or 45-year ownership affordable housing agreement under 15.94.080. Market rate units, including units for median and moderate income households, pay the fee.
- Cycle: rolling (next: Fee due before building permit issuance, or deferred under a recorded secured building agreement (Government Code 66007) to final inspection or certificate of occupancy; the City routinely defers fees for affordable projects to occupancy. Developers may propose an alternative equivalent proposal (on or off site affordable units, land dedication, conversion of market rate units, preservation) with City Council approval under 15.94.070. Petitions for adjustment or waiver under 15.94.100 must be filed within 30 days of the fee determination.)
- Layering notes: Napa replaced its 1999 inclusionary ordinance with this fee in 2012, so market rate apartments owe no on site affordable units and 100% affordable projects (15% or more affordable) pay nothing. The fee stream capitalizes the Affordable Housing Impact Fee Fund record above. Compare the County fee under County Code 18.107 (Pass 2 record), which was overhauled on October 21, 2025 and phases in from January 16, 2026; the City schedule still dates from 2017 until the nexus study update is adopted. A fee exemption is not a City expenditure, but the City's loans are, so prevailing wage turns on the loan not the exemption. Code text read on the ecode360 mirror (source_url) and the 2018 ordinance PDF; the 2017 rate sheet is at cityofnapa.org/DocumentCenter/View/102.
- Source: https://ecode360.com/43395059
- Confidence: verified (researched 2026-11-08)

**Napa Affordable Housing Impact Fee Fund (Affordable Housing Trust Fund) development loans, rolling NOFA**
- Agency: City of Napa Housing Division (Housing Manager Stephanie Gaul, 707-257-9628)
- Type: loan
- Typical award: Gap loans sized by the joint City and County Multi Family Transaction Underwriting Guidelines (Jan 21, 2020). Minimum award $100,000, no set maximum. Fund balance at June 30, 2025 was $8.7 million unaudited, of which $5 million was formally reserved for specific projects; FY 2024-25 fee collections were about $1.7 million. Track record: $2.2 million general fund plus trust fund money each to Heritage House (90 units, 40 PSH) and Valley Lodge (54 units PSH) in 2022; four projects held reservations from the impact fee and TOT funds at the time of the 2023 Prohousing application. Application fee 1% of the loan request, minimum $10,000 ($5,000 cashier's check at pre-application, $5,000 at award).
- AMI requirement: Units must serve households at or below 80% AMI (rents at 30% of 30%, 50% or 60% AMI by tier). 55-year regulatory agreement for rental, 45 years for ownership, recorded under NMC Chapter 15.94. Mixed income projects are funded only for the proportional share of affordable units. Units must count toward the City RHNA (new construction, adaptive reuse, or qualifying rehab); transitional housing and shelters not eligible. Scoring gives 15 points for at least 20% PSH units and 10 points for 100% affordable.
- Cycle: rolling (next: Rolling, first come first served through the Neighborly portal (portal.neighborlysoftware.com/NAPACA/Participant). The 2023 NOFA accepted applications until June 30, 2024 or until funds were allocated; the City states funds are released at least once every two years by NOFA. No 2025 or 2026 NOFA document was found on cityofnapa.org as of 2026-11-08; contact the Housing Division before preparing an application.)
- Layering notes: The largest city controlled pool in Napa County and the normal local gap layer for 4% and 9% deals inside Napa city limits (Heritage House, Valley Lodge, Jamboree Silverado Trail PSH). Terms mirror the Napa County Affordable Housing Fund record: 3.0% simple interest, 55-year term, 50/50 residual receipts split, subordinate to senior debt, 90% maximum senior LTV, $100 per unit monitoring fee. Stack order: CTCAC credits and CMFA or CalHFA conduit bonds first, then HCD programs (MHP, AHSC, NPLH, Homekey), then City impact fee loan, then City 1% TOT loan for moderate income or missing middle units, with HACN project based vouchers for PSH units. County Affordable Housing Fund money is usually not available for sites inside the city (County preference for unincorporated projects) but the two agencies share underwriting guidelines and have co-funded projects. City loans are public funds, so state prevailing wage applies. Sources opened: 2023 NOFA (source_url), FY 2024-25 CAPER for fund balances, Prohousing Designation matrix, 2023 Housing Element APR.
- Source: https://www.cityofnapa.org/DocumentCenter/View/9332/Notice-of-Funding-Availability-2023-PDF
- Confidence: verified (researched 2026-11-08)

**Napa CDBG entitlement program (Community Development Improvements category) and state HOME and CalHome program income**
- Agency: City of Napa Housing Division (CDBG Advisory Committee recommends, City Council approves)
- Type: grant
- Typical award: About $600,000 of CDBG a year (FY 2026-27 estimate about $600,000, HUD amount pending). After the 15% public service cap and 20% administration cap, the remainder (roughly $390,000) funds physical improvements, housing rehabilitation, property acquisition and nonprofit capital improvements with no category cap. Requests typically total twice the money available. FY 2024-25 rehab loans and grants totaled $135,650 for 10 households. The City is not a HOME participating jurisdiction; it recycles program income from past state HOME and CalHome grants into deferred homebuyer loans.
- AMI requirement: Must meet a CDBG national objective (principally low and moderate income benefit, 80% AMI or below) and a Consolidated Plan 2025-2030 priority: housing rehabilitation, emergency shelter services, nonprofit capital improvements, fair housing, outreach for Latino residents, services for youth aging out of foster care, infill sidewalks in low income block groups.
- Cycle: annual NOFA (next: Annual application cycle each winter for the Annual Action Plan adopted in spring (the 2026-2027 draft Annual Action Plan is posted); next cycle for FY 2027-28 applications expected about January 2027. Contact the Housing Division at 707-257-9543.)
- Layering notes: Napa is the only CDBG entitlement jurisdiction in Napa County (the County and other cities are state non-entitlement, see Pass 2 HOME and CDBG record), but the dollars are small and mostly committed to rehab and services, so CDBG is a predevelopment or site improvement layer rather than a construction gap source. Federal Davis-Bacon applies to CDBG assisted construction of 8 or more units and state prevailing wage applies to public funds. CDBG-DR and CDBG-MIT contract reporting also runs through this office. Source page and the FY 2024-25 CAPER and 2025-2030 Consolidated Plan were opened.
- Source: https://www.cityofnapa.org/181/Community-Development-Block-Grant
- Confidence: verified (researched 2026-11-08)

**Napa Density Bonus (NMC 17.52.130) with Supplemental Density Bonus up to 100%, and :AH Affordable Housing Overlay District incentives (NMC Chapter 17.36)**
- Agency: City of Napa Community Development Department, Planning Division
- Type: density bonus
- Typical award: Requirement and entitlement incentive, not a direct subsidy. State density bonus law implemented through 17.52.130 (O2010-3, O2011-2). Local enhancement: a Supplemental Density Bonus allows the decision making body to grant bonuses, incentives or concessions above the state maximum up to a total of 100% for projects that exceed the state affordability tables or provide amenities and public benefits (underground parking, superior design, common space). Small project bonus lets duplexes and triplexes exceed pod density if the extra units are very low or lower income (30-year restriction). :AH overlay sites (over 2.5 acres, under 10% slope, within one half mile of transit or services) must deliver 10% very low plus 10% low income units in RM, MU or MP districts and receive priority processing, fee deferral to occupancy for all affordable units, access to local affordable housing funds, Housing Authority marketing and density flexibility under 17.52.140.
- AMI requirement: State density bonus thresholds (5% very low, 10% lower income, 10% moderate for sale, senior, etc.) with 55-year restrictions; supplemental bonus requires affordability above the state tables or public benefits. :AH overlay requires 20% affordable (10% very low and 10% low) or an approved alternative equivalent proposal.
- Cycle: rolling (next: Applies at entitlement; large project density bonus decisions are made by the City Council. The 2023-2031 Housing Element (adopted October 17, 2023, certified December 5, 2023) found 17.52.130 out of date with AB 682, AB 1551, AB 2334, AB 571 and SB 290 and committed to update it (Program H2-2.1) in the comprehensive zoning ordinance update that was underway in 2024-2025; check the current code before relying on local terms.)
- Layering notes: Napa is one of the few California cities with a codified local bonus above the state maximum (to 100% total), which matters for small infill sites downtown and along the four General Plan corridor focus areas. AB 2334 (unlimited density and three extra stories for 100% affordable projects in Napa County, a very low vehicle travel area) applies by state law even before the local text is updated. :AH overlay sites in the Housing Element site inventory (including City owned sites under Program H2.F) carry the fee deferral and local fund incentives, which pair with the impact fee and TOT loans above. Density bonus alone does not trigger prevailing wage; City funds do. Code text read on the Zoneomics mirror (source_url for 17.52; chapter_18 for 17.36); the Housing Element PDF and 2023 APR were opened on cityofnapa.org.
- Source: https://www.zoneomics.com/code/napa-CA/chapter_27
- Confidence: verified (researched 2026-11-08)

**Napa Permanent Local Housing Allocation (PLHA) formula share and Junior Unit Initiative Program (ADU and JADU forgivable loans)**
- Agency: City of Napa Housing Division (also delegated administrator of PLHA for American Canyon, Calistoga, St. Helena and Yountville)
- Type: loan
- Typical award: Napa's PLHA formula allocation is programmed 80% to Junior and Accessory Dwelling Unit creation, 15% to homeless services and 5% to administration. The Junior Unit Initiative provides forgivable financing up to $50,000 to create a JADU or conversion ADU, an additional $25,000 interest free deferred loan for conversion ADUs, up to $5,000 for ADA improvements, and design and engineering grants. Owner must occupy one unit and rent the other to a low income tenant under a recorded regulatory agreement.

For multifamily deals this is a negative finding: PLHA in Napa County goes to ADUs and rehab, not construction gaps. See the Pass 2 County PLHA record and the County Affordable ADU Forgivable Loan record for the parallel county program. Sources opened: PLHA page (source_url) and the Junior Unit Initiative page.

**Novato Affordable Housing Requirements (inclusionary), Novato Municipal Code Division 19.24 (Ordinances 1576, 1676 and 1718), with in-lieu fees to the City housing fund**
- Agency: City of Novato Community Development Department, 922 Machin Avenue, Novato, (415) 899-8989
- Type: other
- Typical award: Requirement, not a subsidy. In-lieu fee amounts are set by Council resolution (not published on the code mirror); fees are paid before building permit issuance into a separate City fund earmarked for very low, low and moderate income housing (19.24.040). Council approval of an in-lieu payment is discretionary for projects of 7 or more units and by right for 3 to 6 unit projects and for fractions below 0.70.
- AMI requirement: Sliding scale by project size: 3 to 10 units 10%, then one percentage point per unit from 11 units (11%) to 20 or more units (20%). Rental projects: half of the required units at 50% AMI rents and half at 60% AMI rents (very low and low income). Ownership: half low income (65% AMI pricing) and half moderate income (90% AMI pricing). Fractions of 0.70 or more round up. Deed restrictions through a recorded Inclusionary Housing Agreement; one-for-one replacement of demolished deed-restricted units. Exempt: ADUs and JADUs, residential care facilities for the elderly, single or two-unit projects with homes of 3,000 square feet or less, and AHO overlay projects that meet the overlay's 20% requirement.
- Cycle: rolling (next: Ordinance 1718 (Sept 10, 2024) was the latest amendment read. Confirm the current in-lieu fee resolution and any Housing Element Program 3.F (Evaluate and Adjust Impact Fees) follow-up with the Planning Division.)
- Layering notes: Novato's 20% at 20-plus units with a 50/50 very low and low split is the strictest rental inclusionary standard among the three Marin priority cities and matches the County's 20% in unincorporated Marin; State Density Bonus units are excluded from the base count. ### City of Oakland

**Acquisition and Conversion to Affordable Housing (ACAH) Program and Housing Accelerator Fund partnership (rolling ACAH NOFA, Resolutions 90308 and 90118 C.M.S.)**
- Agency: City of Oakland HCD, Housing Preservation Services, with the San Francisco Housing Accelerator Fund (HAF) as program administrator; applications go to HAF
- Type: loan
- Typical award: Since 2017 ACAH has awarded $59,800,000 to preserve 339 units, with set-aside pools for community land trusts and cooperatives. Current structure (June 2024): $10,000,000 unsecured City loan to HAF pooled with private capital (HAF targets 2.5 to 1 leverage, $25,000,000) for short-term bridge acquisition loans, plus $20,000,000 to $30,000,000 of Measure U committed for City take-out permanent loans that revolve the pool. Rolling ACAH NOFA of $22,000,000 released December 2025. 2025 preserved 48 units (1432 12th Avenue co-op with St. Mary's Center, 1534 29th Avenue with Bay Area Community Land Trust).
- AMI requirement: 55-year regulatory agreement; all units rented to households averaging 80% AMI and below; priority to naturally occurring affordable housing in displacement-risk neighborhoods, CLTs and co-ops.
- Cycle: rolling (next: Rolling; the December 2025 $22,000,000 NOFA remains open through HAF until funds are committed. Confirm balance with HAF or Oakland HCD.)
- Layering notes: Oakland's preservation layer. Comparable to Berkeley's Small Sites Program but much larger. Pairs with Measure W acquisition-rehab RFP planned by the County (about $10,000,000) and county boomerang funds. Rehab scopes over bridge period are modest; larger rehabs can later use 4% credits and bonds. Measure U is the primary capital source so City labor standards apply. Source documents are the October 2026 HCD funding authorization report (Legistar) and the 2025 HCD Annual Impact Report (OpenCities prelive host); the ACAH NOFA itself sits on the 403-blocked oaklandca.gov site.
- Source: https://oakland.legistar1.com/oakland/attachments/6fffddd8-44d0-4cb6-9f7a-bd7e5972ecb2.pdf
- Confidence: verified (researched 2026-11-08)

**Affordable Housing Impact Fee, OMC Chapter 15.72 (2025 amendments, Ordinance 13853 C.M.S.), with exemption for affordable housing projects and Fund 1872**
- Agency: City of Oakland Planning and Building Department (collection, impactfees@oaklandca.gov) and HCD (expenditure through NOFAs)
- Type: fee waiver
- Typical award: Requirement on market-rate housing and a funding source for affordable housing. July 15, 2025 amendments converted the fee from per unit to per square foot (AB 602): multifamily Zone 1 $36.17 per sq ft (was $29,658 per unit), Zone 2 $29.18 (was $23,929), Zone 3 $19.73 but set at 0% through FY 2027-28; townhome $14.98 / $10.97 / $5.99 (Zone 3 at 0%); single family $12.66 / $9.08 / $4.40 (Zone 3 at 0%). Annual Marshall and Swift inflation adjustment each July 1. Exempt: 100% affordable projects, projects providing the on-site or off-site affordable units specified in 15.72.100-110, ADUs, 2 to 4 unit projects, single-family homes under 1,750 sq ft, SB 684 projects, and the first four smallest units in larger projects. All impact fee payments deferred to certificate of occupancy for 100% affordable and density bonus projects (SB 937 alignment). FY 2024-25 AHIF fund: start $18,162,106, end $10,737,051, $6,577,455 spent, $5,893,752 committed, $4,843,299 being committed to NOFA pipeline projects.
- AMI requirement: Exemption requires 100% affordable (manager units excepted) or the on-site mix in 15.72.100 (chosen to align with state density bonus thresholds); fee revenue funds 100% affordable developments for extremely low to moderate income households through the NC NOFA.
- Cycle: rolling (next: Fee due at building permit (installments) or deferred to certificate of occupancy for affordable and density bonus projects; rates adjust each July 1. Zone 3 zero rate expires June 30, 2028 unless extended.)
- Layering notes: Oakland has no general permit or impact fee waiver program; the AHIF exemption plus SB 937 deferral of transportation and capital improvement fees is the relevant relief. Affordable projects still pay the Transportation Impact Fee (Ch. 15.74) but are exempt from the Capital Improvements Impact Fee. AHIF revenue (Fund 1872) is one of the non-bond sources commingled with Measure U in the NC NOFA, so this record both reduces developer cost and feeds the Oakland NOFA record. No county impact fee exists for comparison. Fee rate schedule read in the July 2025 Master Fee Schedule exhibit on Legistar; the annual report FY 2024-25 (November 2025) supplied balances.
- Source: https://oakland.legistar1.com/oakland/attachments/b2194064-f7d7-4deb-b57e-d33d286c32be.pdf
- Confidence: verified (researched 2026-11-08)

**Density Bonus and Incentive Procedure, Oakland Planning Code Chapter 17.107 (Ordinance 13684 C.M.S., 2022), and S-13 Affordable Housing Combining Zone**
- Agency: City of Oakland Planning and Building Department, Bureau of Planning
- Type: density bonus
- Typical award: Requirement and entitlement, not a subsidy. Implements Government Code 65915 with the state tables (20% to 50% bonus for 10% to 24% low income; 20% to 50% for 5% to 15% very low; 80% bonus for 100% affordable projects). Local additions: 100% affordable projects within one-half mile of a major transit stop may waive all density maximums and receive up to three additional stories or 33 feet; condominium conversions with 33% moderate or 15% lower income units get a 25% unit bonus or equivalent incentive; incentive counts of one, two, three or four follow state tiers; parking ratio reductions per 65915(p) and no parking required for qualifying transit-adjacent 100% affordable projects; incentives expressly exclude fee waivers and City land.
- AMI requirement: State thresholds (10% low, 5% very low, 10% moderate for sale, 100% affordable with up to 20% moderate); 55-year restriction for rental.
- Cycle: rolling (next: Submitted concurrently with the planning application; no deadline.)
- Layering notes: Oakland does not offer a local bonus above state law except the transit-adjacent height add for 100% affordable projects. Fee relief comes separately through the AHIF on-site exemption (Ch. 15.72), which was deliberately keyed to density bonus thresholds so a mixed-income project can satisfy both with one affordability mix. Code read on the zoneomics mirror because the City's codepublishing site blocks scripts.
- Source: https://www.zoneomics.com/code/oakland-CA/chapter_84
- Confidence: verified (researched 2026-11-08)

**Jobs/Housing Impact Fee (commercial linkage fee), OMC Chapter 15.68, Fund 1871**
- Agency: City of Oakland Planning and Building Department (collection) and HCD (expenditure)
- Type: other
- Typical award: Linkage fee on office and warehouse projects over 25,000 sq ft: $7.87 per sq ft for permits applied July 1, 2024 to June 30, 2025 ($8.05 in FY 2023-24), inflation adjusted; paid 25% at permit, 50% at certificate of occupancy, 25% eighteen months later. The 2025 amendments extended the fee to additional nonresidential categories. FY 2024-25 JHIF fund: start $13,964,433, end $12,546,460, $12,060,074 committed to affordable developments, $486,386 being committed to pipeline projects.
- AMI requirement: Revenue restricted to acquisition, new construction, substantial rehabilitation and preservation of affordable housing, awarded through HCD NOFAs.
- Cycle: rolling (next: Fee collected continuously; funds flow to the NC NOFA pipeline (next round late 2026 or early 2027).)
- Layering notes: Oakland is one of only two priority cities in the county with a commercial linkage fee (Fremont also has one). Revenue is modest relative to Measure U but is flexible local money with no bond restrictions, which HCD uses for early predevelopment commitments. Developers do not apply to this fund directly; it is part of the NOFA sources table.

**Low and Moderate Income Housing Asset Fund (LMIHAF, Fund 2830), boomerang Affordable Housing Trust Fund (Fund 1870) and HOME program income authorizations (Resolution 90894 C.M.S., 2025)**
- Agency: City of Oakland HCD (housing successor to the Oakland Redevelopment Agency) and Community Development Division (HOME entitlement)
- Type: loan
- Typical award: Program income from residual receipts and payoffs: LMIHAF collected $5,634,227 (FY 2021-22), $5,820,444 (FY 2022-23), $2,132,775 (FY 2023-24) and $2,309,139 (FY 2024-25); HOME program income reallocated through the budget. October 2025 resolution authorized HCD to commit accumulated and future LMIHAF and HOME program income to NOFA pipeline projects without returning to Council, alongside an additional $40,000,000 of Measure U Tranche 2 and just under $30,000,000 from other sources. Boomerang Fund 1870 (former RDA residual property tax) seeded the R2H2 program and remains an eligible NOFA source for predevelopment, acquisition, new construction, operating subsidies and homeless prevention.
- AMI requirement: LMIHAF: housing successor rules (Health and Safety Code 34176.1), majority to 60% AMI and below; HOME: 80% AMI and below with HOME rents; boomerang: locally restricted to affordable housing and homelessness.
- Cycle: rolling (next: No separate application; funds are awarded within the NC NOFA, R2H2 RFP, ACAH and Rehab NOFA processes.)
- Layering notes: Oakland is a HOME participating jurisdiction and CDBG entitlement city in its own right (not in the Alameda County HOME Consortium), so its HOME dollars are separate from the County's consortium RFP recorded at county level. County boomerang funds (county record) and City boomerang Fund 1870 are distinct pots from the same RDA dissolution. These sources are the most flexible local money for predevelopment and operating subsidy where Measure U bond proceeds cannot be used.

**Measure U Affordable Housing Bond: New Construction Notice of Funding Availability (NC NOFA), Resolutions 90419, 90552, 90894 and 91377 C.M.S.**
- Agency: City of Oakland Housing and Community Development Department (HCD), Housing Development Division, 250 Frank H. Ogawa Plaza, Suite 5313; Fay Darmawi, Deputy Director, fdarmawi@oaklandca.gov, (510) 238-3714
- Type: loan
- Typical award: Measure U (Nov 2022, $850,000,000 bond, $350,000,000 for affordable housing in three tranches). Tranches 1 and 2 committed $248,000,000 to 32 projects (New Construction 15 projects, 1,172 units, $167,035,412; R2H2/Homekey 6 projects, $31,564,588; ACAH 11 projects, $37,000,000; 5% admin $12,400,000), leveraging about $5 outside per $1 City. 2024 NC NOFA: 24 applications requesting $424,000,000; January 2025 awards $80,500,000 to 5 projects (583 units); November 2025 pipeline awards $63,500,000; 13 unfunded pipeline applications (919 units, $246,000,000 requested) remain. Tranche 3: $50,000,000 appropriated in the FY 2026-27 midcycle budget and authorized by Resolution 91377 C.M.S. (October 2026), about $35,000,000 of it for the NC NOFA. Typical City loans run roughly $8,000,000 to $20,000,000 per project, 55-year residual receipts.
- AMI requirement: At least 20% of units targeted to homeless exits or extremely low income (0-30% AMI) households with supportive services plan; 55-year regulatory agreement; scoring favors public land, ministerial approvals, readiness for tax credits, emerging developer joint ventures, displacement-risk neighborhoods.
- Cycle: biennial (pipeline NOFA with supplemental awards as funds arrive) (next: Next NC NOFA planned for late 2026 or early 2027 after state HDFC rules settle; awards timed to the spring 2027 tax credit round. Existing pipeline applicants may be advanced ahead of a full round. Confirm release date with HCD (NOFA mailing list).)
- Layering notes: Oakland is the largest city funder in the county (42% of Alameda County affordable permits 2024-25). Stacks with Alameda County Measure A1 Oakland base allocation and Measure W Home Together New Construction RFP (five Oakland projects won Measure W in March 2026: Liberation Park, 500 Lake Park, 3135 San Pablo, East 12th Circle, Brighter Bancroft), county PBVs via OHA, and state HDFC/TCAC. City commitment is intended as the first local layer so projects can show match for county and state rounds. Measure U loans carry Oakland local hire, First Source and prevailing wage requirements; a Project Labor Agreement debate for Measure U projects occurred in 2024. Measure KK (2016, $100,000,000 housing) is fully committed and reported with Measure U. Non-bond sources commingled in the same NOFA: Affordable Housing Impact Fee Fund 1872, Jobs/Housing Impact Fee Fund 1871, boomerang Fund 1870, LMIHAF 2830, HOME 2109, PLHA 2145, excess redevelopment bond funds. oaklandca.gov returns 403 to scripts; all material read from Oakland Legistar attachments and the City's OpenCities prelive host.

- Confidence: verified (researched 2026-11-08)

**Prohousing Designation (renewed 2025, Resolution 90836 C.M.S.) and Prohousing Incentive Pilot Program grants**
- Agency: City of Oakland HCD, Housing Policy Unit
- Type: grant
- Typical award: Oakland was the first Bay Area jurisdiction designated Prohousing (December 2022); renewal for a 3-year term authorized September 16, 2025. Prohousing Incentive Program awards: $2,390,000 (Round 1, 2023) dedicated to capitalized service reserves for deeply affordable housing; Rounds 2 and 3 unsuccessful ($1,390,000 requests); Round 4 application for up to $1,600,000 authorized March 2026 for capitalized service reserves for PSH units in R2H2 or NC NOFA projects.
- AMI requirement: Capitalized service reserves for permanent supportive housing and deeply affordable units identified through City NOFAs.
- Cycle: annual NOFA (state PIP rounds, when issued) (next: Round 4 results pending as of March 2026; next state PIP round unknown, verify with HCD.)
- Layering notes: Developers benefit indirectly: Oakland projects receive Prohousing scoring points in AHSC, IIG, TCC and other state programs, and PIP dollars are routed to service reserves that make PSH projects feasible. Hayward and San Leandro also hold or expect Prohousing status. No county equivalent.

**Rapid Response Homeless Housing (R2H2) and local Homekey program (Resolutions 89977 and 90419 C.M.S.)**
- Agency: City of Oakland HCD, Homeless Housing Development unit
- Type: grant
- Typical award: Program capitalized in 2023 with boomerang Fund 1870 and LMIHAF: $10,400,000 capital plus $19,600,000 operating subsidy; $21,000,000 Measure U Tranche 2 capital added September 2024 for $31,400,000 total capital. Four awards to date (Mandela House, Friendly Manor, Covenant House, the Holland), leveraging over $87,000,000 outside funds (about $4 to $1). About $7,000,000 of Measure U Tranche 2 remained available for new applications as of September 2026; Tranche 3 may add more. City also co-applies for state Homekey+: 2025 awards $7,100,000 The Maya (23 units), $33,000,000 Mark Twain Homes (109 units), $6,500,000 34th and San Pablo (15 PSH units).

Operating subsidy is the binding constraint; the Prohousing Incentive Program award ($2,390,000 in 2023, up to $1,600,000 requested in Round 4, 2026) is dedicated to capitalized service reserves for R2H2 and NC NOFA PSH units. OHA may add project-based vouchers or operating subsidy.

- Agency: City of Oakland HCD, Asset Management Services unit

Health and Safety Loan Program: over-the-counter emergency loans to owners of City-subsidized multifamily housing, generally up to $250,000 per project, 0% interest, 55-year term; balance fully committed ($250,000 Christian Church Homes, $100,000 Coliseum Connections) and a $2,000,000 recapitalization was recommended in October 2026.

### City of Petaluma

**Petaluma Commercial Development Housing Linkage Fee (Ordinance 2171 N.C.S. of 2004, as amended 2011)**
- Agency: City of Petaluma Community Development Department, Housing Division; collected by Building at permit
- Type: other
- Typical award: Requirement, not a subsidy. Fee on new or expanded nonresidential square footage, effective July 1, 2024: commercial $3.47, retail $6.00 and industrial $3.57 per square foot of building space (July 2022 rates were $3.36, $5.81 and $3.46), due before building permit issuance, escalated annually by the ENR Construction Cost Index 20-city average. Exempt: public facilities, public and private schools, churches. Fund balance $2,158,717 as of July 1, 2022 (Housing Element).
- AMI requirement: Proceeds fund housing affordable to households between 80% and 100% AMI under the 2004 ordinance; Housing Element Program 12 directs the City to consider widening the target to extremely low, very low and low income households and to add an automatic CPI adjustment.
- Cycle: rolling (next: Fee rate in effect at building permit; FY 2025-26 and FY 2026-27 schedules could not be opened. Program 12 set 2024 for a nexus study review and end of 2024 to consider revising the AMI target; outcome not confirmed.)
- Layering notes: The linkage fund is one of three revenue sources for Petaluma's Local Housing Trust Fund (see Housing Fund record) and is the only local source aimed at 80-100% AMI workforce units, which makes it a possible match for moderate-income or mixed-income deals that cannot use LIHTC. Petaluma's rates are far higher than Rohnert Park's 2008 linkage fee ($0.69 to $1.19 per square foot) and the County's Workforce Housing fee applies only in unincorporated areas. Read from the City's 2024 Development Impact Fee Schedule on City ProudCity storage.
- Source: https://storage.googleapis.com/proudcity/petalumaca/2024/06/2024-Development-Impact-Fee-SCHEDULE.pdf
- Confidence: verified (researched 2026-11-08)

**Petaluma Housing Fund and Local Housing Trust Fund (Inclusionary In-Lieu Fund, Commercial Linkage Fund, PLHA formula allocation and HCD Local Housing Trust Fund match)**
- Agency: City of Petaluma Community Development Department, Housing Division
- Type: loan
- Typical award: No fixed award size and no NOFA; the City negotiates gap loans and grants project by project. Balances reported in the certified 2023-2031 Housing Element: In-Lieu Fund $3,323,128 and Commercial Linkage Fee fund $2,158,717 as of July 1, 2022; PLHA about $250,000 per year with a $470,905 balance from 2019-2020 program years; HOME program income of $900,000 and $1.1 million of in-lieu funds went to MidPen's 43-unit project at 414 Petaluma Blvd North; the City also received a $1,100,000 HCD Local Housing Trust Fund award in 2022 (HCD award list, not a City page). CDBG entitlement about $330,000 per year (FY 2022-23), mostly for public services and rehab, not new construction.
- AMI requirement: In-lieu and PLHA funds target lower income households (PLHA priority at or below 60% AMI); linkage funds target 80-100% AMI under current ordinance. Terms set in each loan agreement; expect 55-year regulatory agreements consistent with inclusionary rental rules.
- Cycle: rolling (next: No NOFA cycle; approach the Housing Division before a TCAC or CDLAC round. Housing Element Program 13 committed the City to explore new revenue (TOT, short-term rental fees, vacant home tax, employer fee) and to pursue options by 2025, and to consider joining the Renewal Enterprise District JPA; status not confirmed. PLHA allocations require HCD applications each cycle.)
- Layering notes: Petaluma is a CDBG entitlement city and its own PLHA recipient, so it is outside the County's Urban County CDBG and County PLHA records; it is not a HOME participating jurisdiction (uses state HOME and program income). Local funds are small relative to Santa Rosa, so the usual stack is City gap loan plus County CFH plus RED Housing Fund (county records; Petaluma was exploring RED membership) plus LIHTC. Housing Element Program 14 lists expedited review, a dedicated project manager, trust fund participation, density bonus beyond state law and waived, reduced or deferred impact fees as incentives (see density bonus record). Current fund balances were not available because cityofpetaluma.org and its housing reports page return 403 to scripts; the certified Housing Element was read from the City's planpetaluma.squarespace.com site.

**Petaluma Inclusionary Housing Program (Implementing Zoning Ordinance Section 3.040, Ordinance 2663 N.C.S.) and Housing In-Lieu Fee (Resolution 2018-142 N.C.S.)**
- Agency: City of Petaluma Community Development Department, Housing Division
- Type: other
- Typical award: Requirement, not a subsidy. Residential projects of five or more units, including residential components of mixed-use projects, must provide 15% of units on site as affordable (rental and ownership alike). Alternatives require City Council approval as alternative compliance: land donation, an in-lieu payment to the City Housing Fund equal to a 20% inclusionary requirement, or other methods. In-lieu fee for fractional units under 0.5 or approved alternative compliance: $10.12 per square foot (2024 Development Impact and Capacity Fees booklet, effective July 1, 2024), collected at close of escrow for for-sale homes and at final inspection or certificate of occupancy for multifamily. Projects deemed complete before January 1, 2019 use the prior rules.
- AMI requirement: Affordability restrictions of at least 45 years for ownership units and 55 years for rental units; the 2023-2031 Housing Element targets 1,000 inclusionary units (400 very low, 400 low, 200 moderate) over eight years.
- Cycle: rolling (next: Applies at entitlement. Housing Element Program 11 called for a 2024 review of thresholds, in-lieu options and fee structure and a fee recalculation at least every four years; no 2025 or 2026 ordinance or resolution amending the program was found (cityofpetaluma.org blocks scripts, so recent council actions could not be checked). Fee schedule for FY 2025-26 and FY 2026-27 could not be opened.)
- Layering notes: Because the 2018 ordinance removed the by-right in-lieu option, most market-rate projects now build units on site and in-lieu revenue to the Housing Fund has slowed; the Housing Element reports the In-Lieu Fund at $3,323,128 on July 1, 2022 (see Petaluma Housing Fund record). Petaluma's 15% rental requirement is higher than Santa Rosa's 8% low income rule and lower than the City of Sonoma's 25%. The County's Affordable Housing Program fee (county record) applies only in unincorporated areas. Fee data read from the City's 2024 fee booklet and schedule hosted on the City's ProudCity storage; ordinance text itself was not opened because petaluma.municipal.codes and cityofpetaluma.org return 403.

### City of Placerville

**Affordable Housing Density Bonus, Placerville City Code Title 10 Chapter 12 (Sections 10-12-1 to 10-12-13; 2015 text, state-law update ZC 24-05 pending under ROI 2024-01)**
- Agency: City of Placerville Development Services Department, Planning Division, 3101 Center Street, (530) 642-5252, pv.planning@gmail.com
- Type: density bonus
- Typical award: Requirement, not a subsidy. The local chapter still reflects the 2015 version of Government Code 65915: bonus up to 35% for 5% very low, 10% lower or 10% moderate (for-sale) units, 20% for senior housing, land donation bonus up to 35% combined; one to three incentives (reduced lot size, setbacks, lot coverage, height, parking, mixed-use zoning, other cost-reducing regulatory relief) and by-right parking ratios of 1 space (0 to 1 bedroom), 2 (2 to 3 bedrooms) and 2.5 (4 or more). Where the chapter conflicts with state law, state law controls (10-12-1), so the current 80% bonus for 100% affordable projects, unlimited bonus near major transit and up to five concessions apply by operation of state law. The 2025 Annual Progress Report (March 2026) reports the full density bonus ordinance update was deferred to 2026 because of evolving state law.
- AMI requirement: Per state law: income-restricted units for very low (50% AMI), lower (80% AMI) or moderate (120% AMI, for-sale) households with a recorded density bonus housing agreement (10-12-12); rental affordability term per Government Code 65915 (55 years).
- Cycle: rolling (next: Request with the entitlement application (optional pre-application conference). Watch for the Planning Commission and City Council hearings on text amendment ZC 24-05 (density bonus update), dates still TBD on the City's project list; adoption targeted in 2026.)
- Layering notes: No local enhancement beyond state law. Placerville has no local housing trust fund, no inclusionary ordinance or in-lieu fee, no commercial linkage fee, no city NOFA and no redevelopment successor housing funds; the City's affordable housing tools are this chapter, the Housing Opportunity Overlay by-right sites, fee deferral under SB 937, SCIP impact fee financing and sponsorship of state CDBG, HOME and PLHA applications (separate records). Stack with the El Dorado County density bonus and the County PLHA, Trust Fund, HOME/CDBG, PBV and welfare exemption records; the County Traffic Impact Fee offset (Policy B-14) does not apply inside the city, which levies its own traffic impact mitigation fee. Chapter text read from the City's own zoning ordinance PDF; the City page links the amlegal code library, which was not opened.
- Source: https://www.cityofplacerville.org/media/Planning%20Division/Zoning%20Ordinance/ZoningOrdinance.DSDMaster-%20Chapter%2012%20-%20Affordable%20Housing%20Density%20Bonus.pdf
- Confidence: verified (researched 2026-11-08)

**City-sponsored state CDBG, Competitive PLHA and HOME loans for affordable multifamily (non-entitlement city; Housing Element Program C-4) and partnership with Housing El Dorado**
- Agency: City of Placerville Development Services Department (applicant and lender of record for state CDBG and PLHA competitive funds) with El Dorado County Housing Authority (HHSA) and Housing El Dorado
- Type: loan
- Typical award: Pass-through loans sized to each state award, no local cash. Mallard Apartments (Mallard Lane and MacIntosh, 72 units): City CDBG loan $756,000 for acquisition, Competitive PLHA (CPLHA) loan $756,000 for architecture and engineering, IIG $1,105,000 for frontage and offsite work, MHP $11,000,000. Middletown Apartments (Cold Springs Road and Middletown Road, 82 units): CDBG loan $861,000 for acquisition, CPLHA loan $861,000, IIG $2,158,000, MHP $13,000,000. The 2025 progress report adds a $400,000 PLHA loan secured for Mallard/Middletown. Program C-4 commits the City to meet annually with nonprofit developers, apply or co-apply for state and federal funds (CDBG, HOME, PLHA, Section 202 and 811, CalHome), and to establish priority processing and fee deferrals for extremely low income projects.
- AMI requirement: Follows the state source: Mallard and Middletown are 100% affordable at 30% to 60% AMI for 55 years; CDBG and PLHA require at least 55-year covenants for rental new construction.
- Cycle: rolling (next: Tied to HCD state CDBG and PLHA competitive NOFAs (typically fall or late winter per the Housing Element) and HUD rounds in late spring. Contact Planning at least one cycle ahead so the City can adopt the required resolutions; no city NOFA exists.)
- Layering notes: Placerville competes in the same non-entitlement state CDBG, HOME and competitive PLHA pools as El Dorado County, so coordinate with the County's Affordable Housing Unit (Housing@edcgov.us) to avoid both jurisdictions applying for the same project; the County's own records cover County HOME/CDBG participation requests, County PLHA formula funds and the County Trust Fund (no development NOFA). County PHA project-based vouchers and the welfare exemption apply inside the city. Gap order used on the two Placerville projects: 4% LIHTC and bonds (CMFA TEFRA via the County), MHP, IIG, City CDBG and CPLHA loans. The City has no local trust fund, inclusionary fee, linkage fee or RDA successor housing funds; a first-time homebuyer program and workforce housing study (Program C-8, CDBG planning grant by spring 2025) were not advanced as of the 2025 progress report. Source is the City's 2023 Housing Element Annual Progress Report tables (October 8, 2024 Council packet); the 2025 APR staff report of March 24, 2026 was also read.
- Source: https://www.cityofplacerville.org/media/City%20Council%20Staff%20Reports/2024/10%2008%202024/7.7_AttA%20APR%20Tables%20A,%20A2,%20B,%20D,%20LEAP,%20and%20Summary.pdf
- Confidence: verified (researched 2026-11-08)

**Development impact fee deferral for affordable projects (SB 937 implementation, Housing Element Program C-5), ADU impact fee reductions, and Statewide Community Infrastructure Program (SCIP) impact fee financing (Program C-7)**
- Agency: City of Placerville Development Services Department (Planning and Building Divisions) and Finance; SCIP bonds issued by California Statewide Communities Development Authority (CSCDA)
- Type: fee waiver
- Typical award: Timing relief, not a reduction, for multifamily: the City reports it implemented fee deferrals under SB 937 in 2025 so impact fees on qualifying affordable projects are collected at certificate of occupancy rather than permit issuance. Housing Element Program C-5 also offers deferment to completion or occupancy, payment over 12 months or longer after completion, or fee reductions where the applicant documents lower facility demand. Impact fee reductions (water, sewer, traffic impact mitigation, park fees) have been implemented only for ADUs and JADUs consistent with state law. SCIP lets a developer finance City impact fees and public improvements through tax-exempt CSCDA bonds repaid by a special assessment on the parcel; the City intends to offer it for all projects, especially housing, but no development had used SCIP as of the 2023 and 2025 progress reports. No general fee waiver for affordable housing exists.
- AMI requirement: SB 937 deferral applies to projects meeting the statute's affordability definitions (generally 100% affordable or qualifying mixed-income projects); Program C-5 options are for affordable housing providers. SCIP has no affordability requirement.
- Cycle: rolling (next: Request deferral at building permit; SCIP participation requires a City resolution and CSCDA application ahead of permit issuance. Confirm the current fee schedule and deferral form with the Building Division.)
- Layering notes: Placerville levies its own traffic impact mitigation, park and utility fees, so the El Dorado County Traffic Impact Fee offset (Board Policy B-14) does not apply to city projects; deferral is the only local fee tool. SCIP assessment financing of impact fees is senior to other liens and must be cleared with TCAC and permanent lenders. Pair with the HO overlay by-right sites and City-sponsored CDBG, PLHA and HOME loans (separate records). Sources read: the March 24, 2026 City Council staff report accepting the 2025 Housing Element Annual Progress Report (SB 937 deferral statement), the City's Housing Resources page describing SCIP (updated March 4, 2025) and Programs C-5 and C-7 of the 2021-2029 Housing Element.
- Source: https://www.cityofplacerville.org/media/City%20Council%20Staff%20Reports/2026/03%2024%202026/12.3_SR%202025%20Housing%20Element%20APR%20(CK,DW-Fully%20Executed).pdf
- Confidence: verified (researched 2026-11-08)

**Housing Opportunity Overlay Zone (HO, Title 10 Chapter 5 Section 24, Zone Change 2016-01) by-right affordable sites and Housing Element Programs A-3 and A-5**
- Agency: City of Placerville Development Services Department, Planning Division
- Type: other
- Typical award: Regulatory. Sites in the HO overlay (and the R-5 Very High Density Multi-Family zone) allow owner-occupied or multifamily housing by right at a minimum 20 and maximum 24 units per acre with compliance with local design standards and no discretionary action (Government Code 65583.2 sites). The overlay covers about 17 acres with three additional sites proposed for 2026. Two of the four original HO parcels produced Mallard Apartments (72 units, 30% to 60% AMI, 55 years) and Middletown Apartments (82 units, 30% to 60% AMI, 55 years), both by Pacific Southwest Community Development Corporation and under construction in 2025 (82 Middletown permits issued in 2025). Objective design standards (LEAP $65,000 and SB 2 $160,000 funded) were still being completed as of March 2025.
- AMI requirement: By-right status is tied to lower income housing need under state law; projects on HO sites have been 100% affordable at 30% to 60% AMI with 55-year covenants. No local inclusionary percentage.
- Cycle: rolling (next: Ministerial site plan review on HO or R-5 sites at any time. Three additional HO sites were proposed for 2026 rezoning; confirm status and the objective design standards with Planning.)
- Layering notes: The HO overlay is where Placerville's deal flow has actually occurred; both recent projects paired by-right siting with City-sponsored CDBG and CPLHA loans, IIG and MHP (see the City state-funding record). The 2025 APR reports 244 lower income units of site capacity against a 90-unit lower income RHNA, so no-net-loss is not a constraint. Combine with the state density bonus (Chapter 12) and SB 35 or AB 2011 streamlining. Source is the City's 2021-2029 Housing Element policy document (Programs A-3 and A-5); the 2016 draft HO ordinance was also read on the City's EvoGov agenda host. No local trust fund or NOFA exists in Placerville.
- Source: https://www.cityofplacerville.org/media/Planning%20Division/Housing%20Element/2021-2029%20Housing%20Element%20-%20Amended/PolicyDocSect%20II%20-%202021%20HE%20(12-16-22,%20lmh).pdf

### City of Redwood City

**Affordable Housing NOFA and Preservation Program (impact fee fund loans)**
- Agency: City of Redwood City, Housing Services
- Type: loan
- Typical award: May 11, 2026 Council action: about $8 million to Rise City Apartments (94 units, 1304 Middlefield Road, 20% to 70% AMI, 24 PSH units including 19 for adults with intellectual and developmental disabilities, construction early 2027) and a commitment to direct about $5.8 million of expected Elco Yards impact fees to MidPen Housing's 79-unit project at 1580 Maple Street (20% to 40% AMI, 23 special needs units, City-owned land transferred by the County, construction late 2027). Staff had recommended about $12.9 million for the two projects; only two applications were received. The City also runs an Affordable Housing Preservation Program (over-the-counter fund for acquisition and deed restriction; amendments adopted May 11, 2026) and is studying 70 to 104 affordable units on Downtown Library Parking Lot B (1016 Middlefield Road).
- AMI requirement: New multifamily rental for low and extremely low income households; all assisted units at least 10% below 80% AMI; 55-year City regulatory agreement.
- Cycle: annual NOFA (next: 2026 round awarded May 11, 2026; the next NOFA depends on impact fee receipts (Elco Yards payment expected mid-2026). Preservation Program is over the counter.)
- Layering notes: County layer: every San Mateo County city project competes for the County Affordable Housing Fund NOFA (AHF 14 closed July 15, 2026, next fall 2027), HEART bridge loans and HACSM project-based vouchers; city money is usually the first commitment that unlocks those. City loans are residual receipts loans repaid from cash flow after operating expenses, hard debt and reserves, and are sized to leverage County AHF, HACSM PBVs and 4% or 9% credits; 1580 Maple shows the City-County land plus City fee money pattern. Marked needs_confirmation because redwoodcity.org (NOFA page, Preservation Program guidelines, fee schedule) returned 403 to automated access and figures come from the May 12, 2026 Redwood City Pulse report (source) and the City's meetings portal; confirm award terms with Housing Services.

**Affordable Housing Ordinance (Zoning Code Article 29): inclusionary units and Affordable Housing Impact Fee**
- Agency: City of Redwood City, Housing Services (City Manager's Office) and Community Development
- Type: other
- Typical award: Requirement, not a subsidy. Rental projects of 20 or more units: 20% affordable (10% moderate, 5% low, 5% very low income). Ownership projects of 20 or more units: 15% moderate income. Projects of 5 to 19 units and nonresidential projects over 5,000 square feet pay the Affordable Housing Impact Fee (Resolution 15462 of 2015; nonresidential rates raised December 20, 2021 to $23.62 per square foot for office, medical office and R&D and $5.91 for hotel, retail, restaurant and services; residential small-project rate reported at about $20 to $25 per square foot, with a temporary 25% reduction for 5 to 19 unit projects that pull vertical permits by June 30, 2027). Fees fund the City's affordable housing NOFA.
- AMI requirement: Rental units restricted at least 55 years, ownership at least 30 years, recorded covenants in first position; fractional units met by an extra unit or in-lieu fee set by Council resolution; 100% affordable projects exempt from the fee.
- Cycle: rolling (next: Applies at entitlement; fees due before the first building permit. The 2026 San Mateo County multi-city nexus study (Strategic Economics, Redwood City is a participant) may change percentages and fees in 2027.)
- Layering notes: County layer: every San Mateo County city project competes for the County Affordable Housing Fund NOFA (AHF 14 closed July 15, 2026, next fall 2027), HEART bridge loans and HACSM project-based vouchers; city money is usually the first commitment that unlocks those. Redwood City is the deepest inclusionary program in the county at 20% for rental with a very low income tier, which is why most downtown projects negotiate on-site units rather than pay the fee and why the impact fee fund grows mainly from commercial projects (Elco Yards is expected to pay about $5.8 million in 2026). Alternative compliance plans (off-site, land, conversions) go to Council. The ordinance text is on the City's code host (source, Article 29, Ordinances 1130-375 of 2018, 2498 of 2021, 1130-387 of 2023 and 1130-890 of 2024); fee amounts are from the December 20, 2021 staff report on meetings.redwoodcity.org because redwoodcity.org returns 403 to automated access. Confirm the current residential fee and the 25% reduction with Housing Services at (650) 780-7000.

**Richmond Inclusionary Housing and Affordable Housing Linkage Fee Ordinance (Richmond Municipal Code Article 15.04.603, readopted 2020) and in-lieu fee**
- Agency: City of Richmond Community Development Department, Housing Division (Jesus Morales, Housing Manager, 510-620-6649) and Planning Division
- Type: other
- Typical award: Requirement, not a subsidy. Applies to residential and mixed-use projects of 10 or more units. Compliance options: for-sale projects 7% of units at low income or 10% at moderate income; rental projects 9% at very low income or 10% at low income. The in-lieu fee is per square foot and geographically tiered, $0 to $12 per square foot (rental projects south of I-580 and on the Point San Pablo peninsula pay $12 per square foot; market-rate projects north of I-580 are exempt from on-site units and the fee after a 2020 feasibility study); for-sale projects south of I-580 and on Point San Pablo must build units and may not pay the fee. A non-residential affordable housing linkage fee was authorized in the same 2020 update. Collections: $803,055 in-lieu fees in calendar 2020 and $677,194 in 2021. Other alternatives: 10% very low income rental units in a for-sale project, off-site construction, or land dedication yielding at least 10% more units than required.
- AMI requirement: 45-year affordability for for-sale inclusionary units and 55 years for rental units under a recorded Inclusionary Housing Agreement; incentives include the Article 15.04.602 density bonus, clustering of units where a funding source requires it, and smaller or different unit types if at least 5% more affordable units result.
- Cycle: rolling (next: Applies at entitlement; fee due per the Inclusionary Housing Agreement. Housing Element Program 2.A called for reassessment of the ordinance and linkage fee by first quarter 2024 and any amendments by third quarter 2025, with annual performance reports; confirm with the Housing Division whether amendments were adopted.)
- Layering notes: Richmond's 2020 rewrite deliberately lowered requirements north of I-580 (Hilltop, North Richmond edge) to make market-rate housing feasible, so most inclusionary units and fees come from the south side (Marina Bay, downtown, Point San Pablo). Fees and linkage revenue fund the City Affordable Housing Fund (separate record). Richmond's Rent Program (Measure L, 2016) caps rent increases on pre-1995 multifamily and sets just-cause rules, which affects underwriting of acquisition-rehab deals. The County's Chapter 822-4 inclusionary ordinance does not apply inside Richmond. ci.richmond.ca.us pages for the ordinance redirect to a login page and the Municode host is blocked, so terms were read from the City's adopted 2023-2031 Housing Element (Resolution 7-23, source_url, Appendix C and Appendix G); the $12 per square foot tier was corroborated in the City of Antioch's January 2026 countywide in-lieu fee comparison (Attachment G to the March 10, 2026 Antioch council packet).
- Source: https://www.ci.richmond.ca.us/ArchiveCenter/ViewFile/Item/12751
- Confidence: verified (researched 2026-11-08)

**Rocklin Inclusionary Housing Requirements (Municipal Code Chapter 17.95, Ordinance 1195, November 11, 2025) and in-lieu fee into the Inclusionary Housing Trust Fund**
- Agency: City of Rocklin Community Development Department, Planning Division, with the City Manager's Office Housing Division
- Type: other
- Typical award: Requirement, not a subsidy. Housing development projects of 10 or more units must provide 15% of units for low income households, or 10% for very low income, or 5% for extremely low income (rental projects provide rental units; fractional units round up). Exempt: projects complete or with SB 330 preliminary applications before the effective date, projects with at least 50% affordable units, historic landmark portions and statutory development agreement projects. Alternatives: off-site construction, acquisition and rehabilitation of market-rate units, or an in-lieu fee once set by Council resolution, paid before building permit into a separate Inclusionary Housing Trust Fund. Council held a January 13, 2026 hearing on a proposed interim fee of $10 per square foot (opposed by the California Apartment Association) and, per the City's June 9, 2026 Council recap found in search results but not opened, approved an in-lieu fee of $2.75 per square foot with further ordinance updates still in progress. Paying the fee does not qualify a project for a state density bonus.
- AMI requirement: Rental inclusionary units restricted 55 years, for-sale units 45 years, by recorded inclusionary housing agreement approved by Council with the entitlements; units dispersed and comparable to market-rate units; the City tenant preference policy applies.
- Cycle: rolling (next: Applies to applications deemed complete after the ordinance took effect (December 2025). The $2.75 per square foot fee and the trust fund guidelines should be confirmed with Planning; a broader fee study (consultant RFP issued 2024) and ordinance amendments were pending in mid-2026.)
- Layering notes: New in 2025, so the Inclusionary Housing Trust Fund has little or no balance yet; over time it will feed the AHIP Low/Mod loans. A 100% affordable project is exempt and instead benefits from the ordinance by competing for the fee revenue. Compare Placer County Chapter 15.65 (10% inclusionary, unincorporated area). The ordinance text was verified on the zoneomics mirror of the Rocklin code; the fee resolution and June 9, 2026 staff report could not be opened (rocklin.ca.gov 403, Legistar API returns 500 for client rocklin), hence needs_confirmation.
- Source: https://www.zoneomics.com/code/rocklin-CA/chapter_65
- Confidence: needs_confirmation (researched 2026-11-08)

**Rocklin impact fee reduction of 40% for affordable units (Ordinance 1159, January 10, 2023) and SB 937 fee deferral program (Resolution adopted August 26, 2025)**
- Agency: City of Rocklin City Manager's Office, Housing Division (Housing@rocklin.ca.us) and Community Development Department
- Type: fee waiver
- Typical award: 40% reduction of City development impact fees for deed-restricted units at 60% AMI or lower, calculated unit by unit (adopted by Ordinance 1159 with the rate set by resolution the same night). Fee deferral: City park development, traffic, community and recreation center, construction tax, park improvement, public facilities and trails impact fees deferred from building permit to final inspection or certificate of occupancy, secured by a promissory note and deed of trust that may be subordinated to construction financing; since the August 26, 2025 SB 937 policy, deferral to final inspection applies to all designated residential projects without interest, and the AHIP deferral is aligned with it. Staff reported in September 2025 that no reductions or deferrals had yet been processed but estimates had been issued to developers for their financing packages.
- AMI requirement: Fee reduction: units deed-restricted at 60% AMI or lower. AHIP fee deferral eligibility: at least 10% of units at affordable rents for very low income households or at least 49% of units affordable to low income households; fees become payable with interest penalties if the promised units are not delivered by certificate of occupancy.
- Cycle: rolling (next: Apply to Housing@rocklin.ca.us with a preliminary title report before building permit issuance; reductions must be requested before signing a deferral agreement. Municipal Code chapters on impact fees were slated for SB 937 clean-up at a future Council meeting (not confirmed adopted as of this pass).)
- Layering notes: A real cost reduction (not just timing), unlike Roseville, which defers but does not waive. Combine with the $40,000 per unit Low/Mod loan (record above). Placer County Capital Facilities fees and school fees are outside the City program. Verified from the September 9, 2025 Council staff report and the City's fee deferral application form (rocklin.ca.gov/DocumentCenter/View/457).
- Source: https://www.rocklin.ca.gov/DocumentCenter/View/457
- Confidence: verified (researched 2026-11-08)


### City of Rohnert Park

**Rohnert Park Affordable Housing Linkage Fee (Municipal Code Chapter 3.36)**
- Agency: City of Rohnert Park Development Services Department
- Type: other

Nonresidential projects (new buildings, added square footage, remodels or changes of use that increase employment density) pay a linkage fee based on classification: commercial $0.69, retail $1.19 and industrial $0.71 per square foot, rates effective July 1, 2008 and apparently never updated (Development Impact Fees handout revised July 16, 2026). Fund 4225 (Affordable Linkage Fee) held $13,430 at June 30, 2023 after $285,000 of expenditures.
- AMI requirement: Proceeds support affordable housing for very low, low and moderate income households under the inclusionary ordinance's use-of-fees rules.

**Rohnert Park Density Bonus (Municipal Code Section 17.08.020) and affordable housing concessions under Section 17.08.010(E)**
- Agency: City of Rohnert Park Development Services Department, Planning Division
- Type: density bonus
- Typical award: Regulatory. Section 17.08.020 adopts state density bonus law (Government Code 65915 et seq.) by reference with no local increase beyond the state schedule; it sets application contents (project summary table, base and bonus unit counts, replacement housing compliance, parking) and ministerial processing without separate Planning Commission action. Section 17.08.010(E) lets the City Council grant for-sale projects exceeding the inclusionary requirement, and rental projects that include affordable units, additional concessions: an extra density bonus or incentives of equal financial value, waiver of City standards, direct financial assistance (loan or grant) from trust funds, and deferral of all City fees on market-rate units until certificate of occupancy. Projects making all inclusionary units affordable at median, low or very low income get an additional 5% density bonus.
- AMI requirement: State thresholds (5% very low, 10% low, 10% moderate for-sale, 100% affordable) for the state bonus; Council discretion for the local concessions, tied to on-site affordable units.
- Cycle: rolling (next: Submitted with the entitlement application; Council concessions requested through the project approval or a development agreement. Housing Element Program HO-3.B (City Density Bonus Program) and HO-2.E (Workforce Housing Overlay, to be presented by January 2026 and adopted by December 2026 if directed) may add local bonuses; status not confirmed.)
- Layering notes: Rohnert Park relies on development agreements and specific plans rather than a formal local bonus, so negotiate fee deferral, rental fee relief and gap funding together. The Workforce Housing Overlay would be the first local density tool beyond state law; check Planning for its status. The County's density bonus chapter applies only in unincorporated areas. Read from the zoneomics mirror of Title 17 (Ordinance 991, January 27, 2026 version).

**Rohnert Park Inclusionary Housing Ordinance, Municipal Code Section 17.08.010 (re-adopted by Ordinance 991, January 27, 2026): for-sale inclusionary units, Housing In-Lieu Fee and Rental Affordable Housing Fee**
- Agency: City of Rohnert Park Development Services Department (Planning and Building)
- Type: other
- Typical award: Requirement, not a subsidy. For-sale projects over 50 units: 15% of units affordable, half low income (80% AMI) and half moderate income (120% AMI), with 99-year resale restrictions; for-sale projects of 50 units or fewer may instead pay the Affordable Housing In-Lieu Fee of $15,891.95 per unit (Development Impact Fees handout revised July 16, 2026). All new rental projects pay the Rental Affordable Housing Fee of $4.11 per square foot at building permit (first adopted at $3.23 per square foot; adjusted each July 1 by the ENR-CCI San Francisco index); market-rate rental projects have no on-site unit requirement since the 2019 amendment. Fee revenue goes to a segregated affordable housing account used for acquisition, construction and rehabilitation of affordable housing, subsidies, and assistance to other entities, with an annual public report. Developers providing all required units at median, low or very low income get an extra 5% density bonus; alternatives (land donation, transferable inclusionary credits, off-site units, second units for up to half the requirement) need Council approval.
- AMI requirement: For-sale inclusionary units: 99-year minimum agreements; rental projects pay the fee instead. Exemptions include projects with vested rights, fire or disaster rebuilds of the same size, and projects whose development agreement sets alternative affordable housing terms.
- Cycle: rolling (next: Fees adjust every July 1 (ENR-CCI); planning and building application fees are being restudied for a July 1, 2027 update. Ordinance 991 (comprehensive Title 17 update) was adopted January 27, 2026. Large specific plan areas (University District, Southeast Specific Plan, SOMO Village, Downtown) are governed by development agreements that set their own affordable housing terms (University District and SESP at 15%; downtown CenterCal project exempted from the rental fee in exchange for pursuing 15 affordable units).)
- Layering notes: The Rental Affordable Housing Fee is Rohnert Park's main local housing revenue source since the 2011 loss of redevelopment; proceeds (budget Fund 4220) plus in-lieu fees fund gap assistance negotiated case by case (see Rohnert Park affordable housing funds record). A 100% affordable rental project would owe the $4.11 per square foot fee unless waived through a development agreement or the Section 17.08.010(I) adjustment process, so request a waiver early. Rohnert Park's for-sale requirement is lower than City of Sonoma's 25% and Petaluma's 15% (which also covers rentals). Ordinance text read from the zoneomics mirror of Title 17; fee amounts from the City's Development Impact Fees handout on rpcity.ca.gov (the former rpcity.org pages redirect and return 404).
- Source: https://www.rpcity.ca.gov/DocumentCenter/View/188/Development-Fees-Handout-PDF
- Confidence: verified (researched 2026-11-08)

**Rohnert Park affordable housing funds (Rental Affordable Housing Fee and Housing In-Lieu Fee account, Housing Fund) and Essential Housing Bond Financing Program (Housing Element Programs HO-3.F and bond program)**
- Agency: City of Rohnert Park Development Services Department and City Manager's office; City Council approves assistance
- Type: loan
- Typical award: No NOFA; the City provides gap loans or grants and land through development agreements and Council action, drawing on the segregated affordable housing fee account (budget Funds 4220 Affordable Housing Rental Fee and 4225 Affordable Linkage Fee) and the Housing Fund named in the 2023-2031 Housing Element as a funding source for Programs HO-1.B and HO-3.F (affordable housing on underutilized City sites, including extremely low income units). The Housing Element's Essential Housing Bond Financing Program commits the City to authorize CSCDA or another JPA to issue an estimated $191.3 million in governmental-purpose bonds for acquisition-conversion of market-rate apartments and new deed-restricted housing, forgoing about $337,346 in property tax and targeting at least 222 units (99 very low, 57 low, 66 moderate). Current fund balances and any adopted lending guidelines were not found; the City's budget and Housing Successor (LMIHAF) reports could not be located online.
- AMI requirement: Fee revenue must serve very low, low and moderate income households (Section 17.08.010(J)); bond program units for very low to moderate income; City-site projects target extremely low income units.
- Cycle: rolling (next: Unknown, verify with agency. Contact Development Services (707-588-2231, Planning@rpcity.org). The Housing Element set July 2023 for joining a JPA for the bond program and January 2026 for the Workforce Housing Overlay; a Council and Planning Commission joint meeting on housing was held February 5, 2026.)

Local money is thin, so the practical stack is County CFH, County PLHA (Rohnert Park is a non-entitlement city within the County PLHA), RED Housing Fund and County PBVs (county records) plus LIHTC, with the City contributing fee deferrals, land (Program HO-3.F) or a modest gap loan. Rohnert Park's former Community Development Commission was a redevelopment agency, so a Housing Successor LMIHAF may exist; no annual report was found (flag for follow-up). **Roseville 10% Affordable Housing Goal in Specific Plan Areas (General Plan Policy LU5.5, Housing Element Programs 6 and 9) with Affordable Housing Regulatory Agreements and case-by-case in-lieu fees**
- Agency: City of Roseville Housing Division (compliance) and Development Services Department, Planning Division (specific plans)
- Type: other
- Typical award: Requirement, not a subsidy. Every specific plan area must designate 10% of total units as affordable (General Plan goal since 1989: 20% of the affordable units at middle income up to 100% AMI, 40% low income up to 80% AMI, 40% very low income up to 50% AMI), allocated to specific medium and high density parcels and secured by Development Agreements and Affordable Housing Regulatory Agreements recorded before building permits or final small-lot maps. Since 1989 the policy has produced 5,167 affordable units (1,357 very low rental, 2,271 low rental, 427 middle rental, 325 moderate rental, plus 787 purchase units), about 140 per year. The City has no formal in-lieu fee ordinance; in-lieu fees are negotiated case by case ($1,036,410 collected 2013 to 2021). A 2025 Housing Tools Inclusionary Housing Policy Analysis recommended standard fee levels, for example $150,000 per required affordable for-sale unit in projects under 20 units, applied in the East Street Subdivision amendment approved November 4, 2026.
- AMI requirement: Rental units restricted by Affordable Rental Housing Agreements (about 2,700 units under agreement in the 2021 to 2029 period); density bonus (Chapter 19.28) may be assigned by the Regulatory Agreement as part of the subsidy. Sierra Vista Specific Plan: 10% of 8,679 units (about 868) allocated to MDR and HDR parcels, with transfers and credits between parcels allowed by Housing Division approval.
- Cycle: rolling (next: Applies at specific plan and Development Agreement approval; the in-lieu fee option is considered case by case at agreement amendment. The 2021 Housing Element also directs work on a commercial linkage fee (nexus study November 2021, draft ordinance posted, not adopted as of this pass).)
- Layering notes: The reason Roseville has a steady supply of affordable parcels and developers: specific plan landowners (Sierra Vista, West Roseville, Amoruso Ranch, Villages West and others) carry a 10% obligation and typically deliver dedicated HDR parcels or partner with USA Properties, Mercy Housing, St. Anton, Eden Housing and others. Hope Way and the County in-lieu fee program (County Code Chapter 15.65) apply only in unincorporated Placer; inside Roseville this goal and the Regulatory Agreements govern. In-lieu fees collected flow to the Local Housing Trust Fund (record above). Density bonus units are excluded from the 10% base. Verified from the adopted 2021 Housing Element PDF, the Sierra Vista Specific Plan Affordable Housing chapter and the November 4, 2026 Council packet.
- Source: https://www.roseville.ca.gov/Documents/Development%20Services/Planning/Housing%20Element/Housing%20Element.pdf
- Confidence: verified (researched 2026-11-08)

**Roseville CDBG entitlement and HOME funds (annual Action Plan) and Permanent Local Housing Allocation (PLHA) Plan adopted September 2, 2026**
- Agency: City of Roseville Housing Division (Dani Calli, Housing Analyst, 916-774-5277, dcalli@roseville.ca.gov)
- Type: grant
- Typical award: Roseville is a HUD entitlement city; the 2026-27 CDBG award was expected at roughly $700,000 with about $730,000 of prior-year carryover and about $50,000 program income (2026 Action Plan hearing May 6, 2026; 2025-26 CAPER public comment August 29 to September 16, 2026). CDBG is mostly used for owner rehabilitation loans (deferred loans up to $100,000, $5,000 grants for elderly and disabled owners), accessibility work (over $1 million earmarked in 2026 for Sierra Gardens accessibility upgrades) and public services, but it has funded affordable housing land acquisition: a $571,850 CDBG loan to Greek Orthodox Housing Corporation on September 4, 2024 for parcel JM-30 (192-unit Sierra Vista Apartments). HOME funds (state-administered) support first-time homebuyer and rehabilitation programs. PLHA: Roseville's formula allocation under HCD's July 2026 NOFA (about $285 million statewide, five-year term) is programmed in the City's PLHA Plan (Resolution 26-327) for Homeless Prevention and Rapid Rehousing, not development; $1,374,763 of PLHA was budgeted for HPRR in FY2026-27.
- AMI requirement: CDBG national objective (low and moderate income benefit; 2026 Sacramento PMSA limits: 1 person $73,600, 4 persons $105,100); HOME and PLHA income rules per program.
- Cycle: annual NOFA (winter) (next: 2026 round: applications were due February 2, 2026, with the hearing May 6, 2026. Expect the 2027 CDBG and HPRR NOFA in December 2026 or January 2027 with applications due about early February 2027 and Council action in May 2027; confirm with the Housing Division.)
- Layering notes: Roseville runs its own CDBG and PLHA; Placer County's PLHA allocation (county record, needs_confirmation) covers the unincorporated area and non-entitlement cities such as Auburn, while Lincoln became its own CDBG entitlement in 2026 and Rocklin receives its own PLHA formula share. CDBG land loans trigger federal cross-cutting rules (Davis-Bacon for 8 or more units, environmental review, Section 3). PLHA is currently committed to HPRR, so do not count on PLHA for development in Roseville. The CDBG page, PLHA notice and the September 2, 2026 agenda were opened; the PLHA Plan PDF link itself was not fetched.
