**City of Sonoma Affordable Housing Trust Fund (established May 2019, funded by 1% of Transient Occupancy Tax and inclusionary in-lieu fees)**
- Agency: City of Sonoma City Manager's office and Planning Department; grants approved by City Council
- Type: grant
- Typical award: Small, case-by-case grants and loans approved by Council. Most recent award: $250,000 grant approved June 18, 2025 (agreement authorized July 16, 2025) to Burbank Housing toward acquisition and 55-year preservation of 18 units at Setzer Senior Apartments (8 units, 673 First St West) and Maysonnave Apartments (10 units, 270 First St East), leveraged with a $4.5 million BAHFA Housing Preservation Loan Pilot loan and San Francisco Housing Accelerator Fund financing; closed fall 2025. Revenue: Council approved on June 10, 2019 the final 1% of the Measure S TOT increase (TOT now 13%) effective September 1, 2019 to address affordable housing, estimated at the time at about $350,000 to $400,000 per year, plus in-lieu fees under Section 19.44.030. Press accounts put the balance at roughly $1.4 million to $1.9 million in 2025-2026; no City balance figure was opened.
- AMI requirement: Grant terms set per project; the 2025 preservation deal requires affordability for at least 55 years with rents averaging 30% of 80% AMI and tenants protected on modest income increases. The fund is earmarked for very low, low and moderate income housing (Section 19.44.030).
- Cycle: rolling (next: No NOFA. Requests go to City Council; the Council's 2026 priorities include creating a funding plan and policy for use of the Housing Trust Fund, so an allocation policy may be adopted in 2026-2027 (verify with the City Manager's office, (707) 938-3681).)
- Layering notes: Sonoma is a non-entitlement city inside the County's Urban County and County PLHA area, so projects in the city should combine this fund with County CFH, County HOME and CDBG, County PLHA, RED Housing Fund and County PBVs (county records); the 2025 Burbank deal shows the pattern with BAHFA regional preservation money. Housing Element Program 7 commits the City to pursue a Prohousing Designation and to request RED JPA membership in 2024 (status not confirmed). The City also runs an ADU fee waiver program (housing strategies page) and lists Policy H-4.6 fee waivers for affordable housing, but no multifamily fee waiver ordinance was found. Council staff reports on the civicweb portal could not be reached by meeting date; the City's press release and TOT page were used as sources.

**City of Sonoma Density Bonus and incentives, Development Code Sections 19.44.040 through 19.44.080 (Housing Element Program 19)**
- Agency: City of Sonoma Planning Department and Planning Commission (reductions in standards); City Council for other incentives
- Type: density bonus
- Typical award: Regulatory. Adopts state density bonus law (Government Code 65915 through 65918) by reference; bonus percentage calculated under 65915(f), inclusionary units count toward the bonus, one bonus per project, Planning Commission may waive or modify standards to fit bonus units, incentives include reduced standards, mixed-use zoning, other cost-reducing incentives and state parking ratios. No local bonus beyond state law, though Housing Element Program 19 contemplates streamlined processing and a density bonus or incentives for projects not otherwise eligible under state law, and reduced parking for affordable and special needs housing (Program 18). Density bonus and inclusionary units are exempt from the Chapter 19.94 growth management allocation.
- AMI requirement: State thresholds; affordable units restricted in perpetuity under Section 19.44.060 (2016 amendments raised the term from 30 to 55 years and 2021-2023 amendments made it perpetual).
- Cycle: rolling (next: Density bonus request filed with the first entitlement application; Housing Element Program 19 schedules an update of Chapter 19.44 to current state law (Program 15 code amendments noticed January 2026).)
- Layering notes: Past projects using the bonus include Firehouse Village and Maysonnave Apartments. In a city with low base densities and an urban growth boundary, the state bonus plus the 25% inclusionary rule is the main production tool; pair with the Affordable Housing Trust Fund and County sources. Read from the zoneomics mirror of the Sonoma Development Code (codepublishing.com and sonoma.municipal.codes return 403).
- Source: https://www.zoneomics.com/code/sonoma-CA/chapter_4
- Confidence: verified (researched 2026-11-08)

**City of Sonoma Inclusionary Housing requirement and in-lieu fee, Development Code Chapter 19.44 (Sections 19.44.020 and 19.44.030, Ordinance 06-2021)**
- Agency: City of Sonoma Planning Department
- Type: other
- Typical award: Requirement, not a subsidy. Projects of five or more parcels or units must make at least 25% of units affordable: rental projects 5% extremely low, 10% very low and 10% low income (sequenced ELI, VLI, LI, then middle income); ownership projects 5% low, 10% moderate and 10% middle income. Projects of four or fewer units pay an in-lieu fee per Section 19.44.030; fractions below 0.5 may be paid as a fee. In-lieu fees are paid before building permit into the City's housing trust fund. Fee amount is set by Council resolution (amount not opened); Housing Element Program 1 called for a nexus-supported in-lieu fee by December 2023 and a July 2024 amendment requiring perpetual affordability. Units of 850 square feet or less, ADUs and additions under 850 square feet are exempt. Affordability is in perpetuity under Section 19.44.060.
- AMI requirement: Rental: 25% of units split 5% ELI, 10% VLI, 10% LI; ownership: 25% split 5% LI, 10% moderate, 10% middle income; restricted in perpetuity by recorded affordability agreement; affordable units must average at least 75% of market-rate unit floor area with the same bedroom count.
- Cycle: rolling (next: Applies at entitlement. Housing Element Program 1 schedules a review of the inclusionary provisions and Development Code amendments by 2026; Program 15 Development Code amendments were noticed under CEQA in January 2026. Check with Planning (707) 938-3681 for the current in-lieu fee resolution.)
- Layering notes: At 25% with deep targeting, this is the strictest inclusionary rule among the Sonoma County priority cities, and the City says it has produced about 293 inclusionary and density bonus rental units inside 40 market-rate projects (about six units a year). Because the required ELI and VLI units can also qualify a project for a state density bonus (Chapter 19.44 counts inclusionary units when calculating the bonus), most market-rate rental projects in Sonoma pair the two. In-lieu revenue feeds the Affordable Housing Trust Fund (separate record). Growth management (Chapter 19.94 Housing Allocation Process) exempts affordable and density bonus units from the annual allocation. Code read from the zoneomics mirror (codepublishing.com returns 403); the City's Housing Policies page confirms the 25% rule.
- Source: https://www.zoneomics.com/code/sonoma-CA/chapter_4
- Confidence: verified (researched 2026-11-08)


### City of South Lake Tahoe

**City direct gap and predevelopment financing for affordable housing (HOME program income, Housing Successor and Redevelopment Agency program income, PLHA formula funds, Prohousing Incentive Program funds, general fund, residential units of use) and state application sponsorship**
- Agency: City of South Lake Tahoe Development Services Department, Housing Division (Housing Manager, mmanuel@cityofslt.gov, 530-542-7417); City Council approves each commitment
- Type: loan
- Typical award: Deal-by-deal Council commitments, no NOFA or written guidelines. Track record: over $2.5 million of HOME program income, Redevelopment Agency program income and general fund to Sugar Pine Village (248 units, Related California and Saint Joseph Community Land Trust on state surplus land; Phase 1A 68 units opened fall 2024, Phase 2A 60 units fall 2025, Phase 1B 60 units summer 2026, Phase 2B seeking financing), plus City-sponsored AHSC ($17,359,470), MHP ($19.6 million), IIG, LGMG, HOME and PLHA awards; a $564,073 predevelopment loan plus $500,000 of Prohousing Incentive Program funds to Novin Development for the 75-unit 3900 and 3908 Lake Tahoe Boulevard project (SB 35 approval 2025, AHSC pending); about $1,791,669 CDBG-CV and $120,000 PIP for rehabilitation of three Homekey properties (72 supportive units) with Tahoe Coalition for the Homeless; 21 multifamily residential units of use donated to Lake Tahoe Community College's 100-bed dorm (about $315,000 market value); three Al Tahoe lots donated to Saint Joseph Community Land Trust. City awards 2020 to 2025 included PLHA formula about $880,000 total, PLHA competitive $15 million over three awards, HOME $6,538,240 and PIP Round 2 $620,000. Legacy RDA Low and Moderate Income Housing Fund loans (AB 987 database) total $16.46 million HOME, $2.15 million RDA and $1.18 million CDBG across 296 units in eight projects.
- AMI requirement: Follows the state source layered in: Sugar Pine Village and 3900 Lake Tahoe Boulevard are 55-year deed restrictions at 30% to 80% AMI; TRPA deed restriction also required when bonus units are used. HOME program income follows HOME rules.
- Cycle: rolling (next: No NOFA. Approach the Housing Division ahead of the AHSC, MHP and PLHA competitive rounds; the City committed to apply for at least one state or federal grant per year (Housing Element Program 2-1). Phase 2B of Sugar Pine Village still lacked a local match as of the August 2026 draft Housing Element. Final 2027-2035 Housing Element adoption was scheduled for a September 8, 2026 Council hearing; confirm the adopted program list.)
- Layering notes: South Lake Tahoe is a non-entitlement city that has out-raised most small cities by sponsoring state applications (PLHA competitive, AHSC, HOME, IIG, LGMG) for a nonprofit or private developer, so the City's own cash is small but its sponsorship is the key to the state layer. Gap order used on Sugar Pine Village: LIHTC and bonds, AHSC and MHP, IIG and LGMG, HOME and PLHA, City program income last. County layers available in the Tahoe Basin: El Dorado County PLHA formula and County HOME/CDBG participation requests, County Affordable Housing Trust Fund (no development NOFA), County PHA project-based vouchers, CMFA TEFRA approvals, welfare exemption, BHSA housing funds; the County Traffic Impact Fee offset (Policy B-14) does not apply inside the city because the City levies its own fees. TRPA layer: bonus units and the allocation exemption are required for any deed-restricted project (see the TRPA record), and TRPA application fees are waived for affordable projects. Residential allocations are scarce (33 market-rate per year citywide, one third reserved for multifamily), which is why deed-restricted projects using bonus units are the only route to scale. Workforce Housing Fund in-lieu fees (inclusionary record) are a separate, newer pool. No local housing trust fund, no city NOFA, no local tax-exempt issuer. Source is the City's August 2026 public review draft 2027-2035 Housing Element on the City DocumentCenter; the City's CivicPlus pages opened directly but council packets were not reachable (Granicus and Legistar hosts not found).
- Source: https://www.cityofslt.gov/DocumentCenter/View/24379/SLT_Housing-Element_Public-Review-Draft_August-2026
- Confidence: verified (researched 2026-11-08)

**City permit fee waiver for nonprofit and public agency affordable housing (City Code Section 6.55.090), lot consolidation fee waiver for deed-restricted units (Housing Element Program 1-7) and Sugar Pine Village inspection fee reduction**
- Agency: City of South Lake Tahoe Development Services Department (Planning and Building Divisions); waivers approved by the City Council at a public hearing
- Type: fee waiver
- Typical award: Case by case. Nonprofits and public agencies developing affordable housing may request waiver of City permit fees, granted by Council resolution (about 45 days from request to approval, run concurrently with permit review). The City also reduced building inspection fees for Sugar Pine Village because HCD inspects the modular units. Program 1-7 commits the City to waive the lot line adjustment fee when the resulting project includes deed-restricted affordable units. City planning fees are modest relative to TRPA fees; City multifamily impact charges are mainly utility connection fees set by South Tahoe Public Utility District (not waived; $7,500 deposit and 10% of capacity fees at plan review). No waiver of TRPA water quality ($1.86 per sq ft) or excess coverage mitigation fees ($8.50 per sq ft), though TRPA application fees are waived for affordable, moderate and achievable bonus-unit projects and the mobility mitigation fee may be waived.
- AMI requirement: Affordable housing project sponsored by a nonprofit or public agency; deed restriction consistent with TRPA affordable, moderate or achievable definitions when bonus units are used. No specific AMI threshold published for the City waiver.
- Cycle: rolling (next: Request with the entitlement or building permit application; Council hearing required. Verify current practice with the Housing Division (530-542-7417) because the code text could not be opened.)
- Layering notes: Fee relief is small in dollar terms; the real cost drivers in the Basin are TRPA mitigation fees, land coverage purchases and development rights, which the TRPA bonus unit program (separate record) addresses. Combine with the TRPA application fee exemption and with the Phase 2 Housing Amendments height, coverage and density relief. Private for-profit developers are not eligible for the 6.55.090 waiver unless partnered with a nonprofit or public agency. The County Traffic Impact Fee offset (Board Policy B-14) is not available inside the city. The City's code host (codepublishing.com) returned 403 and the gocodebook mirror had no Chapter 6.55 page, so Section 6.55.090 was not read directly; the description is taken from the fees and exactions analysis in the City's August 2026 public review draft 2027-2035 Housing Element (pages 4-203 to 4-206) and from Program 1-7 of the adopted 2022-2027 Housing Element.

**Inclusionary Housing Ordinance (City Code Chapter 6.27, Ordinance 1180, adopted December 2024) and Workforce Housing Fund in-lieu fees**
- Agency: City of South Lake Tahoe Development Services Department, Planning Division and Housing Division (fund held by the Finance Director); 1052 Tata Lane, 530-542-7417
- Type: other
- Typical award: Requirement, not a subsidy. New residential construction, redevelopment of 50% or more of a building with dwellings, or condo conversion must provide inclusionary units or pay an in-lieu fee scaled to unit size (habitable square feet): 2,000 sq ft or less exempt; 2,001 to 2,500 sq ft 5% of units or $5.29 per sq ft; 2,501 to 3,000 sq ft 6% or $5.84 per sq ft; 3,001 to 5,000 sq ft 9% or $16.77 per sq ft; over 5,000 sq ft 17% or $17.65 per sq ft. Fees are paid before building permit issuance (by phase for phased projects) into the Workforce Housing Fund for housing affordable to low and moderate income households. Fund balance and collections to date are not published; the 2027-2035 draft Housing Element commits the City to post requirements, fee amounts and annual collections by mid-2027 and to publish a five-year in-lieu fee report under AB 2663.
- AMI requirement: Inclusionary units deed restricted for rent or sale to lower income households (80% AMI or below, El Dorado County), priced at no more than 30% of gross income including utilities, dispersed on site, comparable in exterior quality and bedroom mix, built concurrently with market-rate units. No affordability term is stated in the chapter text that was read.
- Cycle: rolling (next: Applies at building permit; fee schedule in effect at permit issuance. Annual monitoring review each June under draft Program 2-10 with amendments within six months if warranted; first AB 2663 reporting for calendar 2026 due in 2027. Verify any fee indexing with the Planning Division before permit.)
- Layering notes: This is the only locally generated housing fund in South Lake Tahoe. Multifamily rental projects are exempt from both the unit requirement and the fee, so apartment developers owe nothing; the fund is fed by large single-family and condo construction, which is the dominant product in the Basin. Spending the Workforce Housing Fund is at Council discretion with no NOFA or guidelines published; pair requests with the City's HOME program income, PLHA formula and Prohousing Incentive Program dollars (see the City direct financing record) and with the County Affordable Housing Trust Fund, County PLHA and County HOME/CDBG records, which also have no standing NOFA. The ordinance grew out of Housing Element Program 2-11 (2022 to 2027 cycle) and the January 2023 Analysis of Local Funding Sources, which modeled TOT and transfer tax increases, a vacancy tax, a commercial linkage fee and an in-lieu fee against a $3.35 million annual local funding need; Council proceeded only with the inclusionary fee. No vacation rental (Measure T) or TOT revenue is earmarked for housing, and Measure T itself was struck down by the El Dorado County Superior Court in March 2025 and replaced by VHR Ordinance 2025-1200 (effective July 17, 2025) and a 2026 ordinance. Blocked hosts: codepublishing.com (the City's code host) returned 403 and the City Agenda Center search errored; the chapter was read on the gocodebook code mirror, and the adoption date and background come from the City's August 2026 public review draft 2027-2035 Housing Element (cityofslt.gov DocumentCenter View 24379).
- Source: https://gocodebook.com/library/us/ca/south-lake-tahoe-zoning/title-6-development-services/division-2-local-amendments-to-adopted-codes/chapter-6.27-inclusionary-housing
- Confidence: verified (researched 2026-11-08)

**TRPA Residential Bonus Unit Program (TRPA Code Chapter 52), allocation exemption (Chapter 50.5.1) and Phase 2 Housing Amendments as applied in South Lake Tahoe Town Centers (Tourist Core, Tahoe Valley and Midtown Area Plans)**
- Agency: Tahoe Regional Planning Agency (TRPA), with City of South Lake Tahoe Planning Division as lead reviewer inside Area Plan boundaries; City holds a voting seat on the TRPA Governing Board
- Type: density bonus
- Typical award: Regulatory, not cash, but it substitutes for development rights that otherwise must be bought. Deed-restricted affordable (80% AMI), moderate (120% AMI) or achievable (TRPA-set percentage tied to median home price) units receive residential bonus units at no cost in place of a residential unit of use (potential unit plus allocation), are exempt from the City's annual allocation (33 market-rate allocations per year citywide, one third reserved for multifamily), and are exempt from TRPA application fees. About 946 of the 1,124 bonus units set aside in 2018 remained as of the 2026 draft Housing Element, all reserved for deed-restricted housing and prioritized for Centers and multifamily zones. Phase 2 Housing Amendments (TRPA Governing Board, December 2023; MAP settlement July 2024) remove the maximum density cap for 100% deed-restricted projects in Town Centers, allow heights up to 65 feet in Centers (step-back, shade and scenic findings above 56 feet), allow 100% deed-restricted projects outside Centers to transfer in coverage up to 70% of high-capability land if runoff is treated by a public stormwater system, and allow use of the TRPA basin-wide parking study to reduce parking. Affordable projects using these tools have reached 61 to 67 units per acre in the city (Sugar Pine Village, 3900 Lake Tahoe Boulevard).
- AMI requirement: Permanent TRPA deed restriction recorded as a permit condition: occupancy limited to affordable, moderate or achievable households (or local employees for achievable units), no second-home or vacation rental use, annual compliance report to TRPA (penalties up to $5,000 per day), real estate disclosure on transfer; project within one half mile of transit. Height, coverage and density incentives under Phase 2 require 100% deed-restricted units plus stormwater and transportation contributions.
- Cycle: rolling (next: Bonus units assigned at TRPA permit (about 120 days of TRPA review, or City-only review for qualifying projects inside the TCAP and TVAP). Watch: TRPA Phase 3 (Cultivating Community, Conserving the Basin) EIS scoping closed March 16, 2026 with further code changes pending; City Midtown Area Plan (MTAP) adoption was pending a September 2026 hearing; TRPA 2025-2026 income limits and achievable percentages are updated each July.)
- Layering notes: Flag for every South Lake Tahoe deal: the Tahoe Basin is dual-jurisdiction. The City cannot grant a state density bonus law bonus or concessions that exceed TRPA standards; TRPA gives full density relief only to 100% deed-restricted projects and gives no comparable benefit or mandatory concessions to mixed-income projects that set aside a share of units, which the draft 2027-2035 Housing Element names as a continuing constraint (Program 2-8 asks TRPA to allow state density bonus compliance). Land coverage (Bailey system, 30% base outside Area Plans, 70% inside TCAP and TVAP), scenic and height limits and the allocation system govern feasibility more than zoning. Projects using bonus units must carry a TRPA deed restriction in addition to TCAC, HCD or City covenants; coordinate the three so income limits (TRPA uses county AMI for a family of three) and terms do not conflict. The TRPA application fee waiver stacks with the City Section 6.55.090 waiver (separate record). County layers (PLHA, Trust Fund, PBVs, welfare exemption) apply as in the rest of El Dorado County. Source pages at trpa.gov opened directly; City-specific figures (946 bonus units remaining, 61 to 67 du per acre, 65-foot height, MTAP status) come from the City's August 2026 draft Housing Element on the City DocumentCenter.
- Source: https://www.trpa.gov/housing/
- Confidence: verified (researched 2026-11-08)


### City of South San Francisco

**Commercial Linkage Fee fund (Fund 823) and Affordable Housing Trust Fund loans**
- Agency: City of South San Francisco Economic and Community Development Department, Housing Division
- Type: loan
- Typical award: Commercial Linkage Fee (SSFMC 8.69, adopted 2018): office and R&D $17.38 per square foot, hotel $5.80, retail, restaurant and services $2.90 (January 2025 handout). Fund 823 revenue swung from $7.5 million (FY 2022-23) to a projected $1.5 million in FY 2025-26, $19.3 million in FY 2026-27 and $8.5 million in FY 2027-28 (Genentech, Trammell Crow and Healthpeak payments); projected year-end FY 2024-25 balances were $14 million in Fund 823, $200,000 in the Affordable Housing Trust Fund (Fund 205) and $1 million in the housing successor fund (Fund 241). City loans: Rotary Gardens Phase 1, 500 Linden Avenue, up to $7,867,409 (August 11, 2026); Synergy Community Development acquisition of the Metropolitan Hotel, 220 Linden, up to $3,115,000 from Fund 823 (February 24, 2026); 1051 Mission Road (BRIDGE, 158 units, PUC site) $2,000,000 raised to $2,362,000 as the LHTF match plus up to $14.6 million committed April 22, 2026 from the first market-rate phase for Measure K and tax credit applications; 428-432 Baden (For the Future Housing, 36 units) $4,050,000; 201-219 Grand and 418 Linden (ROEM, 84 units) $3,500,000; 201 Baden (Eden, 82 units) $2,362,500 LHTF. City also holds a $28,817,500 IIG grant for 1051 Mission and $890,000 PIP.
- AMI requirement: Trust Fund serves low and moderate income households; LHTF-matched loans require extremely low and very low income units; 55-year City regulatory agreements.
- Cycle: rolling (next: No standing NOFA; the Affordable Housing Financing Plan (May 2025, FY 2025-27) says the City will time NOFAs, acquisitions and rehabilitation around linkage fee payouts, with 66% of projected revenue arriving in FY 2026-27. Requests go to Council through the Housing Division (housing@ssfca.gov, (650) 829-6620).)
- Layering notes: County layer: every San Mateo County city project competes for the County Affordable Housing Fund NOFA (AHF 14 closed July 15, 2026, next fall 2027), HEART bridge loans and HACSM project-based vouchers; city money is usually the first commitment that unlocks those. South San Francisco has the largest city housing fund in the county after the linkage fee rebound and uses it as the first-in local loan (residual receipts) ahead of County AHF, state IIG and LHTF money; the City also waives or pays permit fees from Fund 823 for public housing work (C Street electrification, August 2026) and holds TEFRA hearings for CMFA bonds (Rotary Gardens, August 2026). City-owned sites: 1051 Mission Road (PUC site, Development Agreement amended April 24, 2026), 220 Linden and 905 Linden under negotiation in 2026. Source is the Housing Division funding page; figures from the Affordable Housing Financing Plan PDF and Council files on ci-ssf-ca.legistar.com (Legistar API client ci-ssf-ca).

- Confidence: verified (researched 2026-11-07)

**Inclusionary Housing Ordinance (SSFMC Chapter 20.380) and replacement housing rules**
- Agency: City of South San Francisco Economic and Community Development Department, Housing Division
- Type: other
- Typical award: Requirement, not a subsidy. Market-rate projects of 5 or more units: rental 15% (10% lower income, 5% very low income); homebuyer 15% (7.5% moderate, 7.5% lower income); extended to rental housing in 2018. In-lieu fee amounts are not posted on the developer page. Demolition requires one-for-one replacement, relocation assistance and right of first refusal.
- AMI requirement: County income and rent limits (2026-27 schedule posted), utility allowances deducted, regulatory agreements control; Procedures and Guidelines for Inclusionary Units updated September 2024.
- Cycle: rolling (next: Applies at entitlement; the City is not listed among the 2026 multi-city nexus study participants, so no change is pending.)
- Layering notes: County layer: every San Mateo County city project competes for the County Affordable Housing Fund NOFA (AHF 14 closed July 15, 2026, next fall 2027), HEART bridge loans and HACSM project-based vouchers; city money is usually the first commitment that unlocks those. The 15% rental requirement with a very low income tier plus the linkage fee is why South San Francisco's biotech corridor funds housing elsewhere in the city; 100% affordable projects are exempt and instead draw on Fund 823 loans (see separate record). Source is the Housing Requirements for Developers page.
- Source: https://www.ssfca.gov/Departments/Economic-and-Community-Development/Divisions/Housing-Division/Housing-Requirements-for-Developers

### City of St. Helena

**St. Helena Affordable Housing Program: 20% inclusionary requirement, housing in-lieu fee and nonresidential Housing Impact Fee (SHMC Chapter 17.30, Ordinance 23-4)**
- Agency: City of St. Helena Community Development Department
- Type: other
- Typical award: Requirement, not a subsidy. Inclusionary: at least 20% of all new dwelling units in any residential project (no project size threshold; new units under 850 square feet and ADUs are excluded) must be affordable units of the same tenure, built concurrently. Rental projects with four or more affordable units split them by RHNA need (as of March 2022: 55% very low, 31% low, 14% moderate); three or fewer units are assigned one each to very low, low then moderate. Ownership projects: half the affordable units at or below 100% AMI (or 80% AMI, which earns an extra 5% density bonus beyond state law) and half at moderate income, 45-year resale restrictions renewed at each resale. In-lieu fee (per square foot of net new floor area, set by Council resolution) is available by right only to projects of four or fewer units; larger projects need a Council infeasibility finding that density bonus concessions cannot cure. Housing impact fee on nonresidential development and conversions per the master fee schedule (wineries, nonprofits, schools, public uses and small day care exempt); the Council considered a 2024 proposal to raise the hotel fee to about $41,797 per room and commercial to $14 per square foot (press report, adoption not confirmed).
- AMI requirement: Rental affordable units restricted by recorded agreement (very low, low and moderate by RHNA ratio); ownership units 45 years. The Council may forgive part of a rental project's obligation for undue hardship where the project contributes significantly to affordable housing.
- Cycle: rolling (next: Applies at the first discretionary or ministerial approval through an inclusionary housing plan and recorded affordable housing agreement before building permit. Code is current through Ordinance 26-4 (May 12, 2026). Biennial review of fees and requirements due 2026. Current master fee schedule amounts were not located online; confirm with Community Development (707-968-2740).)
- Layering notes: The strictest inclusionary rule in Napa County (20% with no threshold) means almost every market rate project in St. Helena produces deed restricted units or fee revenue for the trust fund record above. 100% affordable projects satisfy the requirement by definition and pay no in-lieu fee; nonresidential impact fees and in-lieu fees capitalize Fund 751. Chapter 17.29 (Density Bonus) implements state law and is cross referenced for concessions. Code text read on the Zoneomics mirror of the City zoning code (source_url); cityofsthelena.gov pages opened but the agenda search returned nothing to scripts, and codepublishing and gocodebook mirrors return 403.
- Source: https://www.zoneomics.com/code/saint-helena-CA/chapter_4
- Confidence: verified (researched 2026-11-08)

**St. Helena Affordable Housing Trust Fund (Fund 751, SHMC 17.30.050) development loans and project commitments**
- Agency: City of St. Helena Community Development Department and Administrative Services Director (fund administrator); City Council approves commitments
- Type: loan
- Typical award: Fund 751 beginning balance July 1, 2025 of $2,404,218, projected $2,448,125 at June 30, 2026 and $2,492,032 at June 30, 2027 before new commitments; recurring revenue is small (about $60,000 to $65,000 a year of housing impact and in-lieu fees plus interest, with a $583,991 spike in FY 2023-24). Track record: about $2,450,000 committed to Turley Flats (8 units, $700,000 incl. deferred fees), Brenkle Court (8 units) and 963 Pope Street (5 units) through 2021, and the Housing Element states the City has funded every developer request since 2015. Press reports (not confirmed on the City site) describe a $1.4 million loan to Our Town St. Helena for the Christine Apartments and a March 2026 commitment of $2.2 million ($1.5 million early, $700,000 later) to the 40 unit Fountain Street project by Our Town St. Helena and Burbank Housing (about $27 million total cost, land donated).
- AMI requirement: Fund must be used solely to increase and improve housing affordable to moderate, low and very low income households, with priority for extremely low income households and the western part of the city (Programs H-DD and H-MM). Rental affordability agreements recorded; the City targets 55-year terms on assisted rental projects.
- Cycle: rolling (next: No NOFA; developers request funds directly and the City Council acts by resolution (typically one to two actions a year). Remaining uncommitted balance after the Fountain Street pledge should be confirmed with Community Development (707-968-2740, Director Leza Mikhail). The biennial review of fees and inclusionary requirements under 17.30.050(B) is due in 2026.)
- Layering notes: Small but reliable: St. Helena has funded every request since 2015 and pairs trust fund loans with reduced or deferred City fees (Program H-CC) and Measure E money (separate record). Stack order for a St. Helena deal: CTCAC credits, HCD programs, County Affordable Housing Fund (the County funded Turley Flats $798,000 and 963 Pope $200,000, see Pass 2 record), then City trust fund and Measure E, with HACN project based vouchers. City loans are public funds, so prevailing wage applies. Figures from the adopted FY 2025-26 and 2026-27 budget (source_url, Fund 751 worksheet); the 2023-2031 Housing Element draft on hcd.ca.gov and the code mirror were also opened. The City AgendaCenter search returned no results to scripts, so 2026 council actions rest on press coverage and are marked as such.

**St. Helena Measure E 1% Transient Occupancy Tax for affordable and workforce housing (Fund 752)**
- Agency: City of St. Helena Administrative Services and Community Development Departments; City Council
- Type: grant
- Typical award: Special tax of 1% on hotel stays (TOT 12% to 13%) effective January 1, 2019, restricted to programs and services for affordable and workforce housing. Revenue about $300,000 to $315,000 a year (FY 2024-25 estimate $287,718 including interest; FY 2025-26 budget $322,504; FY 2026-27 $328,684). Fund balance $636,312 at July 1, 2025, projected $858,816 at June 30, 2026 and $1,187,500 at June 30, 2027 (includes a $160,000 long term receivable for an affordable housing loan). Only $100,000 of Planning and Building services is budgeted against it in FY 2026-27, so most of the balance is available for projects.
- AMI requirement: Households earning up to 120% AMI (rental and for sale), per the fund description; the City prioritizes extremely low and very low income units in its Housing Element programs.
- Cycle: rolling (next: No NOFA; City Council allocates by resolution. Press coverage indicates Measure E money is part of the two fund total (about $1.5 million) the Council pledged to Fountain Street in March 2026; confirm the uncommitted balance with the City.)
- Layering notes: Measure E is the City's only source for moderate income (81% to 120% AMI) units, which neither the trust fund's nexus based dollars nor state programs cover well; use it on workforce units in a mixed income project while the trust fund covers lower income units. Parallel to Napa's Measure F, Calistoga's Measure D and the County's Measure I, each a separate fund with its own geography. Figures from the adopted FY 2025-26 and 2026-27 budget (source_url, Fund 752 worksheet); the Housing Element estimate of $280,000 a year was also read.

**St. Helena reduced, deferred or waived fees for affordable housing (Housing Element Program H-CC) and Density Bonus Chapter 17.29**
- Agency: City of St. Helena Community Development Department; City Council
- Type: fee waiver
- Typical award: The City reduces, defers or waives application and impact fees for affordable developments case by case; through January 1, 2022 it had reduced, deferred or waived fees for 21 affordable units (Turley Flats, Brenkle Court, 963 Pope Street), in part by lending trust fund money to cover deferred fees. The 2023-2031 Housing Element sets a goal of fee relief for 30 extremely low or very low income units and commits to adopt eligibility criteria and higher incentives for extremely low and very low income units. Chapter 17.29 implements the state density bonus (one to three concessions at 10%, 17% and 24% lower income, etc.) with the 5% local bonus add on for ownership projects under 17.30.030(G).
- AMI requirement: Affordable housing developments, with priority for extremely low and very low income units; deed restrictions required under the City affordable housing agreement.
- Cycle: rolling (next: Request with the entitlement application; Council approves fee relief with the funding commitment. Housing Element program timelines run through 2031.)
- Layering notes: Fee relief is routinely bundled with trust fund and Measure E commitments, so a St. Helena request should ask for all three at once. St. Helena's PLHA share (95% rehab loans up to $60,000 through the City of Napa) and its Housing Services Agreement with HACN (Section 8, regulatory monitoring, loan servicing) round out the local layer; there is no HOME or CDBG entitlement. Waived or reduced fees can count as public funds under Labor Code 1720(b)(4). Source: 2023-2031 Housing Element HCD review draft on hcd.ca.gov (source_url; the City adopted the element in 2023 and the final version was not located on the City site); the City budget and code mirror were also opened.

### City of Stockton

**Affordable Housing Incentives and Density Bonus Provisions, Stockton Municipal Code Chapter 16.40 (State bonus to 50%, Tier-1 to 75%, Tier-2 to 100%; Ord. 2020-12-01-1502, 2022-07-12-1601-02, 2025-06-03-1601)**
- Agency: City of Stockton Community Development Department, Planning Division
- Type: density bonus
- Typical award: Requirement and entitlement incentive, not a subsidy. State Density Bonus up to 50%; Tier-1 supplemental bonus 50% to 75% with 30 eligibility points; Tier-2 76% to 100% with 50 points. Points: one per additional percent of very low or low income units, LEED 15 to 30, CALGreen Tier I up to 20, 10% on-site renewable 15, adaptive reuse of historic buildings 20, plus other community benefits. Projects not qualifying for state concessions get three local concessions: setback reduction up to 25%, parking reductions of 25% to 100% scaled to the share of lower income units, lot coverage or FAR increases of 5% to 20%, lot coverage up to 25%, height plus 12 feet or 10%.
- AMI requirement: State law thresholds (5% very low, 10% low, 100% affordable, senior, moderate for-sale) for the base bonus; supplemental tiers require additional affordable units or community benefits scored under 16.40.050; density bonus housing agreement recorded per 16.40.070.
- Cycle: rolling (next: Applies at entitlement. Title 16 was amended June 3, 2025 and again in 2025-2026 (Chapter 16.20, 16.80.310, 16.244.010) to implement the 2023-2031 Housing Element; check the current code before design.)
- Layering notes: Stockton's 100% bonus exceeds state law and was one of HCD's stated reasons for the Prohousing Designation. Pair with the PFF exemption and the Housing NOFA; the Housing Element also allows duplexes by right in single-family zones. Parking can go to zero for projects with 75% or more lower income units, which matters for downtown and transit sites. Read from the zoneomics code mirror of Title 16 Division 3 because the City's code publisher blocks scripts.
- Source: https://www.zoneomics.com/code/stockton-CA/chapter_3
- Confidence: verified (researched 2026-11-08)

HOME budget: $1,324,906 HOME Housing Loans for multifamily rehab or new construction, $207,384 CHDO set-aside, $150,000 program delivery, $138,256 admin. HOME match is currently 100% waived by HUD. HOME money is the backbone of the City Housing NOFA and has been combined with PLHA, LMIHF, HHAP and PIP in every recent award. **City-Wide Affordable Housing Development Public Facilities Fee (PFF) Exemption Program (with Greater Downtown Residential PFF Exemption; Resolutions 2015-11-17-1602, 2018-02-06-0504, 2018-11-06-1402, 2020-12-15-1105)**
- Agency: City of Stockton Economic Development Department (fee programs) with Community Development Department Permit Center
- Type: fee waiver
- Typical award: Full exemption from seven Public Facilities Fee categories (city office space, libraries, fire stations, parkland, community recreation centers, police stations, street improvements) for qualifying new affordable housing anywhere in city limits; the same categories are exempt for all new residential development in the Greater Downtown area. Dollar value depends on the current PFF schedule (not published on the program page); the program was cited by HCD as a basis for Stockton's 2023 Prohousing Designation. Other PFFs (water, wastewater, air quality, habitat, school fees) and the SJMSCP habitat fee still apply.

- Cycle: rolling (next: Programs sunset when the City completes its Master Infrastructure Plans and PFF Nexus Study and adopts new fees; Resolution 2020-12-15-1105 extended them, and the related Stockton Economic Stimulus Plan (SESP) fee reduction is being phased out over five years from 2025. Apply before building permit issuance through the Economic Development Department.)
- Layering notes: Most valuable local incentive in Stockton after the NOFA; the exemption reduces per-unit soft costs by the PFF categories listed and the downtown exemption applies to market-rate units too, which helps mixed-income deals. A non-residential short-term PFF deferral program (through December 31, 2027) and the non-residential 5 or 10 year deferral do not apply to housing. Stacks with the Chapter 16.40 density bonus and the Housing NOFA; fee exemptions count as public assistance for Labor Code 1720 analysis, so confirm prevailing wage exposure with counsel. **Low and Moderate Income Housing Fund (LMIHF), Successor Agency to the Stockton Redevelopment Agency (housing successor)**
- Agency: City of Stockton as Housing Successor; administered by the Housing Division through the Housing NOFA
- Type: loan
- Typical award: Fund balance not published in the 2026 NOFA documents; the Housing Source Funds Description lists LMIHF as a NOFA source for acquisition, new construction and conversion or rehabilitation for households up to 120% AMI. Recent uses: part of $1,614,000 HOME and LMIHF allocated to Sierra Vista III in 2019 and 2020 (de-obligated March 2026 and returned to the NOFA pool); part of $1,126,893 PLHA and LMIHF to Kentfield Apartments rehab (2024).
- AMI requirement: Housing successor rules (Health and Safety Code 34176.1): 55-year rental covenants, income targeting by statute with at least 30% of expenditures for extremely low income households over each five-year period; City NOFA applies a 55-year regulatory agreement.
- Cycle: annual NOFA (next: Deployed only through the Housing NOFA (next expected about October 2026); no standalone LMIHF application. Check the annual housing successor report filed with the City's HCD Annual Progress Report for the current balance.)
- Layering notes: Stockton is one of the few San Joaquin County cities with legacy redevelopment housing money; Tracy, Manteca and Lodi records show none in active use. LMIHF is the most flexible source in the Stockton pool (local money, up to 120% AMI, no federal cross-cutting rules) and is usually paired with HOME to cover costs HOME cannot. Treat as a small, lumpy source: the only recent LMIHF commitments were under $1.7 million each. Combine with HACSJ PBVs and SJRHF gap loans (county records). Fund description opened from the Stockton Legistar attachment for the April 2026 award item; the Successor Agency meets concurrently with Council.

**Prohousing Designation and Prohousing Incentive Pilot (PIP) funds, City of Stockton (2023 designation, 2026 renewal application, PIP Rounds 1 to 4)**
- Agency: City of Stockton Housing, Homelessness, Events and Parking Department with HCD
- Type: grant

PIP funds are placed in the Housing NOFA for predevelopment, construction, acquisition, rehabilitation or capitalized operating subsidies for households up to 120% AMI, and PIP was part of the $4.55 million 2024 property acquisition NOFA. Stockton Measure M (Strong Communities sales tax) funds libraries and recreation, not housing, and Measure W funds public safety; neither is a housing source despite appearing in the brief. **Stockton Affordable Housing NOFA (annual Housing NOFA; HOME, HOME-ARP, PLHA, LMIHF, NSP, CDBG, HHAP and PIP loan pool)**
- Agency: City of Stockton Economic Development Department, Housing Division (underwriting consultant TDA Consulting Inc.)
- Type: loan
- Typical award: 2025 Housing NOFA released October 30, 2025, closed December 18, 2025: 8 proposals requesting $28.2 million for 522 units; $11,979,838 available after de-obligating $1,614,000 of HOME and LMIHF from Sierra Vista III. Awards: Fairview Terrace (Mutual Housing California, 76 senior units) $2,800,000 gap loan approved March 31, 2026 (Resolution 2026-03-31-1601) on top of $7,037,865 HOME awarded November 19, 2024; Don Shalvey Apartments (Visionary Home Builders, 108 family units, TDC $84.0 million) $5,000,000 and Danny Drive (DCDC, 66 senior units, TDC $39.7 million) $4,179,838 recommended April 2026 after Council deferred them on March 31. 2024 NOFA (January 29, 2024) offered about $16.1 million and funded Fairview Terrace $7,037,865 HOME, Kentfield Apartments rehab $1,126,893 PLHA and LMIHF, Casa de Mariposa $747,055, plus two HHAP projects. Typical award $0.7 million to $7 million per project.
- AMI requirement: 55-year regulatory agreement and loan term at 3% simple interest, repaid from residual receipts proportionate to the City share of permanent financing; projects served 30% to 80% AMI (families) and 30% to 60% AMI (seniors). HOME-funded units carry the HOME affordability period inside the 55-year term. Article XXXIV authority: voters allow Council to approve up to 500 assisted units per year.
- Cycle: annual NOFA (fall release) (next: Next Housing NOFA expected about October 2026 under the Council-approved process (Motion 2025-11-04-1601: release, two-week question window, due date at least 45 days after release, pass/fail review, three-rater scoring, matrix to Council two weeks before award). No 2026 NOFA posted on the housing page as of 2026-11-08; confirm with hhep@stocktonca.gov, (209) 937-8538.)
- Layering notes: Stockton is the only city in San Joaquin County running a competitive gap-loan NOFA, and it is the main local soft source after the SJCOG San Joaquin Regional Housing Fund (county record). Pool is HUD and state pass-through plus housing successor LMIHF, so awards must fit each source's rules and deadlines; the City requires the full stack to be committed before executing loan documents and de-obligates allocations older than three years that cannot start within three years (Sierra Vista III lost $1.6 million in 2026). Scoring: developer capacity 30, proforma 30, populations served 15, design 15, leverage 10; an AI score was averaged with three human raters in 2025. Stacks with HACSJ project-based vouchers, County HOME (Urban County does not cover Stockton), BHSA and managed care plan grants (county records), the City PFF exemption and the 100% density bonus (records below). 2026 awards included HOME-ARP and PIP as eligible sources. Source documents read through the Stockton Legistar API and Granicus attachments; stocktonca.gov Economic Development pages have moved to /business/economic_development/housing_index.php.

**Vallejo Inclusionary Housing Ordinance (Municipal Code Chapter 16.216, Affordable Housing Requirements; Housing Element Program B 2.1.1)**
- Agency: City of Vallejo Planning and Development Services Department, Long Range Planning (Hector Rojas, 707-553-7283)
- Type: other
- Typical award: Requirement, not a subsidy. Introduced October 27, 2026; Council directed the Planning Commission version: applies to residential projects of 10 or more units; rental projects provide 4% affordable (2% very low, 2% low); ownership projects of 10 to 100 units 7% (4% low, 3% moderate), over 100 units 10% (6% low, 4% moderate). Staff had proposed a 20-unit threshold with 5% rental (1% VLI, 4% LI). In-lieu fee may be paid for some or all units, set by a later Council resolution and deposited in a separate City affordable housing fund; fractional units under 0.50 may be paid as fee. Alternatives: off-site units in the same census tract, rental units in ownership projects. EPS feasibility (March 13, 2026) found a subsidy gap of about $369,000 per very low-income apartment and $471,614 per low-income single-family unit, which are the equivalent in-lieu fee ceilings. Effective 90 days after final passage. Exemptions: disaster rebuilds, ADUs, residential care facilities, applications complete before the effective date.
- AMI requirement: Rental units at 30% of HCD income limits less utilities (2026 Solano three-person limits: VLI $61,850, LI $98,950, MOD $134,550); 55-year minimum covenants for rental and ownership units; Affordable Housing Plan and recorded Affordable Housing Agreement required; one-for-one replacement of demolished deed-restricted units.
- Cycle: rolling (next: Second reading and adoption scheduled November 10, 2026; in-lieu fee resolution to follow before the effective date (about February 2027). Planning Commission asked for annual reports and a new feasibility study about two years after enactment. A Commercial Linkage Fee ordinance is to be drafted after adoption.)
- Layering notes: Vallejo's RHNA is 2,900 units with 1,446 lower and moderate units still unmet after 2025. This is the first inclusionary ordinance in Solano County; its in-lieu fund will be a new, small local gap source alongside the Housing Successor LMIHAF (separate record). Developers of 10+ unit rentals should model 4% affordable units or the fee once set. Underwriting in Vallejo is weak (EPS found rental yields of 4.7% to 5.0% against a 5.5% threshold), so the fee is expected to be modest. Staff report and draft ordinance opened on the City's inclusionary project page.
- Source: https://www.cityofvallejo.net/common/pages/GetFile.ashx?key=ovFGARsP
- Confidence: verified (researched 2026-11-08)

- Type: grant
- Typical award: Walnut Creek is a CDBG entitlement city in the Contra Costa HOME Consortium. The 2025-2029 Consolidated Plan estimates $2.12 million in federal resources over five years (PY 2025-26 CDBG entitlement estimated around $350,000 to $400,000) plus $4.14 million in general and local funds through the Community Services Grant and Homeless Services Fund; the five-year goal table programs CDBG of $100,000 to $500,000 per goal with $500,000 of local funds per year for several goals and $2.5 million for affordable housing (AH-1). Historically the City sets aside part of CDBG for the Home Rehabilitation Loan and Emergency Grant Program. Awards are competitive on the Consortium's two- and three-year cycle; the FY 2027/28 to 2029/30 NOFA was released October 15, 2026.
- AMI requirement: CDBG 80% AMI national objective; Walnut Creek has nine low and moderate income block groups (census tracts 3390.01, 3400.01, 3511.01 to 3511.05) prioritized for area-benefit activities.
- Cycle: annual NOFA (three-year cycle; applications due December 7, 2026) (next: Consortium applications due December 7, 2026 at 5:00 PM via City Data Services; Walnut Creek Council adopts its PY 2027-28 Annual Action Plan in May 2027 (the PY 2026-27 plan hearing was May 5, 2026).)
- Layering notes: Walnut Creek's CDBG is small (under $500,000 a year) and mostly funds services and rehab; for development, the City's Local Housing Trust Fund RFP (separate record) and County HOME or Measure X (county records) carry the weight, with HOME requests filed through the same Consortium application the County administers. Davis-Bacon applies to CDBG-assisted projects of 8 or more units. Consolidated Plan read from the County-hosted copy (source_url); Consortium NOFA dates and the Walnut Creek contact were read on the City of Antioch's Community Grants page (https://ca-antioch.civicplus.com/993/Community-Grants) because walnutcreekca.gov returns 403.
- Source: https://www.contracosta.ca.gov/DocumentCenter/View/86762/WC-Strategic-Plan-Draft
- Confidence: verified (researched 2026-11-08)

**Walnut Creek Commercial Linkage Fee (Zoning Code Part IV, Chapter 13, Fee on Commercial Development for Affordable Housing; 2005, amended November 2017)**
- Agency: City of Walnut Creek Housing Division, Community and Economic Development Department
- Type: other
- Typical award: Requirement, not a subsidy. $5.00 per square foot on new commercial development, deposited to the Local Housing Trust Fund. The November 2017 update eliminated the first 1,000 square foot exemption and extended the fee to additional use classifications including skilled nursing facilities and hospitals (effective January 2018). Together with housing in-lieu fees the City projected about $16 million in the Local Housing Trust Fund over the 2025-2029 Consolidated Plan period (including an anticipated State Local Housing Trust Fund matching grant).
- AMI requirement: Not applicable to the payer; proceeds fund extremely low to moderate income housing.
- Cycle: rolling (next: Applies at building permit; Housing Element Program H-2.E calls for a periodic nexus study update (last EPS nexus study 2015-2016) before any rate change.)
- Layering notes: Low rate ($5 per square foot) relative to the housing in-lieu fee, but the downtown office and medical base (John Muir Medical Center area) keeps it producing. Revenue is pooled with inclusionary fees in the Local Housing Trust Fund that funds the City's Affordable Housing Subsidy RFP (separate record). Read from the HCD-hosted Housing Element (source_url) because the City's commercial linkage fee page returned 403.
- Source: https://www.hcd.ca.gov/housing-elements/docs/walnut-creek-6th-draft090622.pdf
- Confidence: verified (researched 2026-11-08)

**Walnut Creek Inclusionary Housing Ordinance (Zoning Code Article 9, Sections 10-2.3.903 et seq., amended November 2017) and housing in-lieu fee**
- Agency: City of Walnut Creek Housing Division (Housing Programs), Community and Economic Development Department
- Type: other
- Typical award: Requirement, not a subsidy. Applies to all residential development of one or more units except ADUs and disaster replacement units. New ownership projects: 10% moderate, or 7% low, or 6% very low income units, or pay the in-lieu fee (ownership projects of any size may pay the fee). New rental projects: 10% low or 6% very low income units, or pay the fee (rental units restored after AB 1505). Condominium conversions: 15% low or 11% very low. Fractions of 0.7 or more round up; partial fee payment allowed pro rata; blended income levels allowed. In-lieu fee reset to $18.00 per square foot effective January 1, 2018 with annual construction-price-index adjustments ($19.27 in 2021; about $26.04 per square foot in 2026 per the City of Antioch's January 2026 countywide comparison). Walnut Creek Transit Village alone paid over $4 million in in-lieu fees and is expected to generate $6 to 7 million for the City's Housing Trust Fund.
- AMI requirement: Rental inclusionary units affordable 55 years and ownership units 45 years; units dispersed on site with the same bedroom mix and comparable quality; one-for-one replacement of demolished low-income units built within 30 years.
- Cycle: rolling (next: Applies at entitlement; fee indexed each January. Housing Element Program H-2.D (6th cycle) continues the ordinance and contemplates an updated nexus study; confirm the current per square foot fee with the Housing Division (brynen@walnutcreekca.gov).)
- Layering notes: Walnut Creek's fee-first ordinance is the engine of its Local Housing Trust Fund (separate record): most downtown and BART-area apartment projects pay the per square foot fee rather than build 6% very low income units, which is why the City can fund 42 to 97 unit affordable projects itself. The County's Chapter 822-4 ordinance does not apply inside the city. walnutcreekca.gov (including showpublisheddocument PDFs) returns 403 to automated access; ordinance terms were read from the City's 2023-2031 Housing Element hosted by HCD (source_url, Chapter 3 Section 3.3.7 and Chapter 6) and the 2026 fee level from the Antioch comparison table.
- Source: https://www.hcd.ca.gov/housing-elements/docs/walnut-creek-6th-draft090622.pdf
- Confidence: verified (researched 2026-11-08)

**Walnut Creek Local Housing Trust Fund and Affordable Housing Subsidy Request for Proposals (annual developer RFP; FY26 round October to December 2025)**
- Agency: City of Walnut Creek Housing Division (Housing Programs), Community and Economic Development Department; contact brynen@walnutcreekca.gov
- Type: loan
- Typical award: The City maintains a Local Housing Trust Fund fed by housing in-lieu fees and commercial linkage fees and projects about $16 million available over the 2025-2029 Consolidated Plan period, with $4.14 million in general and local funds also programmed for housing and community services. Track record: $5 million to St. Paul's Commons (44 units, 2019) plus a $366,642 City fee waiver; $400,000 plus later gap funding to Riviera Family Apartments; $5,150,000 to Habitat for Humanity's 42-unit Las Juntas ownership project; acquisition, predevelopment and development funding for the 95 to 97 unit Civic Crossing at 699 Ygnacio Valley Road (TCAC application CA-24-649 shows $10.5 million of City funds); $300,000 per year budgeted for first-time homebuyer loans. The City's developer page (not opened, 403) describes an FY26 Affordable Housing Subsidy RFP open October 14 to December 19, 2025, Council review March to April 2026 and award notification May 2026; Council retains sole discretion to fund one, several or no projects.
- AMI requirement: Projects must be within Walnut Creek city limits and consistent with the Housing Element; 55-year City regulatory agreements on rental projects; priority to extremely low, very low and low income and special needs households; all other funding sources must be identified before disbursement.
- Cycle: annual NOFA (fall RFP) (next: FY26 round closed December 19, 2025 with awards expected May 2026 (outcome not confirmed). Expect the FY27 RFP in fall 2026 or early 2027; confirm with the Housing Division since the City website blocks automated access.)
- Layering notes: The strongest city-level gap source in Contra Costa outside the County itself: Walnut Creek routinely commits $5 million to $10 million per project, equal to or above County HOME awards, and pairs it with fee waivers and expedited processing. Stack order for a Walnut Creek deal: City subsidy RFP award and fee waiver first (secures local commitment for TCAC tie-breaker), then County HOME or Measure X (county records; Civic Crossing also received $6.8 million County funds), then 4% credits and County or CMFA conduit bonds. The City is also pursuing a Prohousing Designation (program page exists but was not opened) which adds points in State NOFAs. The City is the Housing Successor for its former redevelopment agency but reported minimal boomerang funds. Because walnutcreekca.gov and its PDFs returned 403 (RFP document and developer page not opened), the fund description is taken from the City's 2025-2029 Consolidated Plan strategic plan posted by Contra Costa County (source_url) and the HCD-hosted Housing Element; RFP dates come from search snippets of the City page and need confirmation.

### City of West Sacramento

**Affordable Housing, Density Bonuses and Incentives (West Sacramento Municipal Code Chapter 17.23, Ordinance 19-1)**
- Agency: City of West Sacramento Community Development Department, Planning Division
- Type: density bonus
- Typical award: Regulatory. Chapter 17.23 applies in all zones allowing residential use and grants qualifying developments and qualifying land transfers the density bonus, incentives and concessions specified in Government Code 65915 by reference (no local enhancement, no local cap). Requests are processed with the entitlement and approved if state criteria are met; a continued availability agreement is required before approval. Section 17.23.070 restates Housing Accountability Act limits on denying projects with at least 20% low income units. The 2019 zoning code update raised minimum and maximum densities in medium, high density and mixed-use zones (about 2,025 acres), so the Housing Element targets only about 5 density bonus units for the cycle.
- AMI requirement: State density bonus law thresholds (5% very low, 10% low, 10% moderate for-sale, senior, 100% affordable) with covenants per Government Code 65915(c).
- Cycle: rolling (next: None; request in writing to the Planning Division with the project application. The City reviews the chapter in its biannual zoning code update.)
- Layering notes: West Sacramento's leverage is zoning (high base densities in the Bridge District, Washington and Pioneer Bluff specific plan areas, mixed-use and waterfront zones) rather than the bonus itself. SB 35 and now SB 423 streamlining accepted for 10% or more affordable projects. Chapter 15.40 incentives (parking reductions, priority processing, standards waivers) can be combined. The code mirror (zoneomics) matches ecode360's section list; confirm against the official code.
- Source: https://www.zoneomics.com/code/west-sacramento-CA/chapter_3
- Confidence: verified (researched 2026-11-08)

**CDBG entitlement program (2026-2030 Consolidated Plan) and HOME program income**
- Agency: City of West Sacramento Economic Development and Housing Department, Housing Division
- Type: grant
- Typical award: West Sacramento became a CDBG entitlement city in FY 2016/17 and receives about $546,000 a year (the City's March 2026 notice anticipated an amount similar to the prior year's $546,333). The draft 2026-2030 Consolidated Plan and FY 2026-27 Annual Action Plan were out for comment March 6 to April 7, 2026. Housing uses have been infrastructure for affordable projects ($1,191,428 of CDBG program income for West Gateway Place Phase 1), fair housing services, homeless coordinator staffing, first-time homebuyer help and owner rehabilitation. The City is not a HOME participating jurisdiction but holds HOME program income from earlier state HOME awards ($2,000,000 went into West Gateway Place II). State LHTF applications ($1,000,000) were not awarded.
- AMI requirement: CDBG at or below 80% AMI or area benefit; HOME program income at or below 80% AMI with HOME rent limits.
- Cycle: annual NOFA (next: FY 2027-28 Action Plan comment period expected March to April 2027; subrecipient applications typically open in winter. Confirm with the Housing Division.)
- Layering notes: Use for off-site infrastructure and public improvements around a Bridge District or Washington project rather than vertical construction; HOME program income is the more flexible pot and has gone straight into City-sponsored projects. Yolo County's state CDBG and HOME cover only unincorporated areas. Facts come from the HCD-hosted Housing Element and search snippets of the City's 2026 notices; the CDBG page and Consolidated Plan PDFs on cityofwestsacramento.org returned 403.

**Inclusionary Housing Ordinance (West Sacramento Municipal Code Chapter 15.40, Ordinance 14-4) with Housing Trust Fund Program in-lieu alternative and Urban Infill Area incentive**
- Agency: City of West Sacramento Economic Development and Housing Department, Housing Division (Housing Manager Raul Huerta, (916) 617-4555)
- Type: density bonus
- Typical award: Requirement, not a subsidy. Residential projects of 5 or more units citywide (adopted April 2014, replacing the redevelopment-area Chapter 15.10): rental projects set aside 10% of units (5% very low income, 5% low income); for-sale projects 10% low income, with rental units substitutable. Units on site, dispersed, at least 90% of the smallest market unit size, concurrent with each 25% of market units. Alternatives at Council discretion: payment into the Housing Trust Fund Program at the amount set in the Book of City Imposts Section VIII-N (a regional comparison in late 2025 listed West Sacramento's in-lieu fee at about $7,699 per dwelling unit, assessed per market-rate unit), acquisition and rehabilitation of market units, off-site construction, or preservation of at-risk units. Projects in the priority Urban Infill Area earn a discount on the in-lieu fee based on adjusted density (dwelling unit equivalents for structured parking, public open space and ground floor commercial). Incentives include reduced parking, priority processing, standards waivers and technical assistance; financial incentives only to the extent City programs exist.
- AMI requirement: Rental: 5% very low (50% AMI) and 5% low income (80% AMI) for 55 years; for-sale: 10% low income with a 45-year goal and recapture on early release.
- Cycle: rolling (next: None (ordinance). The Housing Element (Program HE-PR-1.2) commits to refining Chapter 15.40 to target lower incomes and reduce the burden on market-rate housing; six affordable housing agreements were approved 2018 to 2020. Confirm the current Book of City Imposts fee with the Housing Division.)
- Layering notes: The in-lieu alternative is the main revenue source for the City's Housing Trust Fund (Fund 261-9385), which funds gap loans (separate record). Because the per-unit fee is low relative to Davis ($250,000) and Folsom, most subdivisions in Southport pay the fee rather than build, so West Sacramento's affordable production comes from City-assisted 100% affordable projects in the Bridge District and Washington (West Gateway Place I and II, Landmark Lofts, the Grand Gateway 114-unit project). Overconcentration cap: no more than 40% of a project's units may be inclusionary. No county inclusionary applies inside the city. ecode360 hosts the official West Sacramento code and opened directly; cityofwestsacramento.org (Akamai) returns 403 to scripts and WebFetch, and the Book of City Imposts could not be opened.
- Source: https://ecode360.com/43204558
- Confidence: verified (researched 2026-11-08)

**Permanent Local Housing Allocation (PLHA) formula funds, Resolution 25-15 five-year plan**
- Agency: City of West Sacramento Economic Development and Housing Department, Housing Division (Housing Manager Raul Huerta)
- Type: grant
- Typical award: Council adopted Resolution 25-15 on February 19, 2025 (5 to 0) authorizing the PLHA application and a five-year plan for $763,253 of 2021, 2022 and 2023 formula allocations: 55% ($419,789) for the affordable housing component of the Grand Gateway Master Plan, specifically a proposed 114-unit affordable project serving households at 30%, 50%, 60% and up to 80% AMI; 40% ($305,301) for owner-occupied rehabilitation grants up to $30,000 through existing nonprofit contracts; 5% administration. HCD's 2024-2028 PLHA NOFA lists West Sacramento at about $1.04 million over the next five years. The City filed a CEQA notice of exemption for the plan on February 19, 2025.

Any developer of that site should expect PLHA plus Housing Trust Fund plus land, then compete for MHP or AHSC. State funds trigger prevailing wage. Yolo County's own PLHA is unincorporated only. **Redevelopment Successor Agency housing assets, Enhanced Infrastructure Financing District and City-owned land (Grand Gateway Master Plan area, Bridge District, Washington Specific Plan)**
- Agency: City of West Sacramento as Housing Successor and Redevelopment Successor Agency (Economic Development and Housing Department; Yolo Countywide Successor Agency Oversight Board)
- Type: other
- Typical award: Land and tax increment tools rather than a cash fund. With the loss of redevelopment the City repealed Chapter 15.10 and formed an Enhanced Infrastructure Financing District with 14 project areas that, with Measure G sales tax, funds infrastructure for infill, high-density, transit-oriented housing in the riverfront districts (Community Investment Program HE-PR-1.4). The City owns the Grand Gateway Master Plan area (former West Capitol Avenue redevelopment parcels; the Oversight Board approved sale of three Successor Agency parcels at 485 Lighthouse Drive and 2400 and 2600 West Capitol Avenue to the City for $1,310,000 in 2024) where a 114-unit affordable project is planned, and has contributed land to West Gateway Place I and II in the Bridge District. Housing successor Low and Moderate Income Housing Asset Fund balance and SB 341 reports were not accessible this pass.
- AMI requirement: LMIHAF uses follow Health and Safety Code 34176.1 (30% of spending at or below 30% AMI, remainder at or below 60% AMI, 55-year covenants); City land deals carry negotiated covenants.

Developers should ask the Housing Division about (1) City-owned sites in Grand Gateway, Washington and Bridge District, (2) EIFD or Measure G infrastructure contributions that reduce off-site costs, and (3) any LMIHAF balance for extremely low income units. Layer with the Housing Trust Fund, PLHA and state AHSC (the 2016 to 2021 cycle brought $4.13 million AHSC infrastructure plus $2.6 million for West Gateway Place). Blocked: cityofwestsacramento.org and yolocounty.gov (403); the Oversight Board facts come from search snippets of Yolo County documents, so confirm.

- Agency: West Sacramento Housing Development Corporation (501(c)(3), EIN 94-3184534, 2950 Beacon Boulevard) working with the City Housing Division
- Type: other

The Housing Element names the West Sacramento Housing Development Corporation (WSHDC) alongside Yolo County Housing as the City's standing nonprofit partners for pursuing state and federal funds (Programs HE-PR-1.6 and 1.9). WSHDC co-developed West Gateway Place (77 units, 2017, $29.8 million) and West Gateway Place II / The Bridge at West Gateway (60 units, 2025) with Jamboree Housing on City-contributed land, and owns scattered rental properties managed by a third-party manager.

- Agency: City of West Sacramento Economic Development and Housing Department, Housing Division (Housing Manager Raul Huerta; Community Investment Principal Planner David Tilley, (916) 617-4661)

**Affordable Housing Ordinance (Woodland Municipal Code Chapter 15.16, Ordinance 1662 of 2020) inclusionary requirements and in-lieu fee**
- Agency: City of Woodland Community Development Department (Housing Analyst Franklin Cui, (530) 661-2019) with the Community Services Department
- Type: density bonus
- Typical award: Requirement, not a subsidy. Citywide outside the Spring Lake Specific Plan: for-sale and multifamily rental projects of 30 or fewer units are exempt; 31 to 80 units provide 5% low income units; 81 or more units provide 10% low income, reduced to 5% if the project is built at 95% or more of maximum allowed density; in Downtown, Corridor Mixed Use and Neighborhood Commercial areas projects of at least 10 units built at maximum density (and at least 10 units per acre) owe 5% for-sale units. Very low income requirements were dropped in the April 2020 amendments. Alternatives: land dedication valued at the in-lieu fee times required units, or in-lieu fees per an adopted fee schedule (reviewed annually) or, if none is adopted, as negotiated in the inclusionary housing agreement and paid before building permits. Example: Ashley and Main (168 units, 2020) paid $469,413. Fees go to the Affordable Housing Fund (Fund 1327); up to 10% of annual income may fund administration.
- AMI requirement: Low income (80% AMI) rental units must be permanently affordable; for-sale affordable units 10 years minimum reset at each resale with a $1,000 silent second and equity share; rents calculated at 50% AMI for very low and 80% AMI for low income units.
- Cycle: rolling (next: None (ordinance). The 2020 temporary relief provisions were set to expire in April 2022 unless dwelling unit goals were met; the Housing Element (Program A.27) committed to a LEAP-funded study of a standardized square-foot in-lieu fee, including nonresidential. Confirm whether a fee schedule has been adopted with the Housing Analyst.)
- Layering notes: Woodland's inclusionary program feeds the only local soft money in the city (Fund 1327, see the in-lieu fund record). Thresholds are generous to market-rate builders (exempt to 30 units, 5% at 31 to 80), so most revenue has come from Spring Lake development agreements and large projects.
